summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of Lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirchi machine powder was adulterated. The trial court accepted this contention and found that the prosecution had failed to prove that the Lal mirsi powder was 'adulterated article ' of food contained in section 2(1)(f) of the Act. The High Court in revision held that the Food Inspector had found in the sample only nine living meals worm and he has neither stated that it is insect infested nor that it was unfit for human consumption on account of the presence of the meal wyorms, nor that, it is otherwise unfit for personal consumption. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The word 'otherwise ' in sub cl. (f) which contemplates "the whole or any part of the article being "filthy", has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal [1976] 2 S .C.R. 1, applied. The adjectives "favthy" and "putriding" refer to the quality of the articles and furnish the indicia for presuming the article to be unfit for its human consumption. But the presumption may not be conclusive in a case, irrespective of the character of the Article, and the nature and extent of the vice afflicting it. [473 C] 2. It is quite apparent that the words 'or is otherwise fit for human use" indicate presumptive but not absolute criteria as to the quantity of the food being "Filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or insect". In the instant case the evidence led by the prosecution is inadequate to warrant interference with the judgment of acquittal passed by the trying Magistrate and upheld by the High Court. [474 D] 3. The fact that the first clause "or is not otherwise unfit" for human habitation cannot be decisive in a cases, irrespective from the character or extent of its infringement it.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order. The appellant contended that he was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case could be drawn against him. Held, that the appellant is an agriculturist within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Bihar Foodgrains Dealers ' Licensing Order, 1966, and therefore his conviction was rightly pre scribed. Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , followed. Manipur administration vs M., Nila Chander Singh (I.L.R. and Manipur Administration V M.N.uta Chandra Singh (A.I.R.), referred to. Manipur Adminis tration vs M, [70] 76 I.A. 128 distinguished. Manipur Revenue Administration vs P.M. Nika Chandra Singh and contended that the presumption under section 3(2), could not be drawn because storage was not reference to business as a dealer but because storage had reference to employment as a shop and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds, exhibited receipts and proved by oral evidence that he and his brother were in possession of 80 90 bighas of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains found in his pos session were grown and the presumption could not therefore be drawn. The total circumstances in the case show that the appel lant was in fact carrying on agricultural operations. He executed a number Of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. It had been granted for a large sum of money to him and he produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he cultivated 80 9020 bighas of the land, and contended again. In his case, therefore, the presumption against him under para. 3(3) was not drawn.

The defendant was a monthly tenant, under the appellant. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit. He stated that his tenancy had been determined by notice to terminate his tenancy and that he had been paid rent regularly till 1936. In 1926 he obtained an order of eviction against the lessee on the ground that he was in possession of the land as a trespasser and he became a tenant from month to month under section 116, Transfer of Property Act. The suit was decreed on the basis of the terms of the Kabuliyat executed by the defendant on 24th December, 1924. The order of ejectment, which was confirmed by the District Judge and the plaintiff 's suit was dismissed merely on the grounds that the notice to the quit was defective inasmuch as on the expiry of the second annual lease the respondent did not require the land for his own purposes and decided to re settle it, the lessee would be entitled to fresh settlement on enhanced rent and on such terms as might be then agreed upon between the parties. The District Judge, however, held that the tenancy created by payment and acceptance of rent in 1925 was terminable with the end of the Bengali month of the tenancy and consequently a tenancy from monthto month came into existence in accordance with section 116 of the Transfer of . Property Act, and the present suit of the plaintiff having been admittedly brought more than 12 years after the deter mination of the Second yearly lease, was barred by limitation under article 139 Of the Indian Limitation Act. On appeal, the District judge affirmed the findings of the lower appellate court that the defendant 's tenancy was one from month from the beginning a tenancy period from month following which he had accepted payment of rent from him in 1926 and thereby became a monthly tenancy from 1st May, 1922, but as the notice served by the plaintiff upon the defendant did not fulfil this requirement the suit was bound to fail.

Section 138 of the 1961 Act read with Section 137 (2) prohibited a public servant from disclosing his particulars contained in any statement made, return furnished or accounts or documents produced under the provisions of this Act or in any evidence given, or affidavit or deposition made in the course of any proceedings under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 on or after the 1st day of April, 1960 and authorised the Commissioner to furnish or cause to be furnished such information and that decision of the Commissioner is immune from challenge in any court of law. Section 138 (1) (b) of the Income Tax Act provides that for the purpose of this provision, no person shall make an application to the Commissioner for any information relating to any assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the 1961Act on or before April 1, 1960, and authorised by the Commissioner, to furnish such information. Sub section (2), however, provides that where a person makes an application under this Act to the Commission in prescribed form for any particulars relating to the assessee in regard of any tax paid on or on or from April 1st, 1960 or before the date of April 1.1964, in respect thereof, the Commissioner may, if he is satisfied that it was in the public interest so to do, furnish or causes to be supplied information asked for in respect accordingly. The respondents assessee obtained summons from the Income tax Officer under Section 137 of the Act and obtained summons upon the IncomeTax Department to produce evidence relating to M/s Boriseon Industrial Products (P) Ltd, and Bishamber Nath Kaul which were filed after the repeal of section 137 of I.T. Act, 1961. The Income Tax officer refused to apply for and obtain summons requiring the Income, Tax Officer to produce the Income 8 of the defendants, M/S Borisein Industrial Products, (P). Ltd., and BHARishambernath Kaul on the ground that the said record was privileged under Section I. T. Act 1922, as also the interpretation placed by the Bench on section 138 (I) (a) in respect C. No. 64/69, dated April 1 1964, in favour of CO. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal filed by CO, and held that the denial to privilege under section 138(1)(b) had no relationship to the power of the Court to summon that record.

One Mammotty was ill for a long time and was in hospital and he was discharged uncured a month before the execution of gift deed. The gift provided that all property which was given to him by his father were to be valid must he accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say by the father or his executor or by the grand father or of the de facto guardian or the grand parent; and in any event, there was delivery of possession immediately distinguishes gifts from sales. In the present case there was a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammottty and as the gift was by a registered deed no question in this behalf could arise. The trial court held that the gift made by the husband to his minor wife to be an valid gift must be accepted on his behalf by the legal guardian as well as de facto mother and, as the appeal was accepted he filed a suit challenging the gift as invalid. When the first Appellate Court dismissed it the contention of the appellant was accepted and it held that there had been no clear and complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammetty and to transfer the property to the donee. The High Court also did not accept the plea of the respondent that in any view of the matter when a husband makes a gift to a minor wife and there is no legal guardian or guardian 'quasi guardian ' provided there was real and bona fide intention on the donor 's part to transfer, the gift could be completed by delivery of the property. Held:(i) The law is satisfied without an apparent change of possession and will presume that the subsequent holding of the 'property was on behalf of the minor wife. Amritlal vs Lala Chand (1932) 59 I.A. 556 and 504 Bibi Bibi Bai and Anr. vs Abdul Gani, [1933] 59 I,.A. 558, relied on. The ratio in Bhagwan Das and Others vs Ganga Ram & Ors., A.I.R. , and Greaves Cotton Co. Ltd. vs United India Insurance Company, and others, A. 1. R. (1909) 17 Ex Reports 979 to the effect that title to the property should pass from the donor to the executant is good evidence that the property had been given by the donee and had been accepted by the respondent as a gift is not valid unless possessed 'and for the benefit of the father, the fact that possession was not handed over to the minor 's mother or of other near relative or even a stranger. In such cases the benefit need not detain the father because although possession has been taken by one who has done, it must be held to have resigned. The strict view was that the donor must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. If the property is with the donor he must depart from it. The presumption of truth under section 114 of the Evidence Act would apply if there is good authority for these propositions in the ancient and modern books of Muhammadan law and in decided cases of undoubted authority. In Tran vs Abdul Hafia, , referred to. (ii) The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's father when the gift is from the husband is to his mother after marriage of a girl unless he was considered unfit; and (iii) In such a case the benefit to the son and the completion of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. [566 H] 5(a).

The appellant, who was trustees of a religious institution in the State of Madras moved a petition for an order restraining him from enforcing its provisions. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63 to 69 and 89 as amended by Act 27 of 1954 were invalid. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) (a) no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951, and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was without jurisdiction and bad as no rules framed thereunder were in existence at the time when the demand was made; (ii) the High Court erred in relying on irrelevant considerations. HELD:(i) The condition precedent that a fee is uniform and no account is taken of the varying abilities of different recipients, and it was not a postulate of a fee that it must have direct relation to the regular services rendered by the authority levying the fee for generally providing the service and the aggregate of the levy from persons who were to be made subject thereto. [919 E]. H. Sudhindra Thirtha Swamiar vs Commissioner for Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments, Mysore, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 302, followed and (ii). The High court erred in taking the view that under the Act the Government had to make rules applicable to each temple separately and prescribing the method for determining contribution found no support in the provisions of the Act or its scheme was not restricted nor were the rules framed by the Government rendered invalid.[920 E] H. C. Sathindra Thirthubha Swamiari vs Commissioner, Mysore ; , followed.

The respondents, who were the alleged contemner under section 19(1) of the , from an order issuing notice as nothing yet had been decided by the High Court. The appellant filed a petition under section 13 (1) (a) of section 19 of the Act challenging the said orders and seeking a direction that he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt under section 15. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondents, to the effect that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section19 of the . The High Court held that an appeal does lie to this court as a matters of right from any kind of order made by the trial court in the proceeding for contempt, and dismissed the application. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that an Appeal does not lie to the Supreme Court as the matter of 'right under section 20 of the ; (ii) that the initiation of the proceeding by the appellant High Court will be without jurisdiction if it is in violation of section 20. HELD: 1. An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemnor and cannot he appeal against as a question of right tinder section 19. [508 C] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to. Baradkanta Mishra v Justice Gitikrushta Mishra, [1976] S.C. 1206, followed. Barabdakanta Misra vs JusticeGatikrunna Mishra; , distinguished. Barkadakanta Das & Anr. vs Justice Gopal Mishra, SC 1206 and Baradaksanta Mishra V.K.S.Katakakakkatakakkata & Anr., ; applied. Bardakanda Mishra vs justice Gatirushna Misra, (1985) 1 S.L.R. 986, distinguished.

In 1920, the Indian Wireless Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949, section 6(1 A), which was inserted in the 1939 Act of 1933, provided that if any person establishes, maintains or works a telegraph within India in contravention of the provisions of section 3 shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees. The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6 (1 A) of the Act for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention Of the provisions contained. Section 3 of the , provided that any person possesses wireless telegraphy apparatus in contravention thereof shall be liable to fine which might extend to two hundred and fifty rupess. The trial Court acquitted both the accused holding that although section 6 of the East Punjab Police Act, 1933, saved the operation of the amendments that had been inserted by the 1949 Act in 1933, the repealing Act did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the amending Act Of 1949. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. Held: (i) A statute is designed to provide for a different situation, namely, the repeal of an earlier Act which has been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act. Under that section the repeal either of the first statute or of the second one does not affect its continuance unless a different intention appears, the repealed enactment by a third did not effect the continuance. (ii) The language of the relevant provisions of the two Acts is not to give it any legislative effect but to excise dead matter from the statute book. The object of the said Act was not to gave it any legislature effect but merely to excise good dead matter and to remove confusion from the public mind. The word " text ", in its dictionary meaning, means " subject or theme ". When an enactment amends the text of another a, it amends that the subject or | Annexure thereto, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. ' (iii) Even from the history of the legislation it was not possible to say that it disclosed an intention different from that envisaged in section 6 A of the .

Under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act for reopening of decrees as well, the provisions of that section are to reopen any transaction and take an account between the parties. The drafting of section 36 is obscure and somewhat clumsy but it is clear only when the Court permits a decree is reopened, that the new decree is passed only for the purpose of substituting the method of accounting sanctioned by the Act for the calculations upon which the original decree was passed and to give an opportunity to the judgment debtor to pay the decretal dues thus ascertained by instalments. But save and except for those, the old decree as well as the adjudications made thereunder are not wiped out and the parties are not relegated to their rights and liabilities under the original cause of action, for a proper determination of this point it is necessary, in order to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Act. To give effect to clauses (b) and (c), therefore the court has not only the right but is under a duty to make an inquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decree holder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b). But it cannot be disputed that the court theatens a decree under section 36(2) only for purposes and so far as it is required to give protection to the lender in the way provided for by the section.

One M had instituted a suit in the Bombay City Civil Court against the appellant for recovery of certain sums of money and interest which was due by him to the firm. The respondent company resisted execution on the ground that as the decree had been transferred or agreed to be transferred by this document, it could not apply to the provisions Of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the appellant company was the transferees of the decree passed in 1923 and the application for execution filed before the City Civil Judge was a sufficient compliance with the provisions of Order XXI r. 16 of order XXI, Rule 17(1) (j). The contention taken from the respondent that order XXI rule 16 had no application at all to the facts of this case is not correct. There was also no question of transfer of the suit by the transferors to the respondent company by assignment of the right in writing in writing or by operation of law, and the respondent could not claim to be a transferee of the said decree. Kangati Mahanandi Reddi vs Panikalapati Venkatappa & another ([1931] I.L.R. , Bhagwant Balajirao & Ors. vs Rajaram Sajnaji & Others ([1900] L.R,. I 1.A. 98), Malayanji Ambalalai Chettiar vs Kangli Mahanandi Mad. 328) and Kaushalya Devi vs Lakshmi Narain Narain Narain (I.L,R. and Bhagwant Balrajirao and Ors. A.I.R., referred to.

The respondent in the appeal was carrying on his business of fabricating steel doors, windows and windows etc. The contract undertaken by the respondent was to prepare the window leaves according to the specifications and to fix them to the building, but there were no two contracts one of sale and another of service. In accordance with the specification, designs, drawing and instructions in writing referred to in r. 1 hereof, and in Class 11 of the conditions of contract, and with such materials as are provided for by and in all other respects in accordance with such conditions so far as applicable. In respect of "fixing" the windows the respondent offered to execute and complete the "work" mentioned in the written memorandum according to which the respondent had agreed to supply the "black out curtains, curtain rails and battens and their erection at a number of police stations. The price was to be revised in the light of cost revision of the controlled price of steel supplied to the respondent. The rates quoted by the appellant were based on the current price of mild steel billets fixed by the Government. But in the view of the High Court the contract was for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed and it was not a "deed of service" and that the amount received by the res pondent was not taxable. The respondent preferred an appeal to this court. HELD: (i) The object of the respondent being to enter into a works contract is to enter upon a works 'fix" certain articles made by a manufacturer the contract must be deemed one for sale and not of service, and [509 D] (ii)The object of construction of a building became the property of the other party, to the contract only on the theory of accretion. The work was not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. The "fix", of windows in the manner stipulated required special technical skill.

The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 the accused person who was an agent of the respondent company went to Ram Avtar Prasad at Ram Avtar and introduced a deal of foreign goods in favour of one Hari Lal and introduced him as his agent of M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. On November 16, 1967 S.N. Singh lodged a report with the police against Shanker Lal and Saheb Jaman Khan and thereafter filed a revision petition in the High Court on February 9, 1970 which was allowed by the High court on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned no case had been made out against him. The High Court quashed the charges framed against the accused holding, after following the procedure laid down in section 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that so long as the said Raj KumarAggla was not satisfied with the commission of any offence, he would be liable to be discharged as a result of his acquittal. Thereupon the State filed an appeal to this Court by special leave. HELD: On November 8 1967 S had brought to the notice of the High .Court that he was present along with Shankar Lal when the latter brought washer sheets in a taxi and demanded the price of the washer plates from Ram Avtar. That circumstance, as pointed out by the prosecution itself, would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Kumar respondent too was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat, Ram Avtar even though he was not present along along with S.B.A. On the facts of this case there is no infirmity in the judgment of the high Court as might induce us to interfere.

The petitioner took the ground that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil their constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 provides for certain safety measures as well as non provision of adequate facilities to passenger. The petitioner alleged that the Railway Safety Work Fund has been set up and expenses are being met out of it. On June 1, 1982 there were as many as 27233 unmanned level crossings on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. Most of the States have framed rules under the making it obligatory for drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmanning level cross files, observed and then proceed. With a view to educating the users of the roads wide publicity is given through newspapers, cinema slides, commercial broadcasting and the television about hazards involved while negotiating unman heard level crosses. It has been alleged that unmannned level Crossings are gradually being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being provided for efficient operations. Relying on the Sikri Committee Report of 1978, it has been stated that there were nearly 120000 bridges on the railways out of which 195 are important bridges and nearly 9400 are major bridges. It is further alleged that every bridge is annually inspected and continuous record is maintained in regard to every bridge in the bridge register. It was hoped that the total life of 80 years for steel work and 100 years for masonry part of the bridges stipulated in the Railway Code is for the purpose of provision In the Depreciation Reserve Fund. The codal life does not have any direct relevance with the condition of a bridge and there is no necessity of rebuilding a bridge when its codal Life was over. It had been averred that unManned level motor crossings were gradually being replace by man wned ones, improved technical and gadgests are needed to improve and in 1982 83 as manyas 15 works in different States involving an expenditure of RS.22 crores have been cleared. Every accident, it had been pointed out that there are nearly 12000 bridges on Railway track which are important bridge bridges and almost 9400 were major bridges, but the loss from June 6, 1981 to a river Bridge in the Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. The respondents denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been raised in the counter affidavit. According to the petitioner assistance of 500 crores of rupees was to come during the year ending March 31, 1983 and from out of such funds pressing improvements like manning the unmannerned level crossing crossings could be undertaken. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period namely, the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railways with particular reference to accidents and although detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unManning level Crossing of new level cross sheets in consultation with appropriate State Governments. The Joint Director (Safety) filed a counter affidavit stating that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as manned level counterings are concerned there wereas many as 14471 of them as on March 1,1982; unmanunned levelrossings were provided mostly on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. It further averred that periodic review is undertaken about manning of unmenned level sub crossings, drawing a heavy toll on human lives every year.

The Collector of Baroda, passed an order dismissing the appellants ' applications for restoration of their proprietary jagirs. The appellants ' appeals were dismissed in Iimine and the first question before the High Court was whether the orders passed by the Tribunal under the Act dismissing the appeals were illegal and ultra vires because the Tribunal dismissed the appeals for non prosecution. The Tribunal rejected these applications holding that they were time barred under section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41, rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. On appeal by special leave : HELD: (1) The language of section 17(1) has no application to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a ease where the A appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Tribunal may decide the same on merits. [143 H] (2) The application for restoration should be disposed of under section 13(2). If an appeal is dismissed for want of prosecution it cannot be said that the Tribunal has decided the appeal and 'recorded its decision ' within the meaning of section 13 of the Abolition Act. If there is default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal, the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases were well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. [144 A B] (3) In view of the express language of Section 17(I), the Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the application of restoration and deciding it on merits even though there was default on their part.

Tallibandha was dedicated by Dinanath Sao, a wealthy inhabitant of the locality. They were worshipped for very many years and for the maintenance of the temple. One village by the name of Hirmi was dedicated for several years. For the expenses of worship of the deities and for its upkeep, one village by name of Telibandha and for accounts. The appellants ' case in the plaint was that Teli Murat fell to the share of Saijobha who had three sons, Sarjoo Prasad and Kalyan Chand Moosad, both descendants of Dinanath, Sao brought the present suit under section 92 Of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for removal of the respondent Kamal Narayan, another descendant of Dinnath Sao from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandraji Swamy for the village of Tellibandha, and for account. The appellant 's case was that it had been dedicated absolutely to the temple of Shri Ramchandraaswami Swamy who had thereby become a public religious trust for which the trust was created, was a public institution. The trial Court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village Telivancoreakia since 1936 and to allot the village to the members of one branch of the family with only a moral obligation to look after the temple but this later award had all along remained a dead letter and did not affect the respondent 's property. The High Court ordered that a Commissioner would be appointed later on to enquire into the alienations made by the respondent and to take accounts of the trust from the year 1936. It was further directed that a commissioner should be appointed, who submitted his report in writing to the Board. The Board forwarded his report to the High Court for its opinion. Held, (i) The suit was not maintainable as it had not been filed within the time given by the trial court. (ii) There was no complete dedication of the property for the purpose of the endowment being made 905 in favour of the idol or whether the temple was given in full proprietary estate to two big members. (iii)The word 'Malik ' in section 92 of the Code , means that son should be son and not a son but an alienation by the will or deed of gift and not by any other of his coparceners who may be fit to do that work. The words "in cases where the intention of the testator is to grant an absolute estate, an attempt to reduce the powers of the owner by imposing restraint on alienation would certainly be repelled on the ground of repugnancy; but where the restrictions are the primary things which the testator desires and they are consistent with the whole tenor of the will, the Court is not right in construing the intention instead of the words "Malik." The use of the word ' Malik ' was merely a presumption which can well be displaced by what follows in the same document as regards this very property. When all these different provisions are considered it appears to be clear beyond any shadow of doubt that the intention was not intended to make Ramsaran Lal the absolute owner of the land but gave him possession and management of the house for the benefit of one of the co shares for the under mentioned purposes. If Ramsaren had not carried out this purpose then out of the joint trust. (iv)The use of words "at that time" in the original means "from the profits and income of Mouza Teli Bhagal, " it is more than likely therefore that the Panchas wanted to say that the purposes mentioned will be carried out with the income and profits and did no expect any surplus to be left.

The two appellants before this Court are the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Kid Sabha. The learned Judge held that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associ ated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of contempt of Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD:(1) The language used by them was unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. [603C D] (2) In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations. [ 604B C] (3) The Chairman of a Chance Committee ofProcedure should have themselves embarked on the path of vilifying the Chief justice of this Court and that it was a single act of the Chief Judge for which the attack was made, there does not propose to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumacious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty though he expressed strong disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeated". [605 E F] (4) The words "I am acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held" should have itself embarked upon the path for vilting the Chief Justices of this court and that they do not want to be over sensitive in the matter, keeping in view the surrounding circumstances in which the contu macious act was committed by them.

The respondent No. 1 entered into a joint Hindu Family with his eldest brother, Respondent No. 2 was entered into an agreement on 28th of January, 1977 in respect of partition of joint movable and immovable properties. On or about 2nd July, 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the same was registered by which the above named arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah, the district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. It was stated by the respondent No 1 that on or about November 28, 1977, the same Agreement was re printed on a new stamp paper which had already been registered by them on a proper stamp paper. On 26th July, 1978 the arbitrators explained their award to the parties and made signed the award. On 14th of August, 1978, the arbitrators published an application calling for return of the award to enable them to present the same before the Sub Registrar for registration. On 2nd September, 1978 and the learned Munsif ordered return of ' the award ' to the arbitrators to enable their prayer to present their examination, which was rejected on 27th November, 1983. The appellants, thereafter, filed an application under section 14 of the . The sub Judge dismissed the said application and did not direct return of it holding that the limitation for registration for the award had already expired. The High Court therefore in Civil Appeal No. 3670 was set aside by the High Court. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal and setting aside the order of the High court, this Court, HELD: 1. In the instant case admittedly during the period from 26th of July,1978 to 24th November 1983 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps; that is to say, 28th January, 1978 till the return of 15th December, 1982, the award was in the court and this was manifest from the order in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1977. The arbitrators had made an application on or around 14th August 1974 for return for the said award but that was not done. The appellant was the tenant for about 20 years and was a part of the building. The respondent gave notice to him to vacate within certain time the premises on the ground that he had been let on June 1, 1948, and the respondent was allowed to be in possession by the respondent. Although it was admitted that the respondent had sub tenants there could not be any new tenancy after the coming into force of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bom. 57 Of 1947). In 1949, the appellant obtained a decree for Rs. 445 on account of rent remaining due and dismissed the respondent 's suit for ejectment. The defence of the appellant was that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises; but so far as the claim on the grounds of non payment of rent could be deposited, the arrears of rent in court were not payable and that he was merely licensee of the landlord ; and that no new sub tenancy had been created. Held, further, that under section 15 Of the Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging Houses Rates) Control Act 1947, a rantation by the appellant of his right to sue for ejectment on the basis that the respond ent did not enforce his rights under section 13(1)(e), was void because of the provisions of section 15 of the Act. The reason given by the plaintiff for this amending Act was that if public policy demands it even an equal participant in the (1) [1945] 1 K.B. 65, 72, 74, 136, 135 and 142 Of 1947, brought about a contract of sub letting, the non obstante clause would be unenforceable as being in contravention of the express provision of the Exchange Act which prohibits it. The appellant pleaded that under sections 13(i)(e) and 15 of Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control might be parted with or renounced by the landlord; and that section 13 Of the Act was not applicable to contracts between the landlord and tenant and as such he could not evict the respondent under section 12(1).

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of answer sheets in each subject, were found tampered with, the marks initially obtained and the marks increased due to tampering. The respondents challenged the notification before a Division Bench of the High Court which directed the Board to take expeditious action to declare the results of the examination within the specified time. Show cause notices were issued to the students on July 30, 1990 informing them of the nature of tampering, the subjects in which the marks were found tallied with the appellant and they would not be entitled to appear through an Advocate but the parents or guardians would be permitted to accompany the students at the time of enquiry, but they are not entitled to take part in the enquiry. The Single Judge by a majority directed that the result of the examinees be declared within the stipulated time. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the Appeals and setting aside the notification dated August 31, 1990 issued by the Board, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Under the scheme of the Act and Regulations, the State Board is empowered to constitute the standing Committee. Therefore, when the Divisional Board is acting in conducting the examinations and dealing with the use of unfair means at the final Examination, it is acting on behalf of the State Government as its agent. When the enquiry was conducted by some members and the Standing Committee was taking the decision thereon, it was acting on by behalf of (a) either the candidate or parents or guardian to their advantage; and (b) after considering the evidence available on the record, it acted on behalf the State in turn is acting upon behalf of its Board as its agents. When general public policy requires that particular information should be furnished to the concerned authorities and unless such information is furnished, a decision given by an authority not supported by any evidence or if the order as passed is not supported with any evidence, the High court may be justified to quash the impugned notification. [799C E] 1.2 In cases where the requirement has been dispensed with expressly or by necessary implication, an administrative authority exercising judicial functions is required to record the reasons for its decision. Ordinarily, the appeals are to be allowed, the judgment of the Single Judge is set aside and the appellants ' orders are quashed and the notification issued dated August 19, 1990 is upheld in toto. [789H] 1:3 The examination Committee, if relies upon such evidence to come to the conclusion that the examinee has used unfair means not only on direct evidence but also on probabilities and circumstantial evidence. If the evidence is such that the tribunal can say: "we think it more probable than not the burden is discharge but, if the probabilities are equal, it would be not discharged". [789D] 2.1 The conclusion reached by the Education Standing Committee that the fabrication was done at a behest of either the student/parents or guardian is amply borne out from the record. Therefore when the evidence justified the examination Standing Committee to record its finding that the examin ingees, parents orguardians were parties to the fabrication and whether their complicity was established from record and whether the evidence was sufficient to support such conclusion reached, the Board would be justified in arriving at its conclusion against the respondent, it will not be reasonable to exclude from consideration of the circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The case of the prosecution was that of a firm and not a partner or a proprietor as the other appellants and that they had withdrawn money with them when the talks were going on between an adjoining room and saw the payment through a hole in the door. The appellants were tried by the Special Judge who convicted both the accused under sections 120 B, 161, 165 and 165 of the Indian Penal code for abetment of criminal conspiracy punishable under sections 5(1)(d) read with section 116 of the Act and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 500. The High Court also reduced the sentence on the term of imprisonment already undergone and a further fine. On appeal by special leave: Held, that before it could be made applicable there must be proof, it was said, that the public servant adopted corrupt or illegal means and thereby obtained for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. In one sense such was no doubt true but it did not follow that there was no overlapping of offences. The words "corrupt or illegal" in section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, shows that before a charge under section 3(1) could be sustained there must have been threat or inducement, or promise proceeding from the public servants or duress or extortion practised by him to obtain pecuniary advantage; it was not necessary for an offence under clause (d) to prove all this. It is enough if any by abusing his position as a public servant a man obtains for himself any pecuniary advantage, entirely irrespective of motive or reward for showing favour or disfavour to any person, or for inducing such con duct by the exercise of personal influence. The section does not come with in the meaning of bribery because it contemplates an offence different from a single act of bribery. A trap was laid for catching the appellants and this circumstance according to the learned counsel for the appellants should be taken into account in the matter of sentence. Harjanam Singh vs The State, Cr. Appeal No. 81 of 1953, referred to.

The appellant Bank instituted a suit against the respondent bank for recovery of certain amount from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor and defendant 2 Chitranjan Rangnath Raja. The surety executed the bond, the promissory note and the promissory notes, simultaneously, the surety executed a letter of guarantee exhibit 32 in favour of the Bank. In respect of some correspondence ensued between the Bank and the surety and ultimately the Bank filed the suit for recovery against the legal representatives of the principal debtor but on appeal by the surety, was dismissed by the High Court only against the surety. On appeal by certificate under Article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution, the appellant contended that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of Guarantee executed by the sureties in favour favour of defendant and endorsed by the principal passed in favour PW 4, all on September 16, 1957 constituted one composite transaction and they evidence that the principal defendant had offered two securities one the pledge of goods and the other personal guarantee of the surety; that the Bank having agreed to grant cash credit facility to the deceased Principal debtor on the security of goods by way of pledge and that though the goods were to be kept in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills Pvt. Ltd., but the godown was to be keep under lock and key of the bank, there was negligence on the part of the appellant Bank; that (1) even if it is found as a fact that negligence or inaction on the Bank was responsible for the loss of security of pledged oil tins, yet the surety would not be discharged from his liability under the guarantee. (2) a surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on behalf of one of the sureties; and (3) even assuming that the appellant 's negligence had resulted in the loss to the Bank it was wholly discharged because it was crystal clear that the respondent Bank had offered substantial security by way Of pledge and, therefore, in view thereof, a decree for the recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. was passed against the guarantor. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant Bank was the plaintiff and its suit was decreed by the trial court, i.e., the Court of first instance and this decree has been reversed by theHigh Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. [936G H] 2. The respondent surety has made an application that in compliance with the decree passed by the Trial Court he had paid the entire amount and he should not be exposed to second round of litigation for restitution of the amount and that this Court should give a direction to the bank as part of this judgment that the amount be returned with interest at current rate to the respondent surety. [927D] 3. The court of first instances is not correct in holding that subject to certain variations section 141 of the Indian Contract Act incorporates the English law relating to discharge from liability of a surety where the debtor has offered more than one security, i6 the loan concerned should be made to the creditor. In such a situation clause (a) in the explanation would be attracted and an application for restitution will have to be made by the court of First instance, i,e., Court of Civil Judge, Senior Division, Gondal. Therefore, it would not he proper for this Court to direct restitution. However, where there is a mortgage security given in respect of a debt which is subsequently guaranteed, the creditor must hold the security for the benefit of surety, so that, on paying the debt, the defaulting surety may obtain a transfer of mortgage in its original unimpaired condition.

Patel and Patwaris Law, 1900, were the princely sovereign authority to resume certain lands which were known as " patelki Inam lands. The jagir was created under the British India. Section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, provided that land which was proved to have been held as inams either under a fixed quit rent or under a valid title. In 1922, the jagirdars thought that they were entitled to take possession of the "patelki inam ' lands" on the footing that they would be recorded in the name of Amritrao and that the appellant and his brother brought suits for recovery of possession. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that (1) the lands in suit were granted by then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for services to be rendered by the patel and their grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume and regrant the lands on the basis that they had no right to resume the lands and regdeed them to respondent No. 1, HELD : The observations in Venkata Jagannadha vs Veerabadrayya, A.I.R. , distinguished. (1)(a) Under Rule VI(2), read with rule V(2) of the Inam Rules, the appellant was entitled to his share in the " pate Patelki inam" lands as an undivided brother of Amritnathrao. [723 B] (b) The settlement to be made with the head member of the family holding the office or enjoying the inam and who will be held alone responsible to Government, is not binding on the jaguvada, but only a substitute.

A Hindu governed by the Mitakshara law does not cease to have any interest by birth in a property inherited by his father from his ancestors (ii) that the rule of Hindu Law applicable to Cutchi Memons governed matters of succession and inheritance only. The Madras Berar Courts Act, XXXVI of1932 was extended to the State of Mysore under which, as from November 1, 1950, there were fifteen years before 1948, the holder of a joint family and a half share each in a total of 45,000 shares of which were to be divided by metes and bounds. In 1958, the Madras High Court held that the said rule did not apply to Cutch Memons, and therefore, when a Cutchi memon widow died issueless, her property would be governed by Hindu law as regards succession and succession only. On appeal by certificate: HELD : The properties of the appellant and the respondents belonged to cutchi Memon sect amongst Hindus there and regulated their affairs as regards their property, succession and devolution according to the Hindu Law which they had retained while in Cutch and to which they were already accustomed. [234 D; 235 G] Queen vs Moore Lait vs Ebrahim Hajee Aboo Bucker Sait , referred to. The principle of relationship between the manager and the members of a family was that both the Khoias and the Cutchi, Memons retained, despite their conversion, considerable portion of their personal law and that the rules of Hindu law were accepted by them as customary law in matters of property succession, inheritance and succession including rules as to joint family properties which they bad had while in cutch they had already migrated. In those circumstances, it would appear from the fact that the Setchi Memolons in Madras had regulated their operations since they had settled down amidst Hindus according to Hindu law not only in matters Of succession but also in matters relating to such matters. [236 B C] The Hindu Law by which a testator is governed by Mitakshara law has now extended its operation on the basis of that fact, and in matters in their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship.

The appellant company manufactures fabric of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage and thereafter subjected to an integrated process in the composite mill of the appellant No. 1 for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants did not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not dispute their liability in respect of yarn which is also removed from the Factory. They filed a Writ Petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the validity of the circular. During the pendency of the writ petition in the Delhi high Court, the Central Government by a Notification No. 20/82 C. dated 20th February 1982 amended rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. It further directed that 'use of goods in manufacture of another commodity even within the place/premises that have been specified in this behalf by the Central Excise officers in terms of the powers conferred under Rule 9 will attract duty". As the said circular was implemented to the prejudice of the appellants, they filed a writ petition before the High Court. During pendency of these writ petitions in the High Courts, the central Government amended rules9 and 49 and introduced by amendment of rule 49 so as to include items such as "place of removal", "place or premises appurtenant thereto", for weaving them into fabrics". The said amendments were given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force. The Writ Petition was allowed by a Single Judge holding that the retrospective effect given by section 5(1) would be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act; further, it held that the yarn obtained and also processed within the factory for the manufacture of fabrics could not be subjected to duty of excise. It was held that if at one stage a commodity known to the market is produced and is transferred, within the Factory for the purpose of production of another commercially commodity there is removal within the meaning of rules 9(1). Further, it was held by the Single Judge that if an intermediate product is obtained in an integrated and continuous process of manufacture involving the use or utilisation of a commodity produced at an intermediary stage of such process for the manufacturer of another article inside the factory, then it will be a case of removal for the purposes of payment of Excise duty. It directed that the subordinate excise authorities to levy and collect duty of Excise in accordance therewith.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and a prima facie case was made out against him by the Special judge who accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant of the charge. The High Court set aside the order with regard to payment of fine or imprisonment in default. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: When a public servant is charged under s 161, Indian Penal Code and it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing or procure an official act, it is not necessary for the court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act. [187 E] Gokulchand vs The King, A I R. , referred to. In view of the finding that the appellant grossly abused his position as a police officer and extorted money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal, it cannot be said that the conviction of the appellant under section 161, Penal Code or section 5 (1) (d) of Prevention of corruption Act,. [188 B] In the second place of the allegation against the appellant is also under s 5(1)(d) and by s 5 (5) of his official capacity as a Police officer was expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and to uphold the maintenance of law. Instead they proved facts that there was a gross abuse of his office position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case, it would be difficult to accept that the sentence imposed is not excessive.

The appellant had filed a suit for eviction of the respondents from two different tenancies one for residential purpose and the other for nonresidential purposes. The allegation in the plaint was that the landlord was allowed to enjoy the rents and profits of the property for her life time subject to certain charges mentioned in the Deed. After the life time of his wife, his son, section M Gopalakrishna (appellant) shall enjoy the rent and profits for his life time with certain charges on account of his two sisters. This was contested by the tenants on the ground that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction to the respondents. The Rent Controller held that the requirements of the landlord bonafide and ordered eviction of tenants. On revision, the High Court agreed with the view of the appellate authority that the land was a life interest in the premises and that it was inherent in such a lifeinterest that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b). Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard to the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter, if any occasion arises [275E] The rights on between section Manicka Chettyar and the rest man have to he worked out by in appropriate proceeding, if necessity and the General law win regulate the matter if any arise. [275C D] M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra & others, A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 4; referred to. On the other hand, the Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/S Raval and CO. vs L R. 276 Ramchandra and Others, [1979] 2 S. C.R 746; followed.

Under section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950, the rights in trees of grove, before they were cut, form parts of 'land '. The appellant 's name was struck off on the ground that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. This Court rejected the contention and held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the , in the State of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the . Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: Under the general law, trees before they are cut form parts 'land joint and is agricultural land. After these clear words of the enactment, it was not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are part of groves, and groves and grove land. The proposition was well settled that trees, before them were cut form part of 'lands '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. [34 C D] In view of this very clear legal position, there is no reason to accept the contention that trees before the came into force could be sold only after the Act came into effect. Therefore, even after that decision which according to a DWellant judgment debtor constitutes a complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect of any part of bhumidhari right rights, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves & the view taken by the executing court, that there is a distinction between trees and grove which are parts of grove, and groveland.

A common occurrence took place on 24th December, 1986 in which one Suku succumbed to the injuries as a result of the assault during the occurrence six accused persons were arrayed by the investigating agency for offences punishable under Sections 302, 324, 323, 147 and 148 I.P.C., that six accused. 1 to 4 were put on trial and the prosecution sought to establish its case by examining as many as six eye witnesses besides other evidence, documentary and oral. At the trial however four eye witnesses, PW3 Devassakutty, PWs 6 and 7 salesman and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Nair @ Velayudhan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The Trial Court convicted Accused 2 to 6 for an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to6 were also convicted for offences under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323 324, 325 read with Section 149 I. P.C. but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On appeal before the High Court, it was contended that the prosecution had failed to establish the common object to murder Suku and that the common intention was only to cause grievous hurt to the deceased; that the injuries caused by him were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the deceased and, therefore, he could not be attributed with the knowledge that with those injuries it was likely that death of Suku might be caused and,, therefore he could be cloathed with the liability of causing culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the conviction and sentence of accused 2 to 4 for an offences under Section 307 read with section 149 I P. C., and convicting him for an other offence under Sections 324, 148 and 149 I A. R. for an additional offence under section 326/149 IPC, this Court, HELD: 1. The existence of an unlawful assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking section 149 IPC. Where the existence of such an unlawful omans is not proved, the conviction with the aid of Section 149 cannot be recorded or sustained. [92F] 2. It is no possible to say that all the four appellants had shared the common common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause the death of his or they were sufficient in ordinary course to cause his death. The appellants would, therefore be liable for the offence com mitted individually by each one of them. [93G] 3.1 In a case like this to determine as to which of the accused is guilty of a particular offence it will be necessary to determine whether all the five appellants had sharing the common cause of such bodily injury on the accused persons as were intended to cause such bodily harm on the par ties with the weapon with which he was armed and the nature and seat of injuries inflicted by him though not on any vital part, he can certainly be attributed to the knowledge of that with these injuries it is likely that the death may be caused. [94H; 93A] 2(a) It is in this background that it cannot be said that all those appellants had teen shared the Common intention of committing such bodily hidly as were dangerous and nature and a seat of the injuries, it is not possible to hold that all these four accused have shared the same common intention. [96D] 3(b) The existence or absence of an overt act on any one of the four accused persons is not a matter which is in doubt. From the ocular evidence read with the medical evidence it stands established that the victims 's evidence clearly shows that the assailants had shared their common intention with causing such injuries on them as were unable to give that with that, those injuries could have been caused by blunt weapons, knife, iron rod, cycle chain and the chopper.

The assessee was a non resident company carrying on business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into an agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd, to the assessee, which was renewed by the Income Tax Department in November 1939, whereby it had been maintaining its accounts of the Indian Company on mercantile basis and later for the two subsequent years it stated as cash basis. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. It did not dispute its liability to assessment. In these returns it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 1,600 and Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. When it came to filing of the return for the assessment year 1969 70 (year ending 30 9 1967) and 1970 71, the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs, 925,257 but filed a nil return saving that it was maintaining its books on mercantile foundation alone and returned moneys, but filed the returns in which it stated that it had maintained its accounts on mercantile account. The I.T.O. completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For the four assessment years 1969 70 70 and 197071, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' plea that it Was maintaining its account on cash basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years no tax was payable by it. It took the stand that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69 it had not been maintaining accounts on cash book basis, that no part of the royalty amount has been received by it and, therefore, nothing is taxable. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had not actually received any royalty income from the Indian company, but merely credited to the account of the assessee in its books for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian Co. Ltd.) it found that there was a mistake in filing the returns for the said assessment years and 196869 and the assessee did never contest its liability on to be taxed on the amounts disclosed and further that it is not open to it to change the method of accounting to suit its convenience without the approval of the Income tax Officer. In reference, the High Court answered the question in the negative, i.e., in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. The appellant in this appeal contended: (1) that it could be said to have received the royalty money only when it receives the same in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own books at Coptry. Since it is maintaining its Account with respect for the aforesaid royalty on cash base, it cannot be said that until it is so remitted to and received in the U. K., the assessee has not received the income.

The appellant was put up for trial along with the approver on the night of the murder. The approver had made a confession of his participation in the offence and suggested that the deceased should be killed. The question arose whether the statement of the approver under section 133, Evidence Act, was corroborated in material particulars and qua the appellant. The trial court convicted the appellant on the testimony of the accomplice and found corroboration for the approver 's testimony in the statement Of the approver. Before this Court it was contended that there should be corroboration of the testimony in material details and qua each accused. 834 Held: (i) It is well settled that under section 134, illustration (b), if an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in evidence. The law may be stated broadly in the words of Lord Reading C. J., in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, , followed. (ii) Since sections 133 and 114, illustration(b) may be said not to have been applied but even so, it would be sufficient if corroboration was made with the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice. Therefore though the conviction is unsustainable, the law being that there must be corroboration in material facts it cannot be doubted that under the section a conviction based merely on the unco orroborated evidence of an accused may not be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the terms of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes, (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, 836 position in which he can hardly fail to have a strong bias in favour of the prosecution; the real danger is that he is telling a story which in its general outline is true, and it is easy for him to work into the matter which is untrue. (iii) Though the conviction was based upon the unciporroborate testimony of another accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will as a matter of practice not accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in Material particulars. The fact that he made a confessional statement to his brother, and his conviction is not sustainable merely because it proceeds upon the incorroborating testimony of a co accused cannot be called in the circumstances of this case to be a corroboration of his accomplice.

In a case under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, by the High Court on a finding that the appellant was acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the , it had held that only when an officer or servant of a Corporation was acting as a public servant he could be said to be a public servants within the meaning of section 21(9) of that Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal Code and therefore a 'public servant ' within the expression 'public Servant ' under section 2 of the prevention of CorruptionAct II of 1947. The object of the Act was to introduce the Board and all its officers and servants as may be required to enable the Board to carry out the functions of the Board. Its powers were definitely limited by the provisions in the Act, namely, the establishment of a Board and the regulation of the affairs of the State by the Government, the laying down that the Board may appoint the Secretary and such other officers and staff as may from time to time be required for discharging its functions under the Act and that the powers conferred upon it by the Act were not confined to the general superintendence of the functions and duties of the Boards. Though section 7 of the Bihar State Electricity Board gives power to the Government to appoint any officer, the function of such a body or authority which has a duty to carry on its functions had been duly delegated but the present case is not concerned with the amendment effected by Act 40 of 1964 because the occurrence took place before the coming into force of the Amending Act but after the enactment of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958. There was a difference between an office and an employment. an officer being one to whom is delegated was appointed, was one who was appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. In the course of his judgment, West J. held that a person, who was a Class Iii servant and was employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops and was working under the Works Manager who was an officers of the Government and the duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to those of the Works manager who was the lead of the office.

% The appellant was tried and convicted by the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Mehkar under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Jowar (Restrictions on purchase and sale) Order, 1964. He was further convicted for contravening Cl. 4)(b). The sentences were directed to run concurrently. On appeal by the State before the High Court it was held that the order regarding forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appellant was maintained. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant for contravention of cl. 3. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: Rule 141(2) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of india Rules. [273C] Section 3 gives very wide powers. It seems to us that r. 141 (2) fell within section section 3 inasmuch as it is incumbent upon the Central Government by a notification in the Official Gazette, to make such rules as appear to be necessary or expedient for securing the defence of India and civil defence, the public safety, the maintenance of public order or the efficient conduct of military operations etc. or for maintaining supplies and services essential to life of the community. [272C E] The fact that the rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the . [272F G] In the present case, the order of the High court maintaining the forfeiture of stock was allegal and liable to be set aside.

% This Court in appeal against an order of acquittal in his favour, was of the view that it was unsafe to convict Shri Ram. The appellant who was a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the court along with the brother lawyers, Brijendra Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. The Sessions Judge and the High Court accepted the evidence that Violet did give the particular shout and in accordance with its usual practice, they would not like to take a different view of these simple facts so that they could watch persons moving about on the road. It was also observed that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State Government except in regard to Shri Ram whom it convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced him to death. The incident took place at about 5 p.m. on October 20, 1970. The deceased Kunwar Singh was a lawyer and while he was working as a Nurse with a doctor, the appellant fired a shot from his gun as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down. All the accused thereafter ran away. Some of the accused who had moved an application before the Additional District Magistrate (Judicial) who was conducting the committal proceedings that he was not known to the witnesses and therefore he should be put up for being identified in an identification par parade. The Public Prosecutor objected to this request, contending, that the request was opposed to genuine and the evidence of Om Prakash Singh could not be made the basis of conviction if the request made by the accused is groundless and the witnesses knew the accused prior to the occurrence. Dismissing the appeal of the State, ^ HELD: 1. The said circumstantial chain of reasoning contains a multiplicity of inferences hardly justified by the solitary circumstance that Viasilet informed Sia Ram and his colleagues of the presence of Kunwar Singh. [626E F] 2. No rule of law requires that the oral testimony of a witness should be corroborated by evidence of identification. In fact, evidence of identifie is itself a weak type of evidence. But the point of the matter is that the court which acquitted Shri Ram was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though At the earliest stages he had called his attention to the greater interest and effectiveness played the swift role of alerting the assailants of Kunwar singh. [625A B] 3. The burden was on the prosecution to establish its case and no adverse inference could be raised against Violets for her failure to explain her utterance. Besides, an accused cannot while being examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure be subjected to cross examination and a bald assertion to explain a piece of conduct almost always fails to convince. [643C] 4.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. It was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted they must have taken part in the assault and there was no basis for his plea of private defence and that as two of the other accused involved the incident along with accused 2, it would be appropriate to quote the words of the High Court itself: "Some of the remaining persons" mentioned in the charge. HELD : (1) The conviction of the appellant under section 148 read with s.149 was illegal. [683 D] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 848 and Mohan Singh v State of Haryana, [1963] Supp 1 S. C. R. 847 applied. (2) The charge disclosed only named persons; it may also be that the prosecution witnesses named only the said accused. But there may be other evidence, such as that given by the court witnesses, defence witnesses or circumstantial pieces of evidence which may disclose existence of named or unnamed persons, other than those charged or deposed to by the prosecution witness and the Court on the basis of the said evidence may come to the conclusion that others named or un unnamed acted conjointly in committing the offence. But what is the position if the court acquits 3 of the 4 accused either because it rejects the prosecution evidence or because it gives the benefit of doubt to the said ac cused ? Can it hold, in the absence of a charge as well and evidence that though the three accused are acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointaneously with one of the named persons ? [683 E F] (3) In the present case, on the findings arrived at by the High court the conviction of accused 2 was clearly wrong.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils, is the petitioner in the application and the Union of India, the Collector of Customs, and Assistant Collector of customs (Bond Department) are respondents. On 11th May, 1983, the licensing authority issued import licence No. 295984545 45% in favour of the petitioner for the supply of M Brahca defective sheets/coils on 30th May 1984. This was endorsed on 24th August, 1984. A Writ Petition filed under Article 32 of the Constitution by the petitioner challenging the validity of section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and the order of assessment was dismissed in limine. The petitioner 's petition for special leave was also dis missed. In the meantime, the petitioner ' s clearing agent filed six bills of entry for ex bond clearance. However, due to circumstances beyond the control of the peti tioner, that it to say, by the order dated 4th April, 1988, that he came to know that the income tax authorities had imposed ban under section 132 (1) was arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional, The petitioner asserted that he was ever ready and willing, rather was anxious, rather than anxious. He also filed six Bill of entry on 30st March, 1988 for warehousing under s.59 of the . Subsequently, the Income tax Department issued a certificate for lifting the ban. On 4th May 1988, the Customs Department issued the necessary no objection certificate, thus lifting the embargo. On 5th April 1988, orders were passed by the IncomeTax Department directing the petitioner to pay customs duty at the rate prevailing on the date of posting of goods. The Petitioner 's clearing agent questioned the validity and legality of this act of the Customs authorities. This Court by its order dated 22nd April, 1987 observed that the penalty was not imposed on the petitioner under s, 132( 1) of Income Tax, 1961. On 15th April , 1988, this Court passed a following order: "An appeal shall be filed against the order directing the Revenue Authority to appear before us." By the notice, the respondent authorities had invo lated the duty at Rs.5,000 per M.T. + addl. duty 45% and CVD. at Rs325 per M.,T. from 1st April, 1989. The explanation submitted by the Respondents that for the payment of customs duty the liability of the Petitioner to pay the duty was the duty on the day when the petitioner was acting upon his willingness to remove the goods. This factor was not of the case of the Respondent 's making, according to the petitioner. On 30th March, 1989, the Respondent authorities filed six Bills of entry, for exvi sition clearance, and the goods arrived at the Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984, against which the petitioner filed a Writ Petition before this Court. The Writ Petition was dismissed by the High Court upholding the validity or legality of that order dated 15th/4th April,.1988. Allowing the Appeal, this court, HELD: 1. Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. If there is breach of the fundamental rights, the petitioners can certainly have recourse to Article 32. [ 625A] 2.
