The petition filed under article 32 ofthe Constitution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. It has further to be reiterated that for enforce ment of fundamental right which is dependent upon adjudica tion or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of the Act, it is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is cage breach of fundamental fight. [644C] 3. Article 31 guarantees the fundamental right to a constitutional remedy and relates only to the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 111 of the constitution.

The appellants who were the legal guardian of a Hindu female bank entered into an agreement for sale of the undivided joint family property in favour of the respondent Bank. Though the sale was under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code in execution of the decree on the father 's debt, the amount was not paid within the due date but was paid off and the properties were sold in satisfaction of the claim made by the respondent. In execution of this payment order a bungalow belonging to the appellants was attached. Thereafter the sale deed was fixed for February 2, 1943, and the proclamation on December 24, 1942, was published under sections 165 and 166 of the Act on March 16, 1943. On January 16, 1944, the appellants sold the property to respondents Nos. 1 8 to 10 who were respondents No. 11 to 12. The respondent Bank again applied for postponing the sale which was rejected, but the auction purchaser was required to pay Rs. 15100 to the respondent bank which consisted of the consideration paid by the appellant and the balance of this amount was to be paid within three months from the date of sale. On February 10, 1944 the appellants filed a suit for partition of joint family properties and possession of their separate share alleging inter alia that the purchase by him of bungalow was not binding on the joint family as "it was not liable to be sold and therefore the right title and interest of the defaulter ' could be sold. The trial Court dismissed the suit, but on appeal the High Court held that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the appellants would have a right to challenge the sale on proof of the debt of defendant No. 1 which were characterised as misfeasance " within the meaning of section 155; that the whole estate including the share of the sons was sold in execution under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that even if it was held that there was no evidence to support the finding of the trial court, the order of confirmation could not be challenged on proof by the sons of the immoral or illegal purpose of the debts and partition could relieve the sons from their pious obligation or their shares of their liability to be attached for immoral or unlawful purposes; and that the suit was therefore maintainable. Held, that where after attachment and a proper notice of sale has been given to the sons and the sale proclamation is published under section 166 of, the whole property including the sons ' share which was attached, is sold and the purchaser buys it intending to be the whole coparcenary estate, the presence of the son eonomine is not necessary because they still have the right to challenged the sale and this will apply even to the divided property which, under the doctrine of pious obligation continues to be liable. There can be no doubt that what was put up for auction sale was the entire whole bungalow 2,0 6,6,8 and the description of the property in the sale certificate were conclusive to shew that the entire corpus of the estate was sold. One could not therefore include the share or interest of defendant Nos.

% The petitioners, who are other guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends, challenged the order of the Delhi Administration by way of a writ petition in this Court contending that the Committee had no power to inquire into the conduct of any person, (1) whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B of the Act before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined; and (2) Whether a party has the right of cross examination or not shall be decided by the Committee in accordance with section 8 C. PG NO 521 PG NO 520 Dismissing the writ petition, this Court HELD: 1. The petitioners ' case is that they did not either wish to delay the proceedings or to show disrespect to the Committee but only wanted to protect their own interest by making the submission which they made before the Committee as per legal advice given to them. This was not a case where the circumstances in which the several incidents that had taken place were not known to anyone else. [519F G] 2. Clause 14 of the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1972 provides that upon examination of the conduct and other peculiar features of the case, the Committee may complete its work as early as possible. The Committee should have considered whether the Petitioners were entitled as persons under section 8B of the , before asking their to get in the witness form for being crossexamined till the end of the inquiry.[520F G; 523A B] 3. On behalf of both the petitioners it is submitted that they do not either intend to delay or to give disrespect to it but only wants to protect themselves by making a submission which he made before a Committee as stated in legal advice made to them, [521B C] 4. The affidavits and other material on record show that there were large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the committee. Taking into consideration all the aspects of the matter, it was felt that the committee should not have in the circumstances of the ease directed the filing of a complaint against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. [525E G] 5.

The petitioners, who were seven in number, challenged the levy of a tax on passengers and goods carried by road in motor vehicles. The Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules 1959, which was first published in Rajasthan Gazette shows that the Act received the assent of the President on April 27, 1959, and was published in the Rajasthan Gazette on April 30, 1959. Rule 8(ii) then provides that "the tax payable under the Act on fare by the owner of a motor cycle, rickshaw or a motor cab shall be paid to the State Government in lump sum, of which the amount is mentioned opposite each such class: 3. Rs. 4 for each calendar day This shall have effect on and from the 1st May, 1959" The petitioners challenged the Act as being repugnant to articles 301 and 304 as being a restriction upon inter State trade, commerce and intercourse between two intra state, in support of their contention that there was a difference, reference is made to Entry No. 89 which provides for payments of lump sum in lieu of tax on fare or freight. The petitioners contended (1) that the tax was borne by the operators because of competition with Railways, and (2) that it being borne by operators because they were required to bear the tax themselves to stand competition with the Railways is a matter of policy ' which the petitioners follow. Held, (per Hidayatullah, J., dissenting), that the levy contained a clear classification made by the Constitution itself, and that the words in the two provisos to section 4 have been used both in Rules 8 and 8A and the notification only lay down what the amount of the lump sum must be, if lump sum payment is made in lieu thereof. If the two Rules and the notifications are read harmoniously, and reading them so it was plain that the apparent mandatory language is limited to the prescribing of the contract rates. In view of the view taken by this Court in Coutts Trotter, C. and the Notification, the mere fact that there may be vacant periods when no passengers or goods are transported but the tax is payable is of any force, because there may, be days when the business done might result in tax in excess of the large lump sum payable. The two Rules lay down certain matters which were required under the suction to be made under the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Act, 1959 " and section 4 deals with method of payment of tax by means of stamps to be affixed to the tickets, and the second proviso thereto is to the following effect: "Provided further that the taxes chargeable on fare and freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route lies outside the State. " The assessment of a lump sum was with the taxpayer who may choose one method of paying or the other." The charge of tax calculated on fares and freight charges involved was not obligatory, because it made the pay ment compulsory and attention was drawn to the word 'shall ' used both under Rules 8 & 8A. A Coutters Tropper, Couttrotter C. , followed.

The appellant company was a private limited company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen in February 1974 alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week, and the mounting loss. Subsequently negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. The workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the Appellant pleaded its inability in view of the mountling losses. Some negotiations took placed place between Union and with the appellant lead to an amicable settlement by which work load was sought to he raised(l. It also provided for revision of wages on the one hand and higher norms of production on the other, but ultimately the settlement fell through. Appellant thereafter served a notice of retrenching 43 workmen effective from 1st August 1974 on 43 workmen. The Labour Court held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1 7 1974 were not the real reasons for affecting retrenchment but the real reason was the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and therefore the retrenchment was illegal. It further directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated to service from 1 st August 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The Appellant challenged the Award in this Court on the ground that even if reinstatement was found to be an appro priate relief, what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full back Wages, would he more than full back pay ment and claimed that the reinstatement was not bona fide and that the non availability of the raw material or recurrent power shedage and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood. Allowing the appeal and modifying the award, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 A free and liberal exercise of the power under Article 136 may materially affect the fundamental basis of such decisions viz., quick solution of such disputes to achieve industrial peace. Though Article 136 is couched in widest terms, it is necessary for this court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where Awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman) ; , Management of Paniltole Tea Estate vs The Workmen [1971] I l L.L.J. 327, Workmen of the Bharat Bank Ltd. Calcutta vs Its Workman and others; , U.P. Sugar Undertakings ' Union Ltd., Kanpur vs Their workmen and Others; , , U P. P. Sugar Undertaking Employees ' Union vs Their Workmen ; , All India Industrial Workers ' Union [Private) Ltd. vs Their workman (1964] 1 L.S.J 241, Management of the P. Ltd. Kanpur vs Its Workmen [1975] I L. L J. 216; Associated Cement Companies Ltd. Delhi vs Their workedman and Others, ; referred to. 2.1 In the instant case since 1976 77 the appellant is making profit since 1976 78 year, it would be appropriate to award 75% of the back wages to the workman to be paid in two equal instalments. This Court has taken this view 1105 also.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC by the Sessions Judge, on account of the incident that took place. The conviction and sentence were confirmed in appeal by the High Court but this Court in accepting the prosecution case sentenced him to death. On reference under section 374 Cr. P.C., the High COurt accepted the confession written by the appellant as well as upon the other circumstances of the case. In support of its reasoning, the High court relied on the confessional statement autho rised by the Head Constable Bhag Singh (PW 10) who had performed post mortem examination On the dead body of the deceased found ten injuries on the body of a deceased. The first information report was lodged at about 9 p.m. and during the investigation of the com plaint there were several other facts which showed that on the day of occurrence, the appellant took Churi along with him to his house. On an application by the prosecution under section 164 Cr.P.C. the High Judge converted it into asecond class Magistrate. The second class magistrate remanded the case for recording the confessional statements of the accused. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) Although the Magistrate dealing with the confession recorded by a second class Magistrate in the course of an investigation is not empowered under section164 Cr. C.P., it is open to a lower 'class magistrate to do so. [433 F] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Singhara Singh and Ors. ; , relied on. (2) When a person committing murder went to a second or more class magistrate and made a statement that he had killed the deceased, the accused would have raised hue and cry and cry immediately after the film show was at about 10 p. m. the Sub Inspector came back with the accused to return to his home after the Film show. There was no reason why the confession be not recorded in evidence under sections 74 & 80 of the Evidence Act. [441 G H] State Of Uttar Pradesh V. Singhara singh and Ors., ; , referred to. (3) It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the progress of an en quiry of trial, and it could be caused by Khokhri P. The accused would thus have had a natural affection for the child and it was difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child,. [442 A B] State 's case; , referred back. (4) On the facts of this case, it cannot be held that the confession made by the accused could not be treated as devoid of force. The quantity of corroboration required to operate in the circumstances of a particular case is not relevant. In view of the fact that the accused was an old one of Churi deceased living with his wife there would be no bar to the admissibility of such confession. [442 C] It cannot be disputed that the 1st class Magistrate recorded the confessional confessional statement after having made it before the commencement of the investigation, in the first instance he recorded the confessing therein the same to the police post from the bazar. This was not done in respect of the second class Magis trate. [444 A B]. (5) It was a case for the prosecution itself that the 2nd class Magistrate did not record any such confession when she recorded the confession. The evidence of the 2, mother of the de ceased to be an accused and that the second about the accused having come back with his house on the date of occurrence cannot be accepted because there was nothing in the confession to show that he was a second category magistrate who had been specially empowered by the State Government to record a confession.

A suit for contribution brought by the son of a mortgagor against the co mortgagors was decreed by the Court of Small Causes. The decree was made final on the 22nd December, 1989. In execution the mortgagee proceeded against the proper ty of the plaintiff alone and during the pendency of the execution assigned her rights in the decree to the Hooghly Flour Mills. The mills continued the execu tion and on the 11th March, 1943, the claim was satisfied in this way. An order for sale of a part of the mortgaged property was made on the 26th December, 1939, which was duly certified by the High Court. On appeal the Chief Justice of the High COurt held that it was not necessary to set out the decision regarding the de tails but only giving an overall picture. On further appeal by the plaintiff the Chief justice of Calcutta affirmed that view and held that the signature of the court in the two wills did not affect the validity of the agreement, as it was proved that of the first defendant himself who had signed the will. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court. HELD : (i) The decision of the Court regarding the amount paid by the defendant 's father for satisfaction of the mortgage dated the 12th June, 1936, is unexceptionable and is not against the true legal position. [181 A B]. 442 In the present case, the suit was so framed without doubt and it was therefore unnecessary to decide any further question in this appeal. [182 H] (ii) Though an order of the District Court framing a charge under section 92 of the Indian , shows that the High court has power to prescribe some rules in respect of all other matters common to them, the only rule is the law of the land where such offences are committed. In deciding whether an enquiry into charges is necessary or not, the High Courts must be satisfied that the order of discharge of the accused must be varying with the nature of the charge viewed in the light of the law prevailing at the time of the trial and give the plaintiff such relief as is appropriate to the case. [184 E]. In the instant case, however, it was only after the trial Judge rejected all the contentions raised by the parties that the agreement was proved and that T 's refusal to pay Rs. 40,253 11 10 with interest against each defendant did not infringe any of the rights of redemption conferred on them under section 82. [185 F]. Slightly to vary the language of the Judicial Committee it is the terms and nature of a transaction viewed in such light as would be clear so that while deciding whether the enquiry has been conducted in accordance with law, the conduct of the parties must be looked at first. The principles of law which have evolved in the Allahabad High Court in matters of subrogation under sections 91, 92, 101 and 105 Transfer of Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code do not show that they are rules or rules made thereunder to provide for the same. [186 G] Mohammad Sher Khan vs Seth Swami Dayal, ; , followed. (iii) The section of the Transfer of property Act confers rights on the mortgagor who redeems and directs that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, he must be taken to know, that the law Of mortgage provides for this very question of contribution. It confers rights upon the mortgagor as opposed to proportionate or equal, distri bution of liability. [174 B D] (iv) There is no contract to that effect in the document, there was a recital that the parties were on good terms and trusted each other, the fact remains that Tarak found it necessary to institute a suit for partition against his brothers and right it to a finish. They were not able to arrange matters amicably but only gave an overall impression about it.

Rule 4 of the Karnataka Public Works Department (Recruitment by Selection) Rules 1973 was made providing that a candidate should secure minimum marks from each and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. The appellant applied for the posts of his choice in the Public Works De partment Department, Government of Karnataka. He also secured 24 marks out of 50 marks in the interview and 68.96 marks in his qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out off 150. Appellant No. 1 secured 29.50 marks out. The 2nd appellant obtained 24.83 marks in that exam. He secured 24.84 marks in this test. Appellant Nos. 1 and 2 secured 24,83 marks out the interview Thus, in all 100 candidates were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appel lant secured higher mark than the appellant. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 was excessive and in violation of the decision laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State , JT. On a direction given by this court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the Selection Committee was produced before the Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large percentage of candidates had been selected although they had secured much lesser marks than appellants in the qualifying examina tion but had secured very high marks in compared to the appellant in the viva voce out of 100 marks kept for this purpose. Thus it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of the total marks and merit list was prepared according ly then both the appe ants were bound to be selected and a considerable number of select candidates would had gone much higher in the merits list than appellants. In view of the fact that the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected chal lenged candidates have already joined the posts, that is, the selection was made according lid ing to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafide in the matter of the said selections. In the instant case it is not just and proper to quash the selections on the above ground. However, the selections were made according to the rules of 1973.

The two appellants in the appeals, along with his father were charged and convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on account of a suddenwl which the District Magistrate raided the Ashram and recovered bombs and several other objectionable articles therefrom. On 14.7.1982, the Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed on behalf of the Ashram. The High Court accepted their contention and acquitted them. In these appeals, it was contended for the appellants (i) that since the prosecution evidence had been tendered, there was no justification to take a view different from what has been said about him by the High Court; (ii) that the prosecution witnesses had attributed the extrajudicial confession before the Magistrate, being Exhibit 44 cannot be used in this case and therefore it would not be admissible against the co accused. The State contended that if the wife had been called he would not have supported her version that she met her husband (the detenu 's father). Allowing the appeals and setting aside the conviction of the appellants, this Court, HELD: 1(a) There is evidence that Yadav was beaten up badly after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bomb broke. [436D] 1(b.) The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. Jail officials were also entertained by Sadanand. This type of evidence even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy.[436E G] 2(a). It is not proper to rely on the same for any purpose. [414D E] Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , referred to. (b) In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrates in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses had occur ed. P.S. Appeals dis posed of. [413D F] (c) In this case, Sadanand must have been the common reaction of all the ashramites including Yadav and Sadiq.[435E G]. (d) There was sufficient material in the evidence to support such visits.

The Industrial Tribunal took into account different rates of dearness allowance and fixed the minimum wage and in one concern, namely, that the maximum gratuity allowable would be upto 20 months and a provision was made to the effect that if an employee was dismissed or discharged for misconduct which caused financial loss to the employer gratuity the gratuity to the extent of that loss only will not be paid to the employee concerned. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants in this Court that (1) the award was as regards wages and dearness allowance; (2) the Tribunal had acted wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wage scales and dearness allowances, but did not consider the total effect of the increase. HELD: The Tribunal acted wrong, because it ignored considerations which would be the minimum for various categories of clerical and subordinate staff prevailing in those comparable concerns and the Tribunal therefore should have followed this pattern. [366 A C] (a) In applying the industrial industry cum regional formula the tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the formula if there were ' large number of concerns in the same region carrying on the same industry; in such a case it would be proper to put greater emphasis on the Industry part of tho formula if that there was no step corresponding to the salary drawn by a clerk in the new scale. [372 D] (b) In fixing the wage structure for the factory workmen must be set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal to fix the wages structure including basic wage and dearness Allowance and for granting adjustments in the light of the observations made by this Court. Thus, the Tribunal has not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and the dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done; but considering that wage scales fixed were less than the highest in the comparable concerns though more than the lowest. it cannot be said that the total wages packet was abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total income packet in other comparable concerns. So long as the increase in the maximum from 15 months to 20 months is concerned, it is difficult to say that there is any discrimination. [368 E] (c) The Tribunal has relied on a number of cases. In view of the fact that the Tribunal was relying on a single case which related to clerical and subordi nate staff 's decision in England in the matter of revisionary wages for subordinate and clerical staff, this Court in exercise of its powers under article 136 of the Constitution, has now laid down that it would not be proper for the Tribunal, in view of decisions of this Court, in applying a previous situation to the present case, to fix wage structure including dearness allowance as the one awarded by it. [369 E] The trend in British Columbia Electric Co., Ltd. vs Its Workmen ; and Indian Aluminium Works vs Indian Aluminium & Ors. , followed.

On January 23, 1888, Shiddappa and Annappa executed a usufructuary mortgage (Ex.D 51) in favour of Lalchand Bhavan Chand Gujar and Tuljaram Bhavanchand Gujar for Rs. 1,300 made up of Rs. 1000 due under a previous mortgage and Rs. 200 presently advanced in cash. The deed provided that the mortgage money would be repaid within a period of three years on failure of the mortgagors to meet the said out goings, the mortgagees would incur the said expenses and add the same to their claim on the mortgage. On March 10, 1900, Sh behindappa 's son Tukaram who was the original plaintiff No. 1 filed suits against the mortgagees for accounts to be taken under the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act. The trial court passed a decree for possession declaring that both the mortgages had been satisfied and O. L.P.A. 22 of 1945 was dismissed. Annaappa died in 1923 after having made and published his last will and testament bequeathing his interest in the mortgaged properties to one Krishna Kallappa, that Krishna Kalleppa did not extinguish the title of the plaintiff 's two half share in the suit land. The mortgagee Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade (1904) L. R. 32 Ind App. No. 15 of 1945 which was filed by defendants 1 to 4, was dismissed on March 15, 1909. An Nnappa also died without any issue, and the mortgagee having died his four sons were added as party defendants to this suit and then on their own application they were transposed to the category of plaintiffs. The High Court in Second Appeal No. 754 of 1942 set aside the decree in so far as it upheld the rejection of the plaintiffs ' claim for redemption of one half share of the mortgaged property and in favour Of the mortgagees and for placing the mortgaged Property in his name, held that in view of the matter he dismissed both the appeals. The question for consideration was whether under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as it stood at all material times, the right of an occupant to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour, of a specified person by reason only of his being the registered occupant or that the registered owner had the right to give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in occupancy. Held (per Das C.J., DAS C. J., DAS and L. P.A No. 22 Of 1945) that under section 77, where there are more occupants than one, the notice of relinquishment must be given by the registered tenant also supports the contention that the Rajinama passed by Shiddppa did no effect on the rights of other occupants. Section 74 of Bombay Land revenue Code provides that when a relinquishment is made in favour o more persons than one of such persons must enter into a written agreement to become the registered allotment and his name shall thereupon be substituted in the records for that of the previous registered occupant. A relinquishment in favour by a specified individual may be made at any time, but when there are only 436 occupants than a one, it is said, makes it clear that so far the revenue authorities are concerned, they are, it was the registered user who represents the entire occupancy and the fact that the notice or relinquishment must, under the section, be given to by the Registered occupant also supports its contention. On a correct interpretation of s 74, where no specific reference is made about the intention of an intending tenant to relinquish occupancy either unconditionally or in order to affect his interests in the occupancy, the registration of one of them as a registered occupant attracts the operation of the Code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupants as laid down in the Code but does not take away the right conferred by section 74.

Notification No. ST 1738/X 1012(4) 1964 dated July 1, 1966 issued by the Governor of Uttar Pradesh in exercise of the power vested in him under section 3 A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 provided that carbon paper and ferro papers used for obtaining prints andOfficial im pens of site plans were not paper sorted out or printed in accordance with the word 'paper ' as used in serial No. 2 of Notification Ng ST 3124/X 1012(4). Rule 2 of the said Notification provides that carbon Paper which is manu factured by coating the tissue paper with a thermo setting ink (made to a liquid consistency) based mainly on wax, non drying oils, pigments and dyes by means of suitable coat ing roller and equalising rod and then passing it through chilled rolls cannot be used for the aforesaid purposes but is used. The respondent claimed that carbon papers were not covered within Entry No.2 of Notification No . ST 173 8/XI012(3) 1964. The Sales Tax Officer taxed the turnover of carbon paper at 6% and disallowed the claim of the respondent under section 2A of the Act. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper was challenged by the respondent in writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal on certificate. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: l.1 A word which is not defined in an enactment has to be understood in its popular and commer cial sense with reference to the context in which it occurs. [839E] 1.2 In popular parlance, the word "paper" in common parlance means paper which is used for printing, writing or packing purposes. [850F G] 1:3 The word ' Paper ' is understood as meaning a sub stance which is intended for bearing, writing, or printing, or for wrapping things, decorating walls etc. ' From the definition it, it is clear that in popular parlance the word commonly means paper. It was understood as a term when people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [85F] 1 :4 In popular North Eastern Railway Co. Ltd., ; , relied on. Attorney General vs Winstanley; , ; Craies,Sixth Edition, Volume 13 page p. 108; Edmondonica 's Dictionary (Volume 2), pp. 222 and Vallonian A. 2d. 404 at 248; referred to. In the instant case, carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by Entry 2 of List II of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

The respondents were employed as seasonal masons in the year 1946. In 1951 the partners of the appellant Mills purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at Bulandshahr in the district of Nainital. They closed it at Kiccha and started it at Bulandshahr. The new factory was named Pannijee Sugar & General Mills, Bulandshahr. On January 19, 1955 the General Manager of the Mills ordered the transfer of the respondents I to 4 from one godown to the appellant mills at Bulandshahr subject to certain conditions under which they were not holders of the works as required by Standing Order No. L(a). The respondents challenged the order of transfer on the ground that the conditions of service mentioned in the Standing Order were not satisfied. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the management was within its rights and that a punishment should be imposed upon the respondents under Standing Order 11 (1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. On appeal by the Management it held that both the concerns i.e., the mills at Amroha and the mills formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. The management appealed to the Labour Appellate Tribn but the High Court held on a reference under section 33 of the Act that the decision of the employer holding that both concerns i were the Mills at Amroha, and the Mills formed one single unit, it had no territorial jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal as the respondents 1 to 4 had disobeyed their order of his transfer. Held: (i) The agreements between the appellant and the respondents had no such right. Under an agreement of service between them or under any statutory provisions, only one connection was in th identity of ownership and, but for it, one has nothing to do with the other. It is not necessary to multiply the citation, for the other decisions relied on by the learned counsel for the appellant pursue the same reasoning followed by the Labour Court. (ii) There is nothing on record to indicate that at that time it was intended to purchase factories at other places or to extend its activities in the same line at different places. It would be enough to point out that even if the appellant had such an intention, he could not have prescribed any term between the contracting parties when the idea of starting new factories at different hours was not in contemplation. (iii) In a case where a person joined service, the Privy Council held that it was impossible to imply a term of transfer and his decision assumed that the business was one unit and the only question raised was whether he should not be transferred to a place different from the place where he was actually discharging his duties. This view is not of any relevancy to the present case. (iv) But in all the said decisions, the workers had been employed in a business or a concern and for the question that arose was whether in the circumstances of each case, the transfer from one branch to another was valid or amounted to victimization. If so, could it be said that such a term had to be necessarily implied between the parties. When the respondents were applicable to employees in an industrial dispute, it was possible to imply the condition of right of the management to transfer the employee from one concern to another of his in the circum stances of this case, namely, whether the appellant gave the right to transfer them to a different concern stared by him subsequent to the date of their employment under the contract of service or under r. 11 (a) of Schedule I and rule II thereof, there was no such question of law within the meaning of section 7 (1). (v) There was nothing on the record to show that at the time it Was intended to purchases factories at any other places; if so could, it be held that such term had not to be implied between tho parties.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A. The scheme could not be implemented straight away by the stages. It, therefore became necessary for Parliament to make certain transitory provisions, which it did by the introduction of Chapter VI A by Act 53 of 1951. The Statement of objects and reasons of the Act 53 may be usefully extracted here. The Central Government has considered those objections and are anxious to avoid any competitive handicap to any region. This may be best achieved by an equitable distribution of the employer 's contribution, even where implementation is affected only in certain areas, among the employers in the whole country employers in regions where the scheme is implemented paying slightly higher contributions. This will minimise the contribution leviable from the employers and spread the incidence of the cost of the scheme equitably. This Bill is primarily intended to achieve this object. " The notes on Clause0 of the Bill which provided for the introduction by Chapter VA was to the following effect: "Clause 20 A new self contained chapter is proposed providing for the collection of employer 'S special contribution throughout the Union". The rate of the contribution which may be varied from time to time was to be fixed by the Central Government after two months notice by notification. The rate and time within which the special contribution was to he paid would be notified by the central Government. Consequentential provisions fitting the employer "s special contribution into the existing scheme of the Employees ' State Insurance Corporation shall be given. "Appropriate Government" under section 2(1) means in respect of establishments under the control of the Central Govern ment or a Railway administration or a major port or a mine or oil field (i), the Central 'Government and in all other cases, the State Government.

The management, in a writ petition, claimed regularisation of the services claimed to be daily rated workmen for a long time in its mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demand was being regularised and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they were discharging the same duties as regular workers. The management denied the petition ers ' claim contending that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid continuously; and a voluntary Retirement Scheme offering considerable amount to these daily rated workers has been framed which is Annexure R V to the counter affidavit. Disposing of this petition, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of regular workmen arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him. [613C] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This principle has been reiterated at the hearing before this Court, in view of the clear findings supported by evidence that there were no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that only for some time, they have continued on their rolls and after paid in spite of the there being no work available for them.

The appellants were the owners of a tea estate. They purchased from the several persons directly or mediately, the entire property as also part of it. The diploma holder claimed (i) that by reason of section 3 of the Crown Grants Act, 1919, he obtained virtue of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act by which he became entitled to full 16 as. share in the property and (ii) that only 2 1/2 as share was sold under the mortgage decree and purchased by the mortgagee was not effective that would not help the plaintiffs so long as they could not displace the title of the National Agency Co. The trial court upheld this claim but the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court by the appellants, it was contended (i). that in view of the provisions of 0. 22 r. 1 of the Limitation Act 1908, the bar was not attracted to cases where the subsequent suit was by the heirs and assigns of that plaintiff; the plaintiffs ' suit was liable to be dismissed by reason Of section 41 which barred the plaintiffs from bringing a fresh suit created merely a personal bar against the plaintiff in the first suit and that in any event the claim could not be accepted without careful scrutiny of the facts. Held, further, that the question whether on the findings regarding the existence of a special right based on the purchase of Ashfaq 's share through Pir Baksh had been raised before the trial Court as in the plaint it was not necessary for the plaintiffs to raise any specific ground touching their rights to this share or they contended that in case the sale was made out and was real, it would result merely a transfer of the rights of the plaintiff. The contention that the suit was bad, must be rejected, must fail, because (i ) while the relief sought for on the basis of the agreement dated April 18, 1931, the plaintiffs did not agitate or press before the courts below any special right; and (2) though in the written statement filed by them the necessary averments were made regarding their obtaining the share of brokerage through P. Palarkaras reviewed by the High Courts and held that the plaintiffs were precluded from bringing the fresh suit formed merely a defence which was not raised at any stage of the proceedings until the first issue had been framed.

The prosecution alleged that the deceased man Baga Rao had separated from his other brothers on the evening of December 26, 1955 and partitions took place between Baga, Rao and Lingarao on the following morning. Beypore was proceeding from his village towards Nirmal side. He saw some of the occurrence and then out of fear hid himself in a hut nearby. The appellant who was an excise Contractor had separated and partitioned the family lands. There were differences amongst the brothers which had led to arbitration proceedings in respect of a matter between Bagana Rao on one side and Lingappa on the other in the field. The parties reside in village Kollamaddi Taluk Sircilla, district Karimnagar. At about 7 a.m. "on the morning of December 27, 1955 Baga Reddy had been proceeding from Baga to Nirmal side with his knife. At that time B had been going towards Baga SircImprolai and he fell down on the cot with his knives. At the time P.W., the father 's brother, the appellant, who was also proceeding towards Nirmal and saw most of the incident and then arrived at a hut near the house of B and asked for copies of the depositions of the witnesses examined by him in detail to the accused persons who had denied their complicity in the crime and who alleged enmity with his two brothers 's brothers. These facts were brought to the notice of all the eye witnesses to them. The Sessions Court convicted the appellant under section 302 read with sections 34 and 109 Indian Penal Code. On appeal the High Court rejected the defence suggestion that it was the duty of the magistrate, while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself whether the documents referred in section 173(4) had been furnished to the appellant and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. The High Court also observed that an omission by a police officer to fully comply with the provisions of section 162 or section 360 of the Code has necessarily the result of vitiating those proceedings and subsequent trial. Held, further, that even though section 173 (4) of the Indian Penal code had not been complied with, since it had not empowered him to do so under section 537(a). The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions Of section 162.

The respondent Municipality on the failure of its duty to comply with section 153A of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, as adapted and applied for permission to discharge the effluent in accordance with a notice dated May 14, 1956, issued by the appellant Municipality tinder section 153 A (1) of the City of Nagpur Municipal Act. The appellant replied that since he had obtained the approval of the Government under section 153 B(3) of that Act, the question whether the discharge of the effluent from the factory of the respondent company was polluting water and adversely affected the fertility of the soil was one for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality. Held, that before a notice is issued to the party concerned the condition precedent for the issue of a written notice would be satisfied; and under the provisions of section 153 (A) of Act if he objects to the requisition specified in the notice or consents to it subject to modification, the Government was not free to act upon the objections raised by the respondent Municipality, and when no objection could be taken from him on any particular day after that date, the notice issued under section 13(2)(i), must, on a request made to him by the Municipality appoint a special judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge. In the present case the resolution of the requisition was not challenged by the owner of the premises in question and it was open to him to ask for permission from the Special Officer to hold an enquiry into that question as to whether, in fact, the nuisance alleged was existed or not but the person concerned objects to that notice and the requisition contained therein absolutely the objection. Section 153A does not in any way affect or in any manner affect the legality of the action of the municipality in issuing the notice on the ground that it should not have been so satisfied. In view of section (3) and (4), the provisions Of section 153(A) are not attracted, and there is no question of making a proper enquiry into the existence of the nuisance after due notice. Consequently the proceedings of this kind ought to be handled with the utmost expedition that because if a nuisance exists it should be removed without delay in order to preserve the health of the community and the fertile soil, then it would not require a judicial officer to enquire and report only as to the manner in which the effluent shall be discharged.

The provisions of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 are a measure providing for punishment of persons in unlawful possession of railway stores who cannot satisfactorily account how they came by the same. By section 2 "railway stores" are defined to mean any article (a) which is the property of any railway administration and (b) which has been used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. Section 3 defines the offence as also the measure of punishment therefore. It reads: "If any person is found, or is proved to have been in possession of any article of railway Stores reasonably suspected of being stolen or unlawfully obtained, and cannot account satisfactorily how he came by him by the said definition. He may for instance show that he had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind are usually sold or that he has bought them from a bona fide purchaser in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the facts in this case are as follows: (1) 30 Cuttack Law Tims, 275 191 The evidence shows that he was examined by the prosecution at the time when he found the material which he classified under 38 heads and described the same as unauctionable property. He also showed his definite averment in the report that he did not state whether these articles belonged to any particular railway administration but merely added that he put the articles 1Sup. C.I./70 14 and they were parts of an engine and that Railway articles were mixed with other goods in the bags. The usual formality of preparing a recovery memo and the sealing of goods in bags in the presence of witnesses was gone through and one Jaswant Singh described as an expert of railway machinery parts and Foreman and Chief Inspector of N.E. Kotwali Chowk, Lucknow examined the material thus classified under heads and describing the same to be Railway stores and kept in 11 bags and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a Railway engine. The police seized the said railway property and kept it in 11 s bags and removed the said bundle when he was questioned by the appellant. On the strength of the evidence adduced by the defence and principally on the report of Jaswant Singh a charge under section 3 of the Act was framed against him, and his plea that they belonged to a particular railway 's head office is highly probable and that they had purchased them from someone bona fide in the faith that the purchaser had lawfully acquired the facts he had lawfully taken the facts. The appellant contended that there was no evidence before the courts to prove that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Indian Railways Act and it was only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecutions that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same, and consequently he had failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his. The High Court accepted this contention and convicted him under section 2. On appeal to this Court HELD: (i) It can be reasonably inferred that as the seized articles were found to conform to the specifications of the 'Indian Railway Standards they held that they belong to any railway Administration and that therefore the question of punishment under section 4 did not arise. [189 F] (ii) The mere description of the goods as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 1 2(b).

The appellants and the respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The demised premises were governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 for short the 'Act '). Section 13(1)(a) of that Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any law or contract no Court shall pass any decree or make any order in favour of the landlord whether in execution of a decree or otherwise evicting the tenant so long as he is ready and willing to pay rent thereof to the full extent allowable by the Act ' unless the landlord proves to the satisfaction of the court, that the surviving spouse, son or daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law as applicable to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential pur poses, ordinarily residing and in the Case of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily carrying on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The respondent landlord terminating the lease under section106 of Transfer Of Property Act but her remained in occupation and enjoyment thereof. The Rent Officer dismissed the suit. He held that Smt. Anandi was the tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended by section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing to s.3 Clause (vii), thus: "Notwithstanding anything contained" in any Law or contract No court shall pass an decree or made any order In favour of t he landlord whether, in execution, of a decrees or otherwise eviction against the tenant, so longas he is allowed and willingto pay rent therefor to the total extent allowable under the Act." The Appellate Court dismissed the appeal. While dismissing the appeal filed by the respondent, the High Court held that as the appellants had not carried on the business with her till date of her death, Smt. Jaya Bai was a tenant holdingover. During her life time she had not com muted the business in the demised premises. The Trial Court dismissed and decree was confirmed in appeal by the High Cou rt. In the Second Appeal before this Court it was contended for the appel lants that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of the tenant in September, 1966 the appellants did not carry on the building with her until date of his death; that inasmuch as the tenancy came to a terminus with its determination by issuance of notice under s. 106 of the Transfer of property Act, and the legal representatives do not succeed to the estate of the deceased tenant so as to prosecute the proceedings, and that the tenancy rights devolve on the heirs u/s 13(i)(a); and that in any case the tenancy right devolved on the heir u/S 14 of the Rent Acts; that since the bequest was in favour o the third party, the testator thereby cannot confer rights under the provisions of the Act on the stranger who was not a member of the family. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The tenancy rights devolved on tho heirs under the ordinary law of succession. The unamended definition of 'Tenant ' in section 3 sub clause (vii)(b) makes the legislative intent manifest that from the date of the amend ment Act came into force, on the death of a tenant, his surviving spouse son, daughter and heir, in accordancewith personal law, as applica ble to him, who had initially been, functioning as a statutory tenant.

The Electricity Board, which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4% per annum for supply and distribution thereof, had been continuously rising from Rs. 59.39 lakhs in 1961. The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution was on the basis of basic wage the Board and the employees contributing equally. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. Alternatively, they had contended that the services were liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under 'the Employees Provident Funds Act and that this would impose additional financial liabilities which the appellant Board would not be able to bear. HELD: (i) The dispute between the parties was that the contribution under the Act is 8% whereas under the Board scheme it is 6.24 per cent whereas under 's Scheme it is 5.25% whereas by virtue of section 64 the State Government may guarantee the payment of principal and interest of any loan proposed to be raised by the Board. Under section 64, the State government may advance loans to the Board in the prescribed manner. [44 C D] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, [1964] II L. J. 131, approved. (ii) The Tribunal did not look into the Act at all but the question whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the Electricity Board under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the appellant company, could be applied is a rather difficult question because in fact the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden Of wage structure in the interest of social justice. [45 C D; 46 G] Gramphone Co., vs Its Workers, ; , followed. (iii) The provisions of section 68 may have to he taken into account. If it is not it would have to meet by loans on which interest will have t been payable and deduction of interest so paid will have. to be taken into consideration in calculating the profits. [46 C D, 46 A] Gram Prabhone Co operative vs Its workmen, ; and Gramophonone Co, vs its Workmen, , referred to.

% Respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence under section 498(A) I.P.C. but refused to live with her husband on the grounds that as he was impotent, it should be a just ground for refusing to live alongwith her husband. The appellant filed Revision Application before the Sessions Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotant, this should be deemed to be a fit one for the wife to refuse maintenance and hence she was entitled to the grant of divorce. In revision preferred by her husband the High Court held that that the appellant was unable and unable to discharge his marital obligation, as she was impetent and unable not to maintain her claim with him and thus inflict on herself a life of perpetual torture. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is now well settled by a long course of decisions laid down by various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse to live in with her deceased husband if there was a just reason for doing so. [701F] 1.2 In the instant case the courts below had taken the view that impetency is not reasonable ground on the part of the wife for refusing him to live along with her spouse which would certainly amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a valid ground as contemplated by the aforesaid proviso for the appeal to this Court. [700G] 1:3 A clear perusal of the provisions manifestly shows that it was meant to give a clear instance of circumstances which may be treated as a just one ground for refusal of the husband 's refusal to livewith her husband, and these circumstances have clearly established that the grounds on which the wife refuses to live should be just and reasonable as contemplated under the Proviso. Similarly, where the wife has a reasonable apprehension arising from the conduct of the father that she is likely to be physically harmed due to persistent demands of dowry from her husband ' parents or relations, such an apprehension also would be manifestly a reasonable justification for the divorce 's refused to living with her appellant 's husband. [800G] 2.1 In the matter of the Petition of Din Mohammad, Mahmood, J, in the Nagpur case, there was clear finding cf fact by the police which had been accepted by the High court that the wife failed to prove by convincing evidence that her father was impatent and is unable to live separately from such a husband. Similarly the Judge who had delivered the judgment in the instant ease had very rightly pointed out as follows: "Jammu Basawamma vs Managevekar Mancherji, ; , referred to.

The suit property was described in two parts in the schedule to the plaint. The first part consisted of Survey Nos. 162, 163, 164 and 165 on which structures of old Lancer 's lines were standing and certain evacuees were Occupying at the time of the suit. This second part is sometimes referred to as Lancers quarters and also sometimes as Rasala Lines. The plaintiffs ' case was that by Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1984 published in the Bhavnagar Darbar Gazette dated 24.1.1948, the State vested the said lands including four plots of land mentioned therein in the survey numbers referred to in part 2 of the Schedule. These three suits were filed on 3rd March, 1964 but the suit was dismissed in respect of the Land comprised in the Rasala line. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in that suit till 7th July, 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of India to the State Public works Department of the State of Saurashtra. However, on appeal, the High Court allowed the appeals filed by the Union of India in respect Of two survey numbers whose lands were situated within the limits of the Municipality and held that these were occupied by the State Government without buildings. Against this judgment and decree of the High court, the appellant came to this Court.

The appellant was a member of the Railway Carriage Workshops, and he was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code with having abetted the said establishment. He was further charged with having committed an offence under section 420 Indian Penal. The Special judge convicted him of the offense under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947 and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same, both the sentences to run concurrently. On appeal by the State against acquittal, the High Court acquitted him but granted certificate of fitness to appeal on two main grounds (i) that the appellant was an 'officer ' within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal code and (ii) that he did not fall within the terms of the last portion of clause (9) Of the section 21. Held, that the question for consideration before the High court was whether a person is an officer of the Government though he might not possibly exercise 'any delegated function of the government. The fact that the duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to those of some one who was an officer in the service or pay of the 'Government did not per se make him an 'Officer ' within section 21 (9). The liability which he performs had been entrusted by the Government to him by the delegation and was therefore, a public servant within the definition of a public servants contained in section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act IIoII of 1947. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, [1952] S.C.R. 1, relied on. Held further that the conviction and sentence awarded to an officer under section 16(1) (d) Of Act IIII of 1946 was illegal and not in order and fell within the term of a 'public servant ' contained in Section 2 of Prevention of corruption Act IIof 1947. King vs Empress, I.L.R., Ahad Shah vs Emperor, , referred to.

% The respondent alongwith his one Gora Lal and Sat Pal were granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The licences paid a sum of Rs. 1,38,000 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated demands. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. Excise and Taxation Department, Patiala (Respondent 's) issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share of the respondent in the property was notified for June 14, 1977 and since the respondent did not challenge his liability to pay the amount claimed from him, he filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C, being Suit No. 472/13 6 77 against the State of Punjab and the collector cum Deputy Excise and the Taxation Commissioner, Patiala Division, for permanent injunction restraining the State and the District Collector cum Deputy excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his said half share. The contention of the Respondent was that a part of the building standing on the said plot of Land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other suitable residential house and, therefore his half portion could not be exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (I) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The trial court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of the provisions of Section 50 of the Civil Court Act, 1887, which makes the provisions applicable to attachment and sale for recovery of revenue under the Act, the properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sold in execution of such a decree would be only those properties as are exempted by the said Section. The said section has no application to an attachment and sales under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said provisions are concerned, it contains a complete code providing for modes and machinery for recovery o arrears of revenue. Allowing the appeal, this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect thereof were not in execution as no decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery recovery of Revenue due to the State. [848E] 2.1 Under Section 60 nothing is contained in the said section which makes provisions of section 60 applicable to attached attachment and Sale for recoveryof revenue under this Act. It contains a non obstante provision providing for the modes and procedure for recovery for arrears of money revenue. The rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary of final and binding.

The appellant was the owner of certain agricultural lands in Moosapet village. In 1962, the former notification was issued under section 59(a) and the latter after his death notice issued on the respondent to show cause why his land should not be acquired for the Hindustan Machine Tools Project Factory of the Indian Drugs & Pharmaceutical Ltd., Hyderabad. In proceedings instituted before the Special Deputy Collector against him the respondent as well as the High Court awarded compensation of Rs. 20,45,000 under section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act. The special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of about Rs. 2 lakhs and this amount was received in April, 1964 by the heirs of Rashid, the deceased son of Rashid (Appellant in C.A. No. In the reassessment proceeding, the Special Additional Deputy Collector did not accept the awards made by the Special Land Acquisition Collector in respect of the aforesaid lands and requested him to refer the question of compensation to Civil Court under section 18 of the Act on two grounds: (a) that after compensation had been awarded by the special Deputy Commissioner under section11 of the land Acquisition Act, the heirs had merely exercised a right to sue for further compensation which was merely a hope or a chance that the compensation might be enhanced, and that such hope or chance could not be elevated to the status of an assets or property and as such not asset or property chargeable to estate duty had escaped assessment and (b) that even assuming that any asset or properties chargeable to Estate Duty had escapedassessment the notice was illegal and without jurisdiction because such escapement was not due to any omission or failure on the part of the accountable person to disclose fully and truly material facts necessary for making the assessment. 20 The respondent challenged the validity of two notices issued by the Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, Hyderabad contending (a), that after acquisition of lands acquired, the right to receive compensation at market value on the dates of the relevant notifications accrued to the deceased and such right was unquestionably property which would pass on the death of the deceased but he contended that during the lifetime of the late husband of the respondent the lands in question had not merely been acquired but even the compensation as determined under the awards passed by the civil court, and (c) that the extra compensation received by the legal heirs of the de fendants belonged to them and not to the Appellant and hence it was not property that passed on the deceased. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands such property had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by it, there was escapement of assessment to duty because the lands had vested in the Government long prior to his death but he could not pass on his death inasmuch as those lands had sepa rately formed part of that estate which passed on his own death, and hence no property escaped assessment. The respondent appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High Courts.

This was a writ petition challenging the election of the Directors to the District Central Cooperative Bank, Chandrapur. The appellant 's election was not called in question in view of the procedure prescribed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 which did not envisage the setting aside of an election as one has been done by the impugned order. On 8.1.1987 the District Deputy Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Act to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of the Bank as per the provisions of section 73FF, and directed him to remain present on 2.2.87 at 1167 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The notice stated that the appellant had borrowed a loan of Rs. 10,000 (Rs. 7,000) from the Bank and he kept the loan constant in arrears till 21.10.1986, and being elected as Director of the bank on 18.8.86. He removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors holding that appellant was defaulter under section 73F(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies, 1960, and rejected the appellant ' s contention that section 73B of the Maharashtra Act came into force on 12.5.1986 which came into effect on 12th May, 1986 while the appellant contested the election and although he paid all the debts on 21.11.86 yet he could not be "absolved of the disqualifications on the day he contested the Election. The Assistant Registrar by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the Appellant from the committee of Directors and holding that the Act came to force on December 12, 1986 i.e. the date when he was declared elected as the Director. He also observed that the dues calculated on 31.1 .86 became recurring dues every following day and on December 6, 1987 when section 73 AB applied. The order of the Assistant Registrar dated 7th December, 1987 was served on the appellant on 8.12, 1987. The appeal against this order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of the Cooperative Societies and the appellant filed a writ Petition in the High Court challenging that order. The Writ Petition filed by him challenging the order was also dismissed by holding that section 78F(I)(b), which came to be applicable from 6.81986 as per Government Notification issued on 18th April, 1986, and since he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21st October, 1986 before his election was only a defaulter, he was not at all eligible to contest the election. He filed an additional reply on 10.11,87 stating that he had not committed any default after the amended section 73 B. The High Court dismissed both the writ petition holding that since the appellant was a defaulter he was lawfully removed and hence the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD:1.1 As has been stated in para 36 of the report in Hundraj Kanayalal Sajnani vs Union of India, ; at 1121 will not be relevant. [684F] 1.2 The appellant to have made default on the first day of his directorship and on every subsequent occasion till the instalment or instalments were paid. The submission has therefore to be rejected. Similarly the submission that the defalult must have been one committed after the Act coming into force has also to be repelled on the same ground that immediately on the Act comes into force the appellant is a defaulter and so long that default continued he must be taken to have making default until repayment. What then would be the consequence of such a default. Sub section (2) of section 74FF says that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section(1), shall cease to be a member of the committee and his seat shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. [681C] 1:3.

Rule 189 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules empowers Government to reduce or withdraw a pension. Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner be convicted of grave misconduct while he was in service or after the completion of his service provided that before any order to this effect is issued, the procedure referred to in Note I to Rule 33 of Bombay Civil Service Rules would be followed. The State Government 's power to reduce/ withhold the pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. 35 The validity of the Government ' 's order was challenged before the High Court which allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government order dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State government had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from service. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of reduction/ withholding pension by 50 per cent was disproportionate to the charges proved against the Respondent. [189 E] 2. Rule 188 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part in the pension payable to a Government Servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service. This rule further provides that before an order reducing or withdrawing any portion of the pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note 1 to Rule 34 of the Rules. The validity and propriety of the Rule was not challenged either before theHigh Court or before this Court. [ 189 E] B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., ; , followed.

Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 provides that a landlord can evict his tenant if he satisfies two conditions. The first condition is that he must obtain the permission of the District Magistrate to file such a suit; and the second condition was that he should prove the existence of one or the other of the seven grounds. enumerated in clauses (a) to (g) of section 3( 1). Sub sections (2), (3) and (4) are mandatory in nature, and the where a plea for eviction is raised by a landlord before the civil court goes to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to that inference. The scheme of section 4 of the Act shows that if a landlord wants to bring a suit to eject his tenant, he has to apply to the District magistrate under section 3 (1) for permission to do so. After the district Magistrate makes an order on the landlord 's application, the party aggrieved by the order can apply in revision to the Commissioner within 30 days and the Commissioner, in exercise of his revisional jurisdiction, has to deal with the revision application under section three(3). If he is satisfied that the District Judge had acted illegally or with material irregularity or had wrongly refused to act, he may confirm or set aside. The appellants further claim termination by a subsequent amendment of section 2(3) which provides for the grant of permission, and, as the said application was found to be without the authority of law, the latter had also been rejected. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) It cannot be seriously contended that the High Court was in error in coming to the conclu sion that the permission granted by the Commissioner in exercise Of his powers conferred on him by section 3 k was invalid in law, and as such, a nullity. [560 F] (ii) The authority under the relevant provisions of the , can be excluded by a statutory provision which expressly provides for it, or which necessarily and inevitably leads to that conclusion. In other words, the jurisdiction of the civil courts could be excluded from a statutory provi sions which deal with special matters; but in the context, the inference that the civil Courts ' jurisdiction was intended to be excluded, appears to be inescapable; there are three ,categories of cases in which the Commissioner can interfere with an order passed by the District Magis trate: (a), (b) and, (c). The power conferred on the State Government under section 7 F is very wide. [561 A] (iii) It could not be seriously disputed that the jurisdiction conferred on Commissioner under section 2 of the . is exactly similar to the jurisdiction imposed on the High Courts under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The present case does not fall within any of the categories covered by clauses (b), (c) and(c) all centre round the question about the jurisdic tion of the Commissioner.

This is a first reference of its kind and nature.
