The prayers in the Reference are "to whether Shri Gopal Krishan Saini, Member of the Punjab Public Service Commission ought on the ground of misbehaviour to be removed from the office of the Member of Commission. " The President of India has referred for consideration the question as to whether Shri Seth of the State Public Service commission ought, on the grounds that : (1) the Chairman or any other member of a public Service Commission cannot be removed; (2) the order of removal can be passed after the Supreme Court has been constituted and (3) the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court. On behalf of Shri Saini it is urged that (1 ) the Constitution of India does not prescribe any time limit or limitation in making a reference under Article 317(1) which is plainly not to be found in it especially a provision in the nature of a condition precedent; (3 ) the power of the President to make a reference to this Court under Article 318(1), is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority; and (4) the High Court has no jurisdiction to embark upon an examination of the facts and that its function is limited to determining whether the circumstances found upon by an independent fact finding has been arrived at. Allowing the Reference, ^ HELD : 1 The judgment of this court in so far as it relates to the procedure which this Court should adopt in a Reference under Article 143(1). [468 C] 2. Even if one may choose the same thing, it will not be conducive to justice to decide the Reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. In the instant case, the argument that the accused has been falsely implicated into the charge of assault because he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the hostility of the posted towards him when trying to ward off the blow is concerned is true and was not correct. The accused have to be summoned and allowed to cross examine witnesses who have filed their affidavits. Considering the nature, and gravity of the matter referred to, this Court cannot prevent Shri Saini against whom a grave charge has been made from proving that the charge is false and motivated. [468 G, 469 A C] 3. If an examination and assessment of facts shows that the President was satisfied prima facie that the allegations made against the Lok Sabha require to be inquired into by the Supreme court, the Court comes to the conclusion that the facts alleged are established, the conviction or a decree for damages may follow as a matter of course. But then, a contrary finding by this Court will equally seal the fate of those proceedings. [470 H] 4. It is not safe to lay down any hard and fast rule. In a reference made by the President under Article 316(1.) this court has the power to summon and examine witnesses, but nothing contained therein can be read to mean that after deciding which witnesses should be summoned, and evidence must be recorded by this court itself. [361 B C] 5. For convenience it is only fair that an opportunity should be given to Shri Saini to prove his case that the charges against him are false at all.

The appellants, who were the plaintiffs and the respondent herein, had instituted a suit under Section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 ( 'the Act '). They contended that the endowment was of a public nature as alleged by the respondent or a family deity as alleged in the plaintiff 's plaint. The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellant 's suit holding that the temple and the deity installed therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the Respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. On appeal, the learned District judge reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the deity installation therein being private endowment fell under the four sentences of section 62(1) of Act and dismissed the appeal filed by the appellants. The High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object which can be gathered from this document is placed beyond doubt by a later document Ext. A and Ext. 1 and Ext A and that the intention was merely to instal a family idol in the temple. [832 D E] 2.1 It is well settled that under Hindu law, however, it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the founder is to instal. a family ship in the Temple and worship the same in order to effectuate the spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and his descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the settlor. [827 E F] 2:2 An idol is a juristic person capable of holding property and the property dedicated to the temple vested in the deity. If the main worshippers are the members of the public who worship as a matter of right then the real purpose is to confer benefit on God. The mere fact that members of a community are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members have a right to worship in the idol. [829 E] 3:1 The bare fact that the interests of the appellants and the palwars were specified individuals, in the latter they are the general public or a section of the same and not a determinate body of individuals as a result of which the remedies for enforcement of charitable trust are somewhat different from those which can he availed of by beneficiaries in a private trust. The members of one institution may not be debarred from entering the temple but their entry into the temple is not as of right. [826 F] 3 :2 An organisation has been created between two different communities in regard to the religious offerings and the ownership of endowment and its administration. It is a contingent provision and here also, the founder did not confer the duty of performing all the work on the members and hence they chose or selected only a particular person belonging to a particular community which also shows that even if the family were to become extinct, the private nature of the endowment could not be changed.

The appellant Bank instituted a suit against the respondent Bank for recovery of money due to the banks and buildings. On September 11, 1952 the attorneys were appointed by the appellant to be the attorney 'for the purpose of carrying out the terms of the arrangement more effectively and to secure the interest of the attorney. The power of attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorney R had agreed to finance contracts and to advance money to the appeLlant for collection. " The document appointed the appellant as attorney 's attorneys of Malhotra "to present and submit supply bills regarding our contracts to the proper officer and/or authority of the Government Departments concerned, to obtain cheques for sums payable to us under the contract directly in their own name or in our name in payment of such bills or other amounts and to cash and to receive the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards repayment of the advances made or to be made hereafter and all other monies due from us to the attorney in any account what soever. " On July 19, 1948 the appellant made out a bill on the military authorities for Rs. 49,633/8/7 then due to him in respect of his supplies under the contracts during 1945 46 and handed over the bill to the appellant for collection, but before the appellant received payment, the amount due under the bill was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained by it against Malhotra. The respondent Bank filed objections in the execution proceedings which were dismissed. On December 12, 1952, the appellant filed a suit in the court of first Additional District Judge Jabalpur against the bank and Takhat Mal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhat had no right to attach it. The trial Court held that the respondent bank was the assignee of a bill and decreed the suit. On appeal by the Bank, the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit filed by the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) An agreement to finance the borrower and a power of Attorney even date to receive monies due to it under certain contracts had the effect of an equitable assignment of the funds. The law on the subject admits of no doubt. [702] (ii) The relationship of the two parties, a payment order and an assignment created an interest in the fund and was not revocable. Read in the light of the power of one attorney the endorsement on the bill dated July 19 1948 created an interests in a specific fund and it was irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment in favour of the appellant. The High Court was clearly in error in holding that there was no equitable assignment. [759E] (iii) An assignment creates interest in a fund and is not rev executable.

Section 17(1)(iv) of the Income tax Act, 1961 provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax under that head if it is not chargeable to incometax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E ' were brought to tax under section 56. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. But the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Act. It further held that the income in ques tion was exempt from tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD : The High Court erred in arriving at that conclusion. [ 439 A] 382 B] Accordingly the word "profits" used in section 13(2)(iv), must be read as including any "profits in lieu of or in addition to any salary or wages". In view of the fact that the assessee was not represented before this Court it is obvious that the meaning of section '17(3)(ii) was plain and unambiguous. Accordingly there is no need to call into aid any rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [439 C] The respondent was not heard. Therefore the appeal must succeed.

In Bihar there is a total ban on the slaughter of all categories of animals of the species of bovine cattle which includes buffaloes (male or female adult and calves) irrespective of their age or usefulness. In order to secure the preservation of stock and in the State it was provided that the imprisonment for slaughter of she buffalo (cattle and buffaloes) cannot be renewed except in accordance with the provisions of article 19 (1) (g). The Bihar Act makes no distinction between she buffaloes, bulls and bullocks (c cattle and sheep) which are useful as milch or breeding or draught animals and those which are not and indiscriminately prohibited slaughter of her buffaloes, bull bulls and working bullocks (dattle and buffalo) without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age and usefulness, though not a complete stoppage, of the business of a considerable section of the people who are by occupation butchers (Kasais). The present Act has been made in implementation of the directive principles laid down by article 48. By virtue of this provision the Bihar Act was amended from time to time and it was continued by the State of Bihar. Since the Bihar Legislature had not enacted any law in respect of the subject, the present enactments infringe the fundamental rights under article 19(1))(g). Held, that the Bihar Acts were constitutionally valid and must be declared invalid. The Bihar Acts imposed a total prohibition on the slaughtering of all animals belonging to the species and those who slaughter 25,02,000 bovines cattle (battle and sheep), without prescribing anything as to its age or capacity. They infringe article 19, ,(1)(g) and was unconstitutional in so far as it prohibited the slaughter Of cows of all ages and calres of cows and cales of buffaloes, male and female, Counsel for the petitioners were right when they attacked the validity of the Act. The impugned Acts created an apprehension that a total number ban on slaughter of prescribing milk or keeping cattle (c continuously as well as sheep) was also reasonable and valid and was in consonance with the directive principle laid down in article 48, and was therefore void.

The respondent company was a public limited Company having its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh and its Manager, and Assistant Manager. Under the Central Provinces and Berar Industrial Disputes Settlement Act 1947 (C.P. and Berar Act XXl of 1947) the expression " Standing Orders " means rules relating to matters set out in the Schedule, and section 3 requires that within six months from the date on which the central Act becomes applicable to an industrial establishment the employer shall submit to the certifying officer five copies of the draft proposed Standing Orders proposed by him for adoption in his industrial establishment. The respondent submitted his explanation on December 1, 1955, in which he said that the charge was vague and that after 1949 he was not in any way concerned with the preparation of summaries and annual statements of accounts of the consumers department; that after the company had been receiving a basic salary of Rs. 245 per month; that he was also not in a position to know why certain double adjustments had been made in the accounts of 1954 relating to the consumers ' department, and that as regards the issue of certain bills, the charge being vague, and (1) the Standing Orders did not apply to him. The management by an order dated December 5, 1955 terminated his services with effect from January 31, 1956, but on January 2, 1956 the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court at Nagpur praying for the issue Of appropriate writs or directions quashing the orders of suspension and termination. The preliminary objection taken were these: (1)(a) that the Standing Order did not applies to its employees who did not possess tickets or to whom tickets had not been issued, and consequently his case was governed by the provisions of the local Act and on a breach thereof the respondent bad a right to move the High court under article 32 Of the Constitution for quashing the order passed against him or for reinstatement, etc. Held: (i) The Standing Orders appear to have applied to the employees working in their establishments in respect of matters which were required to be dealt with by Standing Orders. They do not therefore make a distinction between an employee who marks his attendance and another who presents his ticket, card or token; (ii) if they apply to those employees only to whom seats have been issued; but such inclusion is not an essential characteristic of an employee. The essential content of the definition of an 'employee ' is employment in the Office, Mains Department, eta., of the Company either at Nagpur orAIR and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order No. 16.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by the Government Company, viz., Hindustan Steel Ltd. Alloy steel Project was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1967 68. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under Payment of Bonus Act (Act 21 of 1965) in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either the Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into the production. The Tribunal took the view that the word Establishment ' had been used in section 2(15) of the , to indicate a "Company" as called in common parlance and that it had to be treated as an establishment separate from Hindustan Steel Limited, that under the proviso to section 3 the Alloy iron Project was to be held as a separate part of the parent establishment owned by the company only for the purpose of computation of bonus under .the Act; that, even the establishment employing less than 20 persons will be a part of it, and consequently, a reference was made under the which came up before the Ninth Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal. The main basis of the decision is that 'the word establishment ' has been used to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . Section and that sections 3(3) and 16(1) were applicable even to new departments, undertakings or branches set up by existing establishments. A further contention was raised on behalf of the workmen, that if an establishment of a Company consists of a number of departments, undertaking or branches, the principal part of section 3 will apply and all such departments, Undertakings or branches must be treated to as parts of one single establishment for purposes of computation, of bonus. The appellant company relied on section 3 of the Act to urge that even the employment less than 5 persons would be a unit separate from the other units; and that if section 3(15). is applicable the Bonus Act will apply to establishments consisting of different departments, companies, undertakings etc. By its petition under article 32 the workmen sought computation of their bonus at five per cent on the basis of consolidated profits as envisaged by section 6(d) read with the Third Schedule thereto. The Company contested these pleas. It was urged that a company in one of these two categories, namely Hindustan Steel Company Ltd., could not be treated separately as an "establishment" because under the Act, a company is itself an establishment, so it can be treated only as part of its parent establishment.

The appellant Sugar Industry is a "processing of vegetable product" within the meaning of Entry 15 of Schedule I. The State Government, by a notification dated March 31, 1977 issued under Article 252 of the Constitution with a view to control pollution of river rivers and streams which has assumed great importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urbanation is an activity in the nature of treatment of vegetable products industry. The Act was intended to ensure that the domestic and industrial affluence are not allowed to be discharged into water coars without adequate treatment. This Act is now in force in almost all States and in Union Territories. The main grievance of the appellant (abhavia/s) is that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "process ing vegetable products". It was contended on behalf of the ap pellant that since it falls under item No. 15 which is "processed of vegetable oil industry", it has to be judged normally by what that industry produces mainly. Whether a particular industry falls within the realm of taxation, must be judged by the predominant purpose and process and not by any ancillary or incidental process carried on by a particular Industry in running its business. The respondent State 's contention was that sugar chal lenged item 15 as 'processing vegetable products" and that it could not be given the meaning to the word "vegetable ' as defined in Section 2(c) of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contention is untenable and must fail. [528G] 1.2 In interpreting the word 'veget able ' it is not possible to conclude sugar cane as vegetable because the word vegetable in the context does not attract the botanic meaning. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within entry 15 of List I. [540C D] 1:3 It is a transformation of an article which is commercially different from the one which is converted. The essence of manufacture is the change of one object to another for the purpose of making it marketable. In the context in which the word is used in Entry 15 'veholdgetable product means product of or made out ofulgues, fruit." [540B] 1 :4 An analysis of items 19 and 20 shows that Sugar mill is one of the main source of causing water pollu tion and since it is based generally on how the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it This Court in State of West Bengal & Ors. vs Washi Ahmed etc. ; , with reference to the meaning thereof will include sugar cane which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude.

The respondent an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises and filed an affidavit in support of the said application. The petition was contested on the grounds that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of section 10(3) (a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960. It was further contended that the Court should favour a construction which would be beneficient to the tenant. The Appellate Authorities passed an order of eviction against the appellant on the finding that the respondent bona fide required the accommodation for carrying on its profession as the advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The tenant appealed by special leave to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 There is no reason why a landlord who is a member of the legal or medical professions and who requires the premises For carrying on , the practice for his profession should be wholly debarred from obtaining possession of the premises. It would indeed be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and section 10 (1) which bars the eviction of tenants apply to nonresidential buildings owned by an Advocate but not section 10 of the Rent Control legislation. [14 F G] 2.

The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant plaintiff claimed that it was money lent under an agreement which was payable on demand and so it was bound to pay the loan along with interest. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree. On appeal by certificate to this Court on behalf of the appellant, it was contended : (i) Article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 was the relevant Article because if was a case of money deposited under an Agreement that it Was payable on ' demand and therefore limitation would commence from the date of demand; and (ii) Article 61 of that Limitation Act could not be invoked by the appellant. HELD : (1) The respondent was entitled to the amount above mentioned in the award since there were common partners in various businesses in which the Singhania and Gupta group were common. [578 F] (2)(a) It is an inherent case where money was deposited under agreement that it would be paid on demand. The question whether a transaction is clothed with the character of a deposit of money can depend on facts of each particular case whether the transaction is embodied in a document or in a letter written by him, and the surrounding circumstances at the time of the transaction, the pecuniary position of the respondent are all overwhelming features to adjudats the oral as well as the documentary evidence of the respondents that the amount was deposited with the appellant and that the pecuniary condition for which he made entries in the pass book of the assessee is magnified. [577 C] (b) The finding regarding payment of money by way of deposit has evidentiary value to show as to how the parties treated and understood their financial dealings. It is also important that when the respondent demanded money by a letter dated 27 April 1953 (exhibit 7), it was not open to him to complain of lack of proof of account books when the documents are shown to the witness in cross examination. [576 C] V. E. A. Annamalai Chettiar & Anr. vs section V. section Veerappa Chettiar, I.L.R. , Subbaih Chetty & Ors. vs Visalakshgi Achi, ; Babu Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., A.I.R., (1869) 7 M.I,A. 279, referred to.

The detenu was detained by an order passed on May 2, 1986 made in exercise of powers vested under Section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The writ petition filed against this order had been dismissed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that (i) on February 22, 1987, he was taken into custody around 2.00 p.m. on 27th February, 1986; and on March 3, 1987 the order of detention was passed and since the detenu was already in jail custody, the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for put ting him back in jail; (ii) the period of parole had to be excluded in recokning the period. Allowing the writ petition this Court HELD: 1.1 From the facts and circumstances emerging in the case it is clear that the detenue 's detention was effected on May 3, 1986, in course of investigation of the case. He was produced before the Magistrate and an order was made requiring him to be produced next day in the court. By the time the order came to be made, the detenu had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him. At the relevant time, the petitioner was under trial in the said criminal case. On such facts it was the contention of the peti tioner that the order, of preventive detention could only he justified against the person in deten tion if the detention authority was satis fied that his detention was necessary to prevent the detenu from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order after his release on the termination of the security proceedings under the Code. [848 C] 1.2 When these contentions are advanced no specific provision has been made for summons in the Customs ACt &, therefore, the provisions of Section 61 of the Code of Criminal Procedure will be applicable.

The President is now pleased to decide that the rates of daily wage for the semi skilled, skilled/sskilled Labour who has not completed 7 days of Service over ay period of 3 years, or more, with the Department as on 2 4 1980 and 1st April 1981 respectively will take effect from 1st May, 1980 (viii) A review would be carried out every year as on the Ist of April for making officials eligible for wages indicated in para (ii) and (iii) above. " In respect of categories (ii), and (iv) i.e., for those who have completed7 days of continuous service for purpose of payment of different rates of pay is equally untenable.

The Income tax Officer, while examining the books of account of a partnership firm found that in one account year there were six cash credits aggregating to Rs. 59,026 in the name of the assessee 's wife and that before, however, he included certain sums in the total income of the assesses and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as well the Tribunal rejected his contentions but the High Court on appeal reversed this view of the Tribunal. Held, that the Income tax Act provides a time limit in sub sections (1) and (2) and the failure or omission occurs when that period passes, but sub section (3), allows a locus poenentiae before the assessment is actually made. The notice under section 22(1) can be issued only after the expiry of four years from the end of the year in which income, profits or gains were first assessable. In other words, it could not be said that even a return filed in compliance with a notice under s.22(2), if filed belatedly under section 24(2) would have been sufficient, though for the period mentioned in the proviso to sub section(3) of section 34 had expired. It was open to him, if there was sufficient justification for it, to hold that the amount noted in the footnote was really the assessee his income, in which case an assessable income would have escaped assessment for any year and he might entertain a return showing an income below the taxable limit. The only question is whether the notice issued under section 34(1), was valid in law or not. Having regard to the terms of the section it could be held that a person who had no such income need not make a return, and if he does make a statement, it is not a return which need be considered, being not a ' return in law. The fact of a return under section 23 (1), is an additional stage of assessment for the purpose of determining whether there was a failure or non production of evidence. While the Queen vs Duke , distinguished and explained. Commissioner of Income tax vs Sultan Ali Gharami ; , applied. In the instant case it was open for him, therefore, to raise a contention that the return was not a true one, and fell within the mischief of cl. (c) of sub section. (1).

Clause 3 of Chapter II of the Scheme, which provides: "The Central Government may make a scheme for carrying out the provisions of this Act. The Central Govern ment has framed a scheme providing for appointment to the Board from amongst the specified categories either by election or by nomination where that mode is more appropriate. But the legislature has left it to the Central Govern tion to specify by a scheme the manner in which the election or nomination is to be conduct ed, bearing in mind the true character and objective of the banking industry and its distinguishing features as a highly sensitive commercial enterprise. Neither the election nor the nomination should be conducted in a manner unmindful of the distinctiveness of the Indian banking industry. What is postu lated is such election or nominations as would lend to the Boards of Directors its truly representative character in consonance with the extremely delicate, vital and significant role of the Banking industry in the context of national policy and objectives and economic development. The method of election or tion must, therefore, be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking Industry and the choice of the mode is generally a matter for decision by the Central Government. The discretion as to the mode of representation is, of course, left to the central Govern ment, but it is not an unrestrained or unrestricted discretion, but a discretion which must be reasonably exercised so as to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to its composition of the Board of Directors. The object of the Act is to nationalise the banks in order to, as stated in the preamble to the Act, "control the heights of the economy and to meet progressively, and serve better, the needs of development of the country in conformi ty with the national policyand objectives". The very purpose of the legislation is to enable the Central Gov ernment to specify the manner for which the elections or nomination was to be conducted, bearing, in mind, the true nature and objective result of the scheme.

Section 220 (6) of the Income tax Act, 1961 provides that where an assessee has presented an appeal under section 246(1) , the Appellate Tribunal shall have power to regulate its own procedure and the procedure of Benches thereof in all matters arising out of the exercise of its powers or of the discharge of its functions including the places at which the Benches shall hold their sittings. Under section 220 (11), the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income Tax Officer only when an appeal had been presented under section 254 which will be to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and not to the Tribunal. For all the reasons given above, the appeal must fail. The appellant contended that : (i) the power to stay was a necessary corollary to the power under section 255(1); and (ii) since the Income. tax Officer and the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner have made assessments or imposed penalties raising considerable demands and if the Appellate Court is entirely helpless in the matter of stay or recovery, the entire purpose of the appeal can be defeated if ultimately the orders of the departmental authorities are set aside. ^ HELD: (1) By the provisions of section 254, the power conferred on the Income_tax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. [69 F] (2) The power of suspension by treating an assessee as non being in service during the pending appeal has accrued only when a strong prima facie case was made out that the Tribunal will consider whether to stay the recovery proceedings and on what conditions and the stay would be granted in most deserving and appropriate cases where the Tribunal is satisfied that the entire object of the appealed will be frustrated or rendered nugatory by allowing the recovery proceed ings to continue during the course of the appeals. [70 G] (3) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate,Tribunal with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise and of those powers fully effective. [71 F H; 71 A B] (4) The Appellate Tribunal is not a court but it exercises judicial powers. The Tribunal 's power in dealing with appeals is of the widest amplitude and has in some cases been held similar to and identical with the powers of an appellate Court under the Civil Procedure Code. [72 C D] (5) The High Court was wrong in holding that it had no power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Police Force on December 1, 1945. The Deputy Inspector General of Police who conducted the trial held that seven out of nine charges had been established and that 7 out of the nine charges, had been proved, that the respondent had accepted bribes in his discharge of his duties; that though he was a habitual bribetaker, he had on nine occasions, particulars of which were given in the charge accepted b rupees. The respondent submitted his explanation and after considering the explanation of the respondent dismissed him from service with effect from the said date. Thereafter he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Allahabad. A Single Judge of the High COurt allowed the petition, inter alia, on the ground that the information about commission of offences was not in the first instance received by the Magistrate and forwarded to the police for inquiry. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the Respondent in regard whereto he magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage. If so, the question is whether para. 486 would govern the present inquiry or it would fall out side its scope. C.A. 119/58 (ii) In view of this finding it would be hypertechnical to hold that there was no magisterial enquiry in respect Of the matter which was the subject matter of the departmental trial. On the facts, therefore, it would not be desirable for the State Government or the Inspector General to follow the alternative procedure prescribed by para 486(3) of the Police Regulations but in view of the fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the question, if substantially the subject matters of magisterial Inquiry and the departmental enquiry is the same; (iii) The Superintendent of Police was authorized to follow them the alternative standard procedure prescribed for holding a departmental trial in respect thereof and other new charges, that he had been charged with cognizable offences and therefore the enquiry held without following the procedure prescribed under para 489(2).

The appellant, a highly qualified ophthalmic surgeon feeling aggrieved by the promotion of respondents 4 to 24, though convinced that even if the Court were to accede to his request, he was in no way likely to be benefited by this bizarre exercise. 51 First, the situation was that the 19 unspecified Specialists ' posts and unspecified posts, 28 in number, could be filled in from those belonging to specialists ' grade. The promotion of Respondents 4 to 26 was challenged by the appellant on diverse grounds but the principal contention was that their promotions were in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules. The main contention was (1) that since the initial constitution of service on September 9, 1966 any future promotion to supertime grade II from departmental candidates could be made from amongst those originally belonging to Specialists Grade, ipso facto they could only be filled by promotion and not either by direct nomination or by transfer; and (2) that it was violative of rule 4(3). The respondents contended that the posts were created in specialists " grade" and the strength of Specialists grade posts was reduced by 28 whenever any post out of these 28 posts added to super time grade II was required to be filled, it can only be done from amongst candidates belonging to the specialists Grade. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the promotion order, ^ HELD: (1)(a) It is crystal clear that when a post from amongst unspecified specialists" posts is converted into a specified post and assigned to a speciality it can be filled In either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But, it was very strenuously contended on behalf of the appellant that whenever an unspecifiedspecialists ' post is converted from a specified cadre, it could only have been filled in by promotion from amongst the those originally belonged to Specialist Grade, that is, category I consisting of Specialist Tacter ' and General Duty Officers grade I. [88G H; 89A B] (b) The Central Government in implementing the rule has understood and in fact implemented the rule to this effect that whenever any unspecifiedSpecialists ' Service post is conversion into a certain specified post it can, only be filling in by promotions from amongst persons who might be promoted from General Duty Officer Grade I because General Duty officers Grade 1 are also promotable to superje grade II. The contention was, therefore, rightly rejected by the Central Government.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country, is one of the States where land reform laws are likely to generate great changes by banning big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a few feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform which special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. Naturally the State enacted the Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others peasant proprietorship created. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, though its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before us arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: A thumb nail sketch of the (the Act) is a prefatory necessity. The defines 'small land owner ' '[section 2(2)] having in mind the optimum ownership in the given conditions. 'Permissible area ' [section 2 (3)] is a cognate concept limiting the maximum permissible extent a person may hold and so long as he does not have any excess, he is a small landholder. He can evict the tenants from his holding and bein actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. However, he was given the option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' ' [Section 2(4)] and then he must make available to the State such excess called surplus area as are; under clause (a) of section 10 A or for such other purposes the State Government may by notification direct. The legislature has been amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High court has upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. The marginal note appended to section 2(5) is that 'the surplus area shall be at the disposal of the State Govern ment for utilization under section 10A or for any other purpose notified by Government". The legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible limit and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of law will go to feed the surplus pool. [620H; 633A B] Amar Singh vs State of Haryana, ; , followed. The legislative command is that if the constitutionally envisioned socio economic revolution is not to be a paper tiger, agrarian laws have to be meaningfully enacted, interpreted and executed and the court is not the anti hero in the drama of limping land reform.

The appellants and certain other persons instituted an action in the Court of the Additional District Judge, Chanda for a decree for possession of property within two months of the passing of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951. The question that arose was whether the Zamindari was impartible and that the decision of the Compensation Officer became final and conclusive against the appellants because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two yeks from the date thereof and the plaintiffs were on that account not entitled to claim the compensation paid or payable in respect of the Malguzari lands. The trial court held that the decree was genuine while the will was, set up by the defendants with regard to the Malpali land which vested in consequence of the enactment of theMadhya Pradesh Abolition Of Proprietary Rights Act 1of 1951. In appeal the High Court, however, agreed with the Trial Court and held that on the facts no suspicion as to the genuineness of the will dated December 3, 1950 arose. Held, further, that the villages in question were impartible within the meaning of cl. 5 of the Chanda Patent of 1949 and were confirmed in 1867 in favour of Sitaram. The right to determine it is true vests in the Governor but the power is exercisable in accordance with and not in violation of the custom of the family. When a holder of the Zamindari is removed, the Governor is bound to hand over the Zamindari to the next heir in the order of succession if the Zamindar removed had died. But if the nearest male relative in the line of succession is not selected the estate must be given to the nearest heir who has the prescribed qualifications and is a successor to the Zamindar. In adjudging the plaintiffs claim, the Court must determine whether Pratapshah father of the plaintiffs was the nearest female male relative of Amarshah. The contest between them had to be adjudged in the light of the rules of lineal primogeniture governing an impartible estate which are well established: Succession is governed by the rules which govern succession to partible property subject to such modifications only as flow from the character of the impartible Estate; the only modification which impartibility suggests in regard to rights of succession was the existence of a special rule for the selection of a single heir when there were several heirs of the same class who would be entitled to succeed to the property if it were partible under the general Hindu law; and in the absence of a statutory custom, the rule of primogen Procedure furnishing a ground of preference.

Section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provides that where there is a dispute as to the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under sub section(3). In a suit for recovery of possession based on arrears of rent, the court must grant relief only after granting leave to appeal to the High Court. When a tenant fails to deposit such amount or pay and raises a dispute which distinctly attracts the provisions of the Act, he can file an application in terms of Section 11(3), within one month from the date of service of the notice. The time prescribed for filing written statements expires on March 31, 1956. In any case no decree for eviction shall be passed in a suit if, on the first day of hearing of the suit or on or before such other date as the Court may, fix, the tenant pays or tenders in Court the standard rent and permitted increases then due and thereafter continues to pay or tender in court regularly such rent and allowed increases till the suit is finally decided and also pays costs of the trial as directed by the Court. Section 12(4) provides for an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court periodically, such amount as it considers proper as interim standard rent, or at the option of the tenant make an order to pay to the landlord such amount thereof as the court may specify, pending final decision of the application. Under section 12 if any application for fixing the standard standard rent is made by a tenant who has received a notice from the landlord under sub s.(2) of s 12, the Court shall forthwith specify the amount and such amount together with interest as the rent or per reduced increases which are to be deposited in Court by the tenant and make an Order directing the tenants to pay the rent within such time as may be allowed by it. The appellant contended that the dispute concerning standard rent was one which must have been raised before service of notice on the tenant, and since there was admittedly no dispute in regard to standard rent nor permitted increases at the date when service of a notice under s 12(2) or section 12( 3) (b), it could not be said that the respondent did not comply with the provisions and therefore there was a dispute. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The contention that the suit concerning standard tenant is one which is in existence at the time when the notice terminating the tenancy was issued by the appellant cannot be accepted. Section 11 of the Urban Rent Control Act lays down an embargo on exercise of such powers. if the tenant raises a question of law, he has to approach the Court with special leave and not without the permission of the court. [636 G] The power conferred on the Court is a judicial one and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. It can be exercised only by a person who acts judicially in accordance with the statute. In the present case, after notice was issued, the suit for ejectment was filed within the time contemplated by Explanation 1 to section 12 on March 1, 1956, even if the appellant had raised a dispute about standard rent he could not raise the question of breach of such right.

By article 90 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Company by one of its Directors. The appointment was to vote and/or from time to time appoint a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Limited in respect of shares so held by it in another company. Under article 90 for a period of five years, where a company registered under the provisions Of the Indian Companies Act or not is a member of this company a person duly appointed to represent such company at a meeting of which he represents as if he were an individual member of that company including the power to appoint a proxy whether special or General and the production at the meeting of a company of such resolution appointing such representative duly signed by one director of such company and by the secretary (if any) and certified by them or as being a true copy of the resolution shall on production at a meet be accepted by this company as sufficient evidence of the validity of his appointment. The claim was rejected by the Excess Profits Tax Officer. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner affirmed the decision of the Excess profits tax Officer. Held: (i) Where a shareholder holding the majority of shares authorizes an agent to vote in respect thereof by him, the agent acquires no interest, legal or beneficial, in the shares. The control remains vested in the shareholders. The shareholder may revoke the authority of the agent at any time, but in spite of the appointment of the Agent the shareholder may himself appear at the meetings and cast his votes personally. Therefore, the shares being always subject to his will and ordering, the controlling interest which the holder of the majority share has never passed to the agent. (ii) If he acts in breach of his duty, nevertheless as long as his authority is not revoked, as far as the respondent Company is concerned, the directors, of the company in fact control its affairs at general meetings and as such have "a controlling interest" therein, no matter by what machinery or means that result has been effected.

The Mysore State Electricity Board is constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply.) Act. It is governed by the Indian electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. On 1st October, 1957 the Mysore State Electrici ty Board was constituted under an Electricity ( Supply) Act with effect from that date. In 1960 the respondent opted to the Services under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect From that date he was allotted to the new State of Mysore. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former State of El g erabad. On 29th December, 1966, a circular was issued by the Board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Govern ment referred to in the Resolution itself and by the said order it provided that unless in the Recruitment Rules relating to the service concerned Depart mental Examination had been incorporated and prescribed and unless it was clearly specified for what purpose the tests were prescribed viz., whether for increments or promotions, the passing of Departmental Examination cannot be legally insist ed upon for grant of increments or for according promotion to higher posts. The respondent who held the post held before 1st March, 1970, but before that date opted to continue in the service under the. Board and continued in the Government service. After an enquiry the respondent applied to the Board for relaxa tion on the ground of inordinate delay and laches. The Board rejected his application. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the writ petition could not be thrown out on the grounds of inordinate fice and laches on the part of the respondent and allowed the writ in limine. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. A Resolution was not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the resolution the inference that the allottees are exempt ed from passing the examination is not justified. [511 E F] 2. The resolution dated 5th January, 1970 cannot be understood as altering the position existing "as before". This reasoning is erroneous for for, as pointed out by us earlier Resolution was never intended to covers a case of appli cation allottees and mere because the allottee were excluded fr om operation of it the inference was not justified [511 G H] 3.

% The petitioner 's son, namely, the respondents was taken in police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6 on a railway track near some distance from the railway station. On the night between the 1st and 2nd December, 1987, the deceased came to know that certain dead body of her son Suman Behera was found on the Railway track near a bridge at some distance, from the Jaraikela Railway Station, failing which he had escaped from police custody. The allegation made is that it is a case of custodial death since the deceased died as a result of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police detention. Since this was done in view of the vehemence with which the learned Additional Solicitor General urged, the Court awarded compensation towards the petitioner for violation of the fundamental right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. Allowing the petition and directing the State to pay monetary compensation and also by way of exemplary costs or otherwise, taking this power to be settled by the decisions in Kasturilal upholding the State 's plea of sovereign immunity for tortious acts of its servants is confined only to a declaration that there has been contravention and infringement of the guaranteed fundamental rights. This is how the Court has decided in the instant case whether it was a case or not of custodial murder but of death of the deceased whose fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the constitution, which is invoked by this Court or under Article 32 of the Consti tution, for enforcement of fundamental rights, is confined to the sphere of liability in tort, which a person is entitled to claim under Section 6, and may well be the only practicable form of redress, as by now it is in the case of any violation of constitutional rights.

The two prisoners have been sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, we would like to observe that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, which includes freedom of press is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. The Press itself has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President was rejecting the petitions before the President earlier. Hence this petition under article 32 of the constitution by the Chief Reporter of the Hindustan Times, Smt. Prabha Dutt praying for a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ or direction directing the respondents particularly the Delhi Administration and the Superintendent of Jail, Tihar to allow her to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of death. Disposing of the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no reason why the petitioner should not be allowed to interview them. While considering merits of an application for commutation, there will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed on behalf of the respondents and therefore it does not see any reason why newspapermen who can broadly, and we suppose without great fear of contradiction, be termed as friends of the society be denied the right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549. [1187 C E] 2. The constitutional right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right asserted by her is not a fundamental right nor it confers any right upon the press, to have a unrestricted access from means of Information through the medium of an interviews of the two prisoners who are sentenced to imprisonment for life. [1108 B] 3. Rule 549(4) provides that no newspapermen should be allowed. However, in the instant case, the petitioner has been asked for permission for interview the prisoner right since his President rejected the petitions on the grounds that the prisoners are willing to be interviewed.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden of the estate. The Bank applied for the appointment of a Receiver but he was allowed to do so. On February 26, 1950 the tea garden was damaged by fire which destroyed over 3,000 tea saplings. On receipt of the application from the appellant, the District Judge transferred the mortgage suit to the Court of the Subordinate Judge on May 31, 1956. The transferee court was created under the order of 1950 which came into force on December 31, 1950. Before this could be done, a successor of the District judge who was seized of the suit and who transferred it to the Subordinate judge under the Tripura (Courts) Order of 1950. By virtue of section 150, the Subordinate Court was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of the enforcement of the bond as the District Court himself. The surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District court if he had rendered itself liable under the terms of the surety bond. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 30, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. On October 4, 1961, the appellant filed an appeal against that order but it was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner on December 18, 1959. On January 20, 1950, the respondent filed a petition before the Judicial Com missioner, Tripura seeking (i) that execution do issue against the appellant as directed in the Court; and (ii) under the deed of mortgage dated February 10, 1943 he was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea gardens by fire. The learned Judicial Commissioner rejected the objections and directed that the damages awarded may be recovered from the respondent. On appeal by special leave, HELD : Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other court, the transferee Court has the same power and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The bond was a part of the proceedings pending before a District Judge and on the transfer of the Suit the entire proceeding including the bond. stood validly transferred to the court of the subordinate Judge. [359H] Under section 151(c) of the C.P.C., save as expressly otherwise provided by, where, where a business of which any Court was transferred to another court, a transferee Court had the same right powers and is also entitled to performing the same functions as those conferred and impose by the code upon the transferee court.

The appellants who are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat and paid the price for them, were assessed under section 2(h) of the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the Act on 'sale ' as defined in section 2 (h), but the High Court held that the sales made to the appellants ' were 'sales, and assessed them to sales tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants: (i) that under the U .P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order 1959, only a thing, the absolute or general property in which is transferred from the seller to the buyer; and (ii) that 's sales made by them were not 'dischargeable because there was no 'sale" within the meaning of the Act. HELD: (1) The levy order passed by the Sales Tax Commissioner could not have been issued under clause 10B because the shop in question was a factory zone. [669C] In the case before the Court there was nothing to show that the Sales tax payer supplied certain steel products to various persons in the State pursuant to the directions of the Iron and Steel Controller made under cl. 10B of the Order. The order passed on the application of the State Government did not amount to an offer. [689C] (2) The Powers given by cl. 2 of the order were wide enough to cover transactions relating to supply of cane was not ruled out. Under the Act 45 of 1961 and the rules framed thereunder, the cane grower in the factory zone was free to make or not to make an offer of sale of cane to the occupier of a factory. It did not envisage any consensual arrangement. The agreement by the State of its requirement of sugar to the controller or communication of the allotment order to the assessee did not indicate any consensual agreement. Therefore, the acceptance thereof did not result in a contract of sale. [682D] (3) Although the power given by the Iron & Steel Controller had been delegated under cl.(5) of section 21 of the East Punjab Essential Articles Control and Distribution) Order with a view to securing compliance with this order or to satisfying himself that this order had been complied with, the operation of clause 3 of the Control Order was not affected. The power of taxation conferred by cls.

Allowing the appeal and quashing the order of detention, it was ^ HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are tO strictly complied with if any value is to be attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution al rights guaranteed to him in that regard. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to he made within three weeks of the detention, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it was within three months from the date of the second order of deten tion. [205F G] 2. When the report of the advisory board is obtained before the expiry of three months of the subsequent order of detain ment, where the earlier order of his arrest or beyond the period of three ye ars beyond the prescribed period, is revoked and a fresh order of confinement was made on the same facts on thesame day. Section 15 has to yield. But by reading down the provision, the coll i sion may be avoided and section 15 may be sustained. So avoid ing the collision course it held that if the report is not made within 3 months of detention the detention became illegal notwithstanding the expiry that it is within three yea nt from the day of the first order of previ tating the case, where earlier order is revoked, and a subsequent order is made. [207H; 207A B] 3.1 When there is to. be a collision between article 22(4) of the Constitution and section 154 of the Act it has to be appreciated that if a reference is to an advisory Board is necessary to continue the detention of the person beyond the date on which its report or beyond, the period Or three months after the date o f detention are taken into consid eration. The procedure required in such cases would be strictly comply with if there was no difference in the procedure.

% The petitioner is the father of respondent. Both of them are established Vaidyas in Rajkot. They come from a well to do family. The respondent was advanced in age and both the father and the son have been fighting between themselves since more than a decade. The High Court found that the suit was barred as res judicata for setting aside the decree passed in Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977 on 23rd February, 1988 as it is stated by the arbitrator that he had called both the mother and the child at his residence on 18th January, 1977. This letter also stated that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the petitioner and the respondent agreed to such entrustment. Thereafter followed a spell of litigation. The parties filed an application before the court for setting it aside the award under Section 17 of the , and obtained directions from the Court regarding payment of interest on the amount awarded to the respondent. During the course of the execution proceedings, the appellant made an award dated 18th February, 1977, which was signed by both the parties as well as their respective advocates. The agreement was in the form of a letter addressed to the arbitrator wherein it was stated that both of them had appointed him as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them and that he has given an award on 20th January 1977 in respect of which award, there had been continued objections but now they have agreed that both the petitioner should abide by the award dated 20th February. 1977 and that its interpretation would be binding on both the party. The court held that the First Appeal and Civil Revision Application were withdrawn and the judgment of the trial Court on 23/2.1988 became final. The main objection to the award was that there was no written agreement signed by two parties, which is stated in the application to file the award, that the arbitrator had called all the father & the son at his office on 18.1.1977, and that the petition was not filed within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award; (2) the time for making an application to set aside the Award had expired and no such application was made, and (3) the award had not been remitted under Section 16(5) of the Act. The learned trial Judge made a decree in terms of the order. On appeal, the High Court held that both parties had re affirmed the acceptance of the Award. Allowing Civil Revision application filed by the petitioner in this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitration of the named arbitrator and therefore their interpretation should be left to the Arbitrator himself. [539C D] 1.2 In view of the matter, it can certainly be construed to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms Of Section 2(a) of tho Act. In this case, there was not such express or implied prohibition nor any inability of the Judge concerned. In the instant case, on this aspect the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award.

The respondent was appointed receiver of the estate in question for a period of 999 years by the Court of Subordi nate Judge, Asansole. The Receiver with powers mortgaged these properties to the said firm as security for the due repayment of the loan advanced by that firm became the lessees for 999 one year. By various processes not necessary to be detailed, the appellants were declared the successors in interest of the mortgagors and they thereupon filed a suit against them claiming the mortgage money from out of court auction. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the decree holder had com preeded out of Court and the prayer for withdrawal of the attachment was merely consequential and would follow as a matter of course on full satisfaction of the decree being recorded. In execution a final decree for sale was made I on February 26, 1929. The respondent appealed to the High Court. It was contended that the order was substantially and correctly entered in column 20 of exhibit F which is a certified copy of extract from the Register of applications for executions of decrees relating to execution case No. 118 of 1936 and 675 of 1936 which contains an assignment of debt due under the original mortgage debt and of all the rights of the mortgagee, the position appeared to be free from difficulty. Held, that in dealing with a petition under section 36(5) of the , it is not necessary for the Court to consider the other question raised by the respondent on the strength of section 36 (5)of the Act and I express no opinion as to the con sideration which arises if the sub mortgage contains only a charge on the original mortgaged debt but when it contains an assign ment of that debt, and of certain rights such as the right transferred to a sub mortgagee under his sub modates not to the sub mortgagee and that the transferee still retains a legal (1) 64 I.A. 594 of the mort gage should be liable by privity of estate for the burdens of the lease.

On the death of his widow and sons, both the appellant and the respondents jointly executed a deed purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exts. A 1 and A 2). In 1947, after the execution of exhibit A 1 & A2 there was a disruption of the joint family and a severance of the Joint status between the parties. The appellant instituted against his widow N and sons for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the document dated April ' 15, 1945, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court dis missed the suit holding that the transfers were made by N, in favour of the appellant in view of past illicit cohabitation 45 with her, such past cohabitation was the motive and not consideration for the transfer under exhibit A I and PW 2. The High Court confirmed the decree but on a reference by the High Court, the High court held that the transferees were made in consideration of past cohabitations, having regard to section 2(d) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) the transfers which were effected by N in favour, were invalid because they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services; and (ii) the appellant were parties to an illicit intercourse. HELD: The appeals must be dismissed. There will be one set of costs and one hearing fee. [216F G] In 1.I.R. , 195, followed.

The respondent husband of the appellant was the wife of the deceased who died in the year 1962 and her heirs, after his death, filed a writ petition in the High Court for setting aside an order directing respondents to pay interest on the amount after maturity of the policies. The High Court held that the award of interest on first two policies from the date of their maturity till 31 12 1975 could not be made by the L.I.C., and since the said amounts were paid only on 5 1275 i.e., a few days before or after 5 1276 when the statement on oath under section 226(3) was made by it, it would fall within the ambit of section 281 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 till 5 12 75. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave against the said order of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. Under clause (vi) of sub section (1) of Section 226 of the 1922 Act, which came into force on 5 4 76, no further question survived in that writ petition and the consequent civil appeal in this Court since the further questions including payment of interest were to arise only at a subsequent stage. This writ petition had to be filed because in spite of the L .I. C., having made the requisite statement under section 227(3)(vi) the Income tax Act, was not made within two months. Such an objection is untenable. [543C E] 2. It was incumbent on the Ll.I C. to make the requisite state ment on oath in accordance with the section 226 (3)(vii) of the Act, within two reasonable time. performance of this statutory obligation by the respondent in exercise of its powers under section 225(1)(vi), as also that raising an objection about the amount payable against the policy to the L L.l.l lord C.P.C. cannot be said to have caused prejudice to personal liability as the defaulter of the income tax dues. [542D E] 3. The delay in making the requisite declaration under section 32(3), by the appellant, being after inordinate delay, award of Interest to the assignee of the policy, must be justified. [541G H] 4. Not providing for time, without objecting to the demand by denying its liability to the assessee, it could not make payment to the respondent, since it involved the risk of exposing the L 'I.c. or its officer making the statement, on oath, has to come to an end automatically and such a course is impermissible under law.

The appellant, a firm consisting of three branches of the United States, who was one of the Part B States of India, filed an application in this Court for the trans ference of certain properties enumerated under section 29(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, that is, proceedings under the , and the provisions contained in section 12(2): "that where any special or local law prescribes a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that Schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of Limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any specialor local law (a) the provisions Of this Act shall not apply." The appellant contended that under section 116A(2), a period different from that prescribed therefor ought to have been specifically provided for in that subsection, and an appeal under the Act would be deemed to be one in respect of such proceeding. Held: (1) that the expression "appeal" in article 156 of the , means an appeal governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, and is not introduced by the Indian . Limitation Act. (2)that the appeal contended for by the appellant was covered by cl. (a), and they were time to obtain a copy of the order appealed against; (3) that even if the appeal could be regarded as one falling within the first limb of section 29, sub section(2). was not attracted because it was enough if the special law prescribes for such an appeal a period limitation which is different from any period prescribed in the First Schedule. The word "actually" used in cl. 2 of article 156 refers to proceedings under special or municipal law but does not necessarily include proceedings under ordinary law, and therefore the suit would be governed by section 29 of the Limitation Act; and (4) that a finding laid down by this Court against the appellant on points of limitation was erroneous. Sections 29(1) and (3), sections 12(1), 12 and 10 of the . were clearly intended to be exhaustive and independent and separate, therefore the appeal should not be treated as one under article 156. This court held in Chiman Lal Das vs Lala Nachiappa Chettiar, A.I.R. 1955 Cal. 1002, that where a different period of time of limitation for appeal is expressly prescribed by the First Scheduled to the Limitation , that period of 60 days prescribed by section 116(1 ) will not apply and, as such, section was not ultra vires, it was not necessary in order to render the provisions relating to these matters, to which the first part did not apply.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, under which he purported to pass the impugned order. According to the appellant the power to fix any area as a bus stand was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having juris diction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. The District Magis trate imposed the impugned ord er on the appellant by holding that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand/halting place ', and that since the impugned orders did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get down and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as an bus stand. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the District Magigrate had no power to appoint any area in a regional area under section 76(1) of the . Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1. The City Area Committee can derive assistance from this rule. It only authorises the District Judge to exercise the powers under section 86(2)(rr) of tho Act which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Re porty as held by this Court in T.B. Ibrahim 's case [." The High Court was, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned decision passed by the District Collector.[717D E] 2.1 Section 76 of . is a complete code dealing with "control of traffic" conferred by section 76. It, therefore. cannot be said that the Town Area Committee could derive any assistance from the rule. [718 F] T.P. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Officer, Tanjore; ; and T.L.P.(C.) No. 501 of 1986 dated 27th April, 1988 referred to. 2.2 The District Magistrate had fixed the area within its jurisdiction as a Bus stand for purposes of the , and therefore, the order passed under that provision was open to revision under section 64A by the State Transport Authority.

Section 3 (1) of the , provides that if any person contravenes any order made under section 3 (a) he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and also be liable to fine. Section 7 states " Againstfeiture of certain property used in the commission of the offence, when any offence relates to foodstuffs which is punishable under s.7 has been committed the court shall direct that all the packages, coverings or receptacles in which they are found and any animal, vehicle vessel or other conveyance used in carrying the said property shall be forfeited to the Government: " The appellant 's truck was stopped at Samalkha Barrier. On the ground that it was a personal letter from one of the consignor and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commit it. The preparation consisted in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission which the offence has been com puted. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt to export goods, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit the offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the actor is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commissionof a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt fo commit it". Therefore the appellants should not have been convicted under section 7 of the .

The Sassoons agreed to transfer their Managing Agencies of the said Company to Messrs. Agarwal and Company, Chidambaram and Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd., for the years 1943 51 and 1943 respectively by letters dated the 3rd September, 1943, 16th April, 1943 and 27th April 1943 respectively. The Sassoon executed in favour of Messrs. G. M.
