Sen and Company obtained from them Rs. 57,80,000/ as remuneration for the period that they continued to be the Managing Agents and the transferees had rendered the services for the balance of the periods completed the full year of accounting, and had earned the proportionate commission and therefore the amount of commission which the latter actually received included the Sassoors ' share of the commission in respect of which they were not liable to tax but the Sassoonons. The Income Tax Officer included this sum as income in the hands of the Sascoons but the Tribunal rejected the claim on the ground that the Sasiffs earned by them was a source of income, and it was not exempt from taxation. The High Court on reference held that the Managing Agency Agreement was an indivisible contract for a whole year 's remuneration on the completion of a particular period of service and that as such it was to be considered as an income bearing asset. Held, further that the managing Agency Agreement in Agarwals case had been the effective source of the year 'T 's income and: the services so rendered were the source of his income. The fact that the assignor and the assignee are to be treated as one entity and that on assignment the assignee becomes the Managing Agent as if his name had been inserted in the Managing Office Agreement from the beginning, and that the continuity of the managing agency was preserved thereby and that whoever satisfies the description of the Managing Family Agent at the time when the commission for the year becomes due, is also the person entitled to the amount by way of remuneration not, as per section 26(2) of the Indian Income tax Act. Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Shaw Wallace & Co., (1922) L.R. 74 I.A. 105 and Dhakad Parshad Singh Deo vs State of Madhya Pradesh, (1933) L .R. 75 I. A. 95, relied on. Held further, that even though the terms of the agreements showed that the only effect thereof was to bring about the result specifically stated in the second portion of the clause 10 of the agreement that clause (which had been side lined) i.e., that on assigning, the assignee firm shall be entitled to demand and obtain from the principal company a fresh Managing Agency agreement in its own favour for the residue of the term outstanding and with like powers authorities remuneration and emoluments subject to the like terms and conditions, but the mere existence of a clause in a Managing Agency Contract between the principal and the agent entitles only the assignee to receive the year his remuneration and negativing to the assignmentor any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of income. No such right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee either, as part of the deed of transfer or independent thereof. In computing taxable income of the assignee can it reasonably be said that the remuneration for him is not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the remuneration of the years, such a right may be arise by reason of a mutual arrangement between the assigner and the benefit of the service rendered by him as Managing Agents of the Companies for the broken periods. Commissionerof Inland Revenue Ltd., Bombay vs The State of Bihar, , followed. C. Arton vs James, (1887) 13 I.T.R, referred to.

The appellant was a resident of something in Lucknow, and his wife (mother) was residing with his father. The other inmate of the house was the appellant 's second son, who died in August, 1963 while he was living with his brother. The only other inmate, of the residence was his first son, whose second son was employed in Lucknow. The appellant brought her buck and after some wordy altercation between them they slept in the room inside the house and came out at 60 'clock in the morning of August 13, 1963, and thereafter he was taken to the hospital where she died on August 26, 1963. It is alleged that the appellant brought his buck, to his house by giving him some apology, but when he came back home, he saw his father going with a knife. He then went out of the room but she had noticed his father coming out of her house and hacking him. Thereafter the appellant was taken into custody for trial before the Court on a charge under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. On appeal the Division Bench confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. Hence the appeal. The main contention raised by the appellant in this Court was that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be inadmissible, as the courts below did not hold it to amount to an extrajudicial confession as that the courts as well held it as the distinction drawn by them had not been made out. HELD: (i) A confessional solilhinoquy is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience, and an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as a the case may be. [90 F G] (ii) A confession is a voluntary statement made by an accused admitting His guilt. What does the expression "statement" mean? The dictionary meaning of the word 'statement ' is "the act of stating, reciting or presenting verbally or on paper". The term 'statement" therefore includes both oral and written statements. [91 F] (iii) A statement whether communicated or not admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional ray solil crooquy relates to a written confession brings out the said idea: "A kills B; enters in his diary that he had killed him, puts it in his drawer and absconds. When he places his act on record, he does not communicate to another; indeed he does have any intention of communicating it to a third party. Even so, at the trial the said statement of the appellant can certainly be proved as a confession made by him. If that be so, in the case of a statement in writing there cannot be any difference in principle in the cases of an oral statement. Both must stand on the same footing. [92 G H; 94 A B] (iv) The circumstances found by the High Court lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. No other reasonable hypothesis was or could be suggested. Further, in this case, there is no reason why the statement implied in the confession should be given (1) [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 310 referred to.

Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules, (for short "the Rules") as unconstitutional and void offending Article 14 of the Constitution of India read thus: "No person who has an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days ' notice in writing of his intention to do so will entail forfeiture of the pay of the month. " A direct recruitee can be removed from service on completion of 55th year unless the Board continues him for an extended period as may be determined from time to time. The appellant was kept under suspension pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973 in response thereto the appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The services of the appellant and others stood transferred to and vested with the custodian. The Central Govt. framed a New India Assurance Co. Ltd. Merger Scheme 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. All under the provisions of the Act the services of an employee or employee of an existing insurer appointed in connection with his General Insurance business immediately before the appointed day, were transferred and vested in the custodian of the New India Insurance Company Ltd., the management of Orissa Insurance Society Ltd., filed a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed. The appeal preferred by special leave by way of additional grounds also against their dismissal was dismissed by a learned single Judge on November 11, 1983 and hence the appellant preferred an Letters Patent Appeal before the Division Bench. The respondent contended that a Rule 5 has been ultra vires of Articles 14 and 19 (1) (g) of the constitution of India and that the rule is valid and therefore the impugned order terminating the services was illegal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the Rule is valid. But from the facts it is clear that the Board of Management did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of the employee. Obviously due to loss of confidence as his honesty and integrity became suspicious and his continuance in service was felt inexpedient and not in the interest of business of the respondent, but for Rule 5. [225B C] 2. The scope of Rule 5 is same. [226A] 3.1 Rule 5 does not become arbitrary. unreasonable or void offending article 14.

The appellants who were bidders in lease of country liquor for a sum of Rs. 34,000/ per month in one lot for Rs.34,000 per month at the auction held on February 3, 1970 submitted tender forms to the Collector of Mayurbhanj. After the dir lisation of the tenders, the Collector invited tenders for the grant of the licence and copies thereof were sent to the successful bidder. The State Government and the other respondents denied the allegations and pleaded that the bids at the auctions were not satis fied and in the interest of the State revenue, the State Government had passed orders for not accepting the request made by the appellants and after termsing all the decided cases, issued a re quirection to the State Govt. and also the Bihar Excise (Orissa Amendment) Ordinance of 1970 with retrospective effect from August 19, 1970. The validity of section 6 was challenged in the High Court, which quashed its earlier order and declared that rule 103(1) of the Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act, 1971. Hence these appeals by certificate or special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29 (2) (a) does not authorise the exercise of such absolute and naked powers in determining the sum of money. [884C D] 2. The High Court has taken the view that under the mistaken impression that the State was not entitled to collect a tax "under the garb of a fee" and the "auction price for a license is not duty within the meaning of Entry 51 of List 11 of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution". [889E] 3.

The prosecution alleged that one of the accused was an employee of a firm. The second accused was also charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with another person. Accused No. 3 was further charged with offences under section 120B read with sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code. Both accused Nos. 2 and 3 were convicted for having committed murder and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction on the ground that there was corroboration in material particulars in regard to the offence of theft but also with murder. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) An accomplice is competent to depose but as a rule of caution it will be unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [637 B] (2) It is unsafe to rely on the reasoning that there must be corroboration of the actual participation in the crime and it would be unsafe at all times to convict on his testimony again. [625 E] (3) The rule as to corroboration is based on the reason that there should be corroborative evidence in material facts particulars to connect the accused with the time. When the court, when it is said that an accomplice is lawfully competent tous depose but, as a Rule of caution, it will he unsafe to act upon his evidence alone [638 B] In the present case, the criminal proceeding was one composite unit of murdering Narendra and committing theft. The discovery of articles in the godown of Takalkar was as a result of statement made by accused No. 2 at the foot of it and that was the list of the articles sold to Gadekar. There were civil and criminal proceedings between him and Dr. Nanavati. Both the pieces of evidence proved the connection of accused No 2 with the crime. With regard, accused No 3 had tile motive not only to make it impossible for Dr. Daiyan but also to commit theft in his house. The place of occurrence was known by accused no. 2. The F.I.R. and the theft formed the same transaction and were committed by the same persons. Narendra was seen alive in the company of accused NO.2 and Dinkar. That was the evidence of the tailor who was a classmate of Narendra said that Narendra wore a chain similar to the one that was shown. The statement of P,W. 2 that he had kept the bag of utensils in his godown and gave the key of the godown to accused No, 3 who afterwards returned the key, would not corroborate the evidence that it was the tailer 's shop on 26th December 1967.

The appellant was a building site owner. On the date of notification, the Town Planning Officer granted sanction to the draft scheme. Before the Town planning Officer the appellant claimed compensation for deprivation of his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. by his order dated November 4 1971. The Town Planning officer awarded compensation against his land at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq . The appellant challenged the order of the Town Development Officer before the Gujarat High Court by filing a writ petition which was dismissed. On appeal, this Court, HELD: Under section 64(1) (f), if the owner of an original plot is not provided with a plot in the final scheme or if the contribution to be levied from him under section 66(1), is less than the total amount to be deducted therefrom under any of the provisions of the Act, the net amount of his loss shall be payable to him by the Local Authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. Under section 65 increment means the amount by which the total value of the plots included in the provisional scheme estimated on the assumption that the scheme has been completed would exceed the market value of which the owner was deprived by the scheme estimated for the market price on the date on which the declaration of intention to make a scheme, the market Value of such plot calculated on the basis as if the improvements contemplated in the scheme had stood completed on that date exceeds the market valuation of the same plot when taken into account without the improvement. The increment is thus the difference in the market values of the land with the improvements and without the improvements on the aforesaid date. Clause (v) of rule 17 mentions a "redistribution and valuation statement in Form 'B showing the estimated amounts to be paid to, or by each of the owners included in tile final scheme".

One Viswanatha Iyer, who was a foster son, died in 1934. The appellant claimed title on to the properties contending that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one veli nanja land and one vehi land from out of the land in question in accordance with quality but that after the death of the testator his father took possession of them and thereafter a sum of Rs. 175/in cash towards his properties after deducting the kist each year. The claim was resisted by the appellant on the ground inter alia (i) that the will was for the benefit of the daughter who had, in law, been in possession of the entire property and thereafter on his death their daughter remained in possession; (ii) that it was for him to keep the interest of his minor daughters; and (iii) that as his brother had died without making the selection the lands devised to them must now be partitioned. Held, that the intention of the deceased was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the award in the order in which they were named in the will. The circumstances showed that the testator intended that the daughters would get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the lands. Under the terms of the deed the son was given the right to select and give the devised land to his daughters in the case of the property which he was bequeathing to his daughter in the event of the legatee dying without having made it. The gift could not be said to be void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, because the cancellation of the bail was for uncertainty. There were no words from which it could be inferred that the deceased intended that each daughter should select the land to be handed over to the two daughters. The testator meant something different in the matter of partition between his sons and " he shall deliver possession". The intention of a testator was clearly clear to select, the house itself to be be given on to each child and therefore it could not have been intended that shares should have come partly from the fully paid up shares. The provisions of section 88 were applicable only to those cases where a will is so indefinite that it is not possible to give any definite intention to it at all. The rule was evolved by English Courts in order that where the testator 's intention to make a gift was clear and there was only some uncertainty, but not such complete uncertainty as could be resolved at all) that may be avoided by giving a choice to the legatee. There are no words in the Will from which the latter could be held to lead to the inference that the propounder intended that those daughters would secure their lands while taking into consideration the good quality of it and bad good quality.

The appellant is the widow of one of their brothers. She has executed a registered sale deed in law in respect of her share of the property from the part of his grandfather in law 's share and with a deplorable design, seeks to deprive her of their legal share and deny her legal rights under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950 (for short, 1947). The appellant filed a suit for joint possession of the land on the ground that she was living with her sons at Lucknow and her husband 's cousins were looking after the lands which consisted of agricultural lands and groves. It was alleged that she went to the village from time to time and got her share. The plaintiff further alleged in her statement that during consolidation proceedings separate plots were carved out, but she was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants and was under the Impression that her share was being properly looked after. The trial court decreed the suit for partition and possession in respect thereof the appellant filed an appeal before the district judge who allowed the appeal of the appellant on merits as also confirmed the decree of the trial Court. In second appeal the High Court set aside the judgment of the District Judge and restored that of the lower appellate court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The possession of defendants apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees would be in law the possession of plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the witnesses or by someone else as a result of which the rights were sought to be extinguished. In the present case the fact remained that the possession was of the defendants, apart from having been in the manner as contemplated under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act 1953, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. [868H; 869A] 2. The High Court erred in law while holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U .P. consolidation of Holdings act of 1953 or that the defendants assured the plaintiff that their name shall be entered in the record during the Consolidation proceedings, and was assured by the appellants that they would take proper care of her own share in any proceeding that may be instituted. This is not a case here made out by the appellant that any fraud was practised on the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. [ 866B] 3. The District Judge has come before the clear finding that some sort of fraud must have been committed by the defendant.

The petitioner who was a Deputy Prime Minister of India, filed a writ petition challenging the appointment of Respondent No. 1, Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Ministers of India: (i) that the oath administered to him as Deputy Chief Prime Minister was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution; and (ii) that he was still functioning as the Chief Secretary of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to Respondent No 1. In reply, the Union of India had stated that the form prescribed in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of Article 75(4) of the Constitu tion is only for a Minister of the Union and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. It was further contended that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. The Court allowed the writ petition taking the view that the Constitution described him as the Prime Ministers while being sworn into office, he describes himself as the chosenabinet. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) In view of the clear statement made by the Union Government that Respondent No . 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Superintendent Prime Minister but the description of him as a Deputy Chief Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime minister, along with his other submis sions, he is a Minister and there was no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. [3D F] (2) The necessary requirement of article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India.

An industrial dispute between the employer and its workmen was referred to the Industrial Tribunal by the Madras Government to which by an order dated the 11th July, 1949 made under section 10(1) (c) of the (XIV Of 1947), referred this dispute along with certain other disputes to the industrial tribunals. The adjudicator gave the award on 12th October 1950, but it was published in the Gazette on 12rd October, 1950. By his award the adjudicator found that there could be little doubt that the stoppage of work by the night shift workers on 1st November, 1948, amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the Factories Act, 1947 (XXV Of 1934) and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strikes were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B(1). On appeal by the Union before the Labour Appellate Tribunal it was contended on behalf of the Mills that since the strike had been included in the definition of 'strike ' under section 2(q) Of the Factories, Act, the provisions of sections 49 A and 49B were not attracted to it and that there was no justification for making a distinction between the stoppage and discontinuance of work for two hours on 1St November, as under the leave rules of the mills which prevailed prior to the coming into force of the Industrial , the workers had no right to deprive them of leave by reason of the strike. Held, that since articles 52, 54, 55 and 56 Of the , did not make any distinction between discontinuance and discontinuing work for a period of two to four hours and they were not therefore attracted to attract section 49 A of the Act which provided that every worker who has completed a period Of 12 months continuous service in a factory shall be allowed during the subsequent period of twelve months, holidays for a term of ten years, or if a child fourteenConsecutive days, inclusive of the day or days, if any, on which he is entitled to a holiday under sub section (1) of section 35.

Section 292 I.P.C. provides remedies. Section 79 1.P(1A) of the Act provided that nothing was an offence which was done by any person who was justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason is of a err of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by Law, in doing it. The respondent complained that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and he had acted mala fide whenever it came to light that he had seen that the picture was great and was the audience may lose lucre and culture in the bargain. Section 82 I. P.C., however, allowed prosecution under section 292 IPC to the respondent, but without making a declaration that the certificate of the Board of Censors would not be granted; and that that the film having been duly certified for public exhibition of a film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censorors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that it misdirected section 292(1) Cr.P,C., and violative of article 19(2) from the angle of public order decency or morality; that the prosecution has failed to prove that the respondent had acted in a bona fide belief that the Certificate was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) A special legislation viz., the Act of 1952 sets up a Board of CAensors of high calibre and expertise, provides hearings, appeals and ultimate judicial review, pre censorship and conditional exhibitions and wealth of other civil policings strategies. [507C] (2) The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. [ 516D E] (3) It is immaterial whether the offence was actually justified by a law or was bona fide believed by mistake of facts to be so justified. If, as here, the Board. blunders, the Act provides remedies.[502A B] (4) The distinction between section 292 I(1)(a) and section 79(2), according to Black 's Legal Dictionary means that in certain special circumstances it is not to be regarded as an offence. [ 517F G] K. A. Abbas, R. Maybe art cannot be imprisoned by the bureaucrat and aesthetics can be robbed of the glory and grace and free expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any department, more so in cinema pictures.[505C] K . A. A., Abbas, Maybe, art cannot not be imprisoned By the bureauccrat & aesthesis can be put back upon a study of the anatomy and the efficacy of a certificate under section 5A as a justification within the meaning of section 79 I.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader for the Patna District, was appointed as an Advocate in court in connection with criminal cases. During the currency of his term a plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government like any other litigant to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instructions in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case". He himself tried to persuade the High Court for the universal panacea of a writ because, he bad felt that his client 's claim as the sole representative of government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The locus standi of counsel to writ petition was not questioned as he had the prospect of income without effort not been offered by Government Rules but this Court granted special leave subject to the condition that the petitioner shall conduct the case and shall have enough time for it. But the High court declined to dispense with the magic remedy because, an ordinary litigant and is not bound to encourage monopoly within the profession. With great deal of litigation, the State Governments considered the importance of the matter. But before this Court, the petitioner contended that his clients ' claim as representative of Government in courts was not a proper legal cover and for vindictifying the inviollability or by profession dressed in `litrue] and that the Government Pleader 's legal grievance had to be looked into on its own merits but not before the High Courts. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The basic purpose of article 226 is to protect the individual against arbitrary discrimination in some cases by the Government or other public sector undertakings and others and that this would suppress the mischief which has resulted from manifest injustice, there is no other open sea open to the High Judges ' Court, but this court cannot shut out the door. [766 B] 2. The policy of legal remuneration is a vital connection for any State if resources are to be husbanded to reduce rather than increase its involvement in court proceedings. A Government pleader is more than an advocate for a litigant. He holds a public office and may depute other lawyers and exercise control over such surrogates.

Under section 2(6A), "dividend" means a dividend as normally understood and includes in its connotation several other receipts set out in the definition. The question for determination was whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, distribution of the right to apply for the shares of the Bank of India by Navjivan Mills Ltd., amounted to a distribution of "docividend". Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the distribution of this right amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2 (6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act. The distribution of shares for each share held by the shareholders of the Mills amounted to distributed of dividend; but by the form of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the Resolution could not be altered. The creation of the new shares amounted to 'distribution of dividend". Therefore, the company was entitled to sell the right in the market and distribute its proceeds among the shareholders. Such a distribution would undoubtedly have been distribution of dividends and it was open to the Mills to renounce the offer. The Mills had three options; (1) to accept the shares (2) to decline to accept those shares or (3) to surrender them in favour of its nominee. It was open for the Mills, however advantageous it might have been to the mills to renounse the offer and to allot the shares to its nominees did not distribute any dividend and the Mills wanted to surrender their shares in favour to its nominee, because, the Circular letter had not stated that the company had distributed any dividend. The Mill had three option for acceptance of the shares and for allotment to its members, but this last option could be exercised by nominating the persons who were to take over the shares, and since there was nothing to indicate that the mills did distribute any dividends, the Mills could not furnish it to accept it. Held, further, that while the ownership of the share of the company as dividend is indisputably the value of the ' right. The Board had rightly held in favour.

On May 3, 1983 the High Court made an order in favour of the appellant. The order of the High court was challenged before this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: Since the obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule(1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the Court is t necessary, and this ought to be so because the court wants to be satisfied about the necessity and relevance of the evidence of such witness whose presence will be procured with the assistance by the Court. [534C] The scheme is that after the Court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list of witness with the gist of the ' evidence of each witness in the Court within the prescribed time. [525H; 532A] Rule 1A is subject to sub rule (3) of rule 1 and therefore the court must ascertain how far sub rule 3 would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1 A. There is no inner contradiction between sub rule 2 (1)(a), 1(b) and 1A of Order XIII. Sub rule (2) of Order XVIII confers a wider jurisdiction on the Court to cater to a situation where the party has failed to name the witness in a list and yet the party is unable to produce him or her on his own under Rule 1.

The appellant a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal issued by the Committee of Management of the College. The Selection Committee constituted under section 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 held that the interview on April 12, 1981 was on April 1, 1981. After considering these facts the District Inspector of Schools wrote a letter to the Manager of the Institution that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post and he had convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on that day after college hours in the teachers ' room. Being aggrieved by this order, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which dismissed it holding that the radiogram contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee had no power to make any appointment. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant, it was urged that (i) assuming such a power to issue radiograms was available to the State and if the appointment was made without the knowledge of the order contained in the radiatiram it could be declared that the appellant continues to hold the post; and (ii) the appointment of the appel lant alleged to have been made on May 1,1981 was not valid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The power of wide amplitude will comprehend the power to stop all appointments for the time being being, and the power appears to have be exercised as Government was contemplating taking away the power of private management of non government aided schools to make appointment of teachers including Principals. [942 C D] (b) It is not possible that under section 11 of the Act read with Regulation 978 the State Govern ment enjoys the power, to control and conduct the affairs of the institution. Judicial discretion of an executive authority must be exercised with great care and caution and should not be interfered lightly or lightly but must be guided by considerations. [943 H] (2) The provisions of section 16A are of a drastic nature and it is imperative that such a duty should be cast on the State Govt.

The respondent a manufacturer of tyres, used it for the purpose of impregnating it with rubber. There was no dispute that from year 1966 to 1969 the respondent commercial Tax Officer was not subjecting the goods of this description to sales tax and accepted the case of the petitioners that they were exempt from taxation, and that the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption. The High Court did not go into the merits of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent appellant that the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product". Allowing the appeals, HELD: (1) It is well settled that in all cases it is a question on which two views seem possible on apparent facts. And neither of these two views can be rejected outright as untenable. [503C D] (2) The High court was right in not interfering with the decision of the taxing authority at this stage. [506D] (3) The goods now moved to a place for purpose of "textile" fabrics and not for any kind of fabric. [ 506E F] (4) In the entry, it evidently means a fabric which is also a textile. The question whether the goods under consideration constitute the "withsel" or not is a matter on which both views are possible. The meaning of the term "fabric" given in the Oxford English Dictionary is: "A product of skilled workmanship". [506E F, F] In the entries, it apparently means a fabrics which is again a textile fabric. The contention that, if the tyre cord fabric was the beginning product for the Delhi Cloth Mills, the crucial question is: Is this product constitute a fabric and therefore a textile cloth does not cover everything which could be made into a fabric. Even if the tyres cord fabric may be the end product for Delhi Cloth Mill, the material question is whether the products under consideration constituted the "Vend product" for which the Delhi pointed mill claims exemption exemption Is a textile fabrics and in not any other kind of cloth.

Section 33 B of the empowers the appropriate Government to withdraw any proceedings pending before a Labour Court or Tribunal and transfer it for disposal to another Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal. The State Government notified that such proceeding may be transferred without intimation to the management. The appellant company filed an application under section 10(1)(c) of the . The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties which contained the Government 's approval to transfer the pending case to the Labour Court Patna. The respondent appeared in person and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour court, Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would not be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred from Labour Court Dhanbad and transfer the said proceeding to the labour Court, Patna. That application was made without intimation of the management to the respondent. The Government acceded to the request of the respondent and without giving opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Court Pat tee. The Notification issued in that regard reads as follows: " NOTIFICATION Patna dated 8th August 1988 S.O. In exercise of powers under sub section (1) of Section 33B, the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the applica tion of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he had prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Ranchi regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before the Labour Compa ny. The management moved the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to have the Notification quashed. The High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the Writ Petition with an observation that " Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, we are not inclined to interfere with the order under challenge. This application is dismissed" In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that section 33 B which provides power to transfer pending cases before a labour court or Tribunal carries out an administrative function and the Government cannot transfer a case on the basis of allegations of one party without giving reasonable opportunity to other party to represent its point of view. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions contained in section 33B are itself discretionary. When once a decision is taken to transfer a pending case then it the requirement of giving reasons becomes mandatory. [295A] 2.1 In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the pending refe rence from the Labour petitioners, without getting it veri fied from the management and transferring the case from the labour courts Dhanbad to Labour court Patna. Denial of that opportunity is a fatal flaw to the decision of the Government.

The appellant was the manager of a Hotel Imperial, New Delhi. On a report submitted by the Director of Industries and Labour, Delhi under section 12(4) of the as amended, it appeared that an industrial dispute existed between the management of the Hotel Imperial and its workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi Chandni Chowk, Delhi. The appellant contended that the reference was incompetent inasmuch as the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and (2) the reference in this form was incompetent. Held, that there was no force in the contention that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was that it related to the dismissal of particular workmen, and could not therefore be called vague at all. Held further, that even if the workman is entitled to be represented by an officer of a trade union of which he was a member, the reference made under the section 10(1) cannot be held to be invalid merely because it did not specify the disputes or the parties between whom the dispute arose and the Tribunal has no power to make a reference under section 10. The words " as represented" in section 2(k) of ' the Act give power to the appropriate government where it is of opinion that an Industrial Dispute exists or is apprehended to refer the dispute to a tribunal for adjudication. Held also, further, (i) that in view of the fact that more than three years have passed since the reference being made there was, it would be neces sary duty on the Government to ascertain particulars of the disputes before making a reference. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy ([1953] S.C.R. 334), followed. (ii) that even assuming that the workman was entitled to represent by an Officer under section 36 of the Act, the case did not fall within sections 10(2) and 16 Of the Act as it might be desirable to mention the names of the workmen concerned. State Of Madras vs K. C.

The appellant was engaged in the manufacture of tyres and on its own behalf, imported certain goods described as 'parts thereof '. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of exemption under the Notification No. 281 Cus/76 granting part exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by the appellant. Both the authorities held that the bushings and bearings are one and separate, and that even assuming that Heading No. 84.06 is also included under another Heading, the question of any exemption under Notification does not arise. The Customs 'Appeals Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appel lant on the ground: (1) The appellant was the Road Transport Corporation and (2) Even assuming that heading No.8406 covers 'part 's of such engines, such parts will get the benefit thereof as provided by the Notification in order to avail of the benefit under the Notifications. Hence this appeal by the Union of India. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (i) The Notification is not only intended to grant exemption to internal combustion piston engines but also to 'part the 's thereof. When, therefore, the intention is clear and manifest, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notification and not to extend its benefit to the parts of the engines referred to in Heading No 84.606. [226H 227A] (ii) The object of the notification is clear enough to provide that the parts are of the engine or engines, mentioned under heading No, 84,06 will get their exemption under that Notification and in the absence of any provision to the contrary, it would be unreasonable for taking a narrow interpretation of the Notifications and not at extending its benefit. [227B] (iii) The contention that the Heading No., 84.04 is also inclusion under another heading other than Heading No, has given rise to a controversy between the parties. It may be that the functions of the busi ture and bear ingings are the same, seems ence both as that of the bearings, sometimes bushies are also called bearings as pointed out by the Appellate Tribunal. But when these two articles are known in the market by two different names, it is difficult to uphold the contention that they are parts of internal combustion Piston engine, as mentioned under Heading No . 84.07 and not a few parts thereof. [228C E] (iv) The Appellate Tribunal was influenced by the fact that the function of the Bushings & bearings is the same.

In the suit filed by the plain tiffs for declaration that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of Saint Syed Moosa Shah Khadiri Dargah, Madras for a period of 27 days in all the months of February, March, June, July and November each year and to restrain them from interfering with the plaintiffs ' right and management in the Dargah. The case of the plaintififfs as set up in the plaint was that the Dargah in ques tion was being managed by the members of the family of one person who died in 1957. However on account of some dissensions, the first defendant who is the son of another deceased maternal uncle were preventing the plaintiffs from exercising their right and enjoying the income of the Dar gah. The plaintiffs served a notice on 23.3.1972 calling upon the defendants to recognize the right of management of the plaintiffs in the revocation and further pleaded that they claimed through female were not entitled to any right in the management or share in offerings in the said Dargah and even if they were enti tled to any rights or conces sions, the same was barred by limi tation. The defendants sent a reply on 22.4.1972 stating that the plaintiffs claiming through female members were not enti tice to claim any right of Mujawar and since they were denied by the brothers which would be considered as an ouster they were also paying such share to their sisterunnissa (lOth de fendant) in the Hundial Col lections, the plaintiffs who were claiming through Fathima Bee were also not entitled lo any relief. The widows of Sayed Gulam Gastagir also could not claim any rights of Mujwar by way of inheritance or succession. On 8.5.1972, the High Court allowed the second appeals and while setting aside the judgments of the Courts below dismissed the suit in limi ter. Aggrieved against this Judgment, the appellants plaintiffs have preferred these appeals to this court. In CA NO. 650/81, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Fathiya Bee had never participated in the Management of the Dargah because he was a Mujawar along with his father and that even if she had got any right, the said same was lost as she did not claim anything till her death. The respondents also submitted that R was aware of the filing of Civil Suit No. 116 of 1909 against the appellants for a declaration that the decree passed by the First Appellate Court on 11.8.1910 passed in Civil Suit NO. 117 of 1909 also nega tived the right to manage was recognised for 9 days in a year and that the said 27 days shall be Febru ary 1 to 6, June 1 to June 1st and October 1 to and 10th July for the first plaintiff and that they are entitled to perform the duties of Mujikawar of theAIR in turn. The contesting respondents contested the suit contending that the females were totally excluded from the right or claim of any share in themanagement or offerings. On behalf of some of the defendants it was further contended that the nature of the right was that only those members had a right to management and possession of all the co heirs; that there was no ouster in the facts of the instant case. The trial court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the appellants were entitled ted the management for 27 days. In the appeals by defendants, it con tended that there would be clear presumption of ouster and the courts below proceeded upon an erro neous assumption as if it was the duty of the respond ent to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster had been established. The High Court also took the view that the Courts were not right in holding that the rights of Fathna Bee had become barred by hit by ouster and as such Hindu Law.

The 1st respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. The 'employer which represented by the appellant started, admittedly be was not entitled to any such house rent allowance. His claim was rejected by the Authority by an order dated 28th September 1951 under section 15(1) of the , which provided that where there were no rules governing the grant of houses rent allowance make it compulsory for the employer to grant house rent allowances without anything more. The appellant contended before the authority and by his written statement contested the claim on the ground that the house rent was not "wages" as defined in the Act; that the employee posted at any one of those places would cease to be entitled to the allowance if either the Government provides accommodation to the employee in question or the employee refuses to occupy the accommodation so offered to him. Held, that there can be no doubt that the rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted in one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled, to house rent Allowance. A house rent payment which may in certain circumstances be included under "wages ' is not the same thing as the value of any house accommodation referred to in the section. The definition of "wages " contained in section 2(vi) of, the Act cannot include the value Of any house accommoda tion supplied by the employer for the employee; otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages. The house rent paid may in some circumstances be includible in "wages".

% In Writ Petition 435 of 1980, the detenu was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 439 of 1980 the detenu is alleged to have infringed an order of detention passed under Section 3(1) COFEPOSA by the State Government. On November 16, 1979, the Customs Officers at Bombay raided the premises of the firm and seized two cameras and three wrist watches worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. On September 23, 1980, an order was authenticated by the Under Secretary to the State Govt. wherein it stated that in view of the non supply of copies of certain statements to the detenus on April 3, 1980 the detenus moved this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of habeas corpus on the ground that they could, praying for revocation of the order of their detention. On March 11, 1980 an order purporting to have been made under Section 11 of COFEPOSA was served on the detenus alongwith the grounds of detention. The detenu also sent a petition through the Central Government complaining of the failure of the authorities in refusing to supply copies and conveyed rejection of this request by two letters dated March 31, 1980 which, were received by the detenus under their covering letter. The Secretary to Government of Maharashtra, Home Department, ex parte, informed the State government that the copies had been refused on April 8, 1980. On February 18, 1980 when the detenu again sent a representation to the Central Govt. requesting him to furnish them with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds and that their request for revocation had been rejected. Thereafter, the wife of the detenu received a letter dated March 14, 1980 from the State Gov ernment requesting him not to supply these copies so as to enable him to make an effective representation against his detention. This letter was received by him only on March 25, 1980; the State then being under President 's rule. The detaining authority calledously and deliberately refused to supply them and conveyed acceptance of this communication by a letter. On April 3.1980, copies were received from the detenus and were actually received by them on April 4, 1980 i.e., after more than one month, but on March 27, 1980 and were still actually received under the President 'S rule. During interrogation, the detenus claimed that they had purchased the gems in question from those persons who had sold these diamonds in question or gave them on 'jhangad basis ' was communicated to them by the Customs Department. These statements also alleged that the detenu made a written request to the detaining authori ty and that the goods seized were not smuggled goods but were local materials, locally acquired. They also gave the names of four persons from whom these gems had been acquired. Both the father and son were arrested and interrogated during interrogation; the detenus demanded that they would attend daily before the Customs officers and cooperate in investigation. The detenus claimed the gemas and other articles seized were neither smuggled goods nor local materials but were extra commercial materials, extraneous or locally acquired . They also produced before a Magistrate. They were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they did not attend daily when the Customs Officer visited the premises and meet certain circumstances. While considering their representation, the detaining Deporting Authority, however, called for copies of the statements and documents relied upon in the ground of detention, these facts did not satisfy the requirement of Article 22(6) of the Constitu tion. The State Government however advised the State Govern ment to furnish the detenus with the necessary material relied on by the detenu in the order dated April 3 but it further advised the Union Government to supply the copies and convey rejection of their request by a reply letter, dated March 18,1980 which is received by it only on July 27, 1978. The latter also asked for copies. Thereafter the detenu applied for copies on February 18 1980.

The Gujarat High Court in its order referred to ss 258, 410, 417 and 423 of the Code. The five accused persons, jointly tried and convicted were acquitted by the trial court. There was a revision to the Supreme Court against the acquittal of all the accused persons. A learned single Judge of the High Court recorded a very lengthily order though the reasoning in support of the non maintainability of the joint appeal is confined to a couple of pages only. The High Court however held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Criminal Procedure provides as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against a common order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The learned Judge also recorded the main judgment only in Criminal Appeal No. 60 of 1965. It was contended for the State that r. 6 does not prohibit a joint appeals by the state against more than one accused persons and therefore, not legally prohibited. On behalf of the respondents it was urged that r .6 did not permit a joint petition to be maintainable under section 482 in view of section 494 A of the Indian Penal Code. Allowing the appeal, HELD : The Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High court rightly distinguished and explained this decision. In Rabari Ghela Jadav 's case it is clear that once a view of two judge of the same High Court based on the construction of that section is plainly unacceptable it gives effect to that view, the result would be utter confusion. The true reading of sections therefore seems to be wide enough to permit a Joint appeal. Section 417 which provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal empowers the State Government to direct the public prosecutor in any case to present an appeal from an order of acquittal. This section does not suggest any bar or prohibition against presentation of a Joint Appeal against several accused person acquitted in a cases. On the other hand it provides for An appeal in the same case and not against an accused person, who has been acquitted. The plain reading of this sections therefore shows that there is no bar or prohibited by presentation of joint appeal against two accused persons acquitted in one case.

The appellant was a firm, who carried on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States. It was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, to income tax for the year 1939 40. The total income of the foreign business from April 13, 1938 to June 2, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by virtue of section 25(3) and (4). [908 C] Section 2(a) of the 1922 Act provided that "the provisions of sub section (4) shall apply also in respect of all income other than those under the 1918 Act". The appellant firm discontinued its business on June 30, 1947. The question for determination was whether the foreign accounting business of the assessee was at any time charged under the provisions of the 1918Act. It claimed by the assessee that it was not assessed under section 3 of the Act but only receipt received from the profits of the Foreign business. The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family, but rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal held that there was no discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 2(b) and the assessee firm was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3) of 1922 Act. In a reference to the High Court under section 256 the High court held that it had taken over the entire business of it and, therefore, the foreign income could not be deemed to have been charged under provisions of 1918 Act. On appeal by certificate, HELD: The assessee was entitled to both parts of relief contemplated under section 2 (a) only on the receipt in British India and as the income received by the joint family could not have been charge under the head "Profits and gains of business, profession or vocation"

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to them, for construction of Capital Project, Bhadohinagar. Large quantities of bricks were manufactured and supplied under the agreement with the appellant. The assessee applied under section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 for determining the question whether the said supplies of bricks by the respondent to the Public works Department were sales or works contract, but the Deputy Commissioner held that the supply was sales. On appeal, the Tribunal following its decision in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of Orissa and Ors., came to the conclusion that the supplies of brick were sales; at the instance of the assessee, the tribunal referred the question, whether the aforesaid supplies of lime by the appellant to the public Works Department were Sales or works Contract. The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent and held that as the contracts in this case were a works contract and not a works contractor, the transaction was a works contracts; accordingly, held with the decision of the Supreme Court in Chandraan Bhan Gosayain vs The State of orissa and others, ; , that since in Chandrah Bhan Gosai 's case, the contracts would govern the present case also, the property in the bricks was entirely of the assesee. In coming to this conclusion the High Court held as follows: 1. "Clause 6:The contractor shall have no right to sell these bricks at all unless they belonged to him. The contractor will be entitled to reject the said articles on such portion thereof as may be discovered not to conform to the specifications and quality on such rejection the articles will be at the sellers ' risk and all the provisions herein contained relating to rejection of goods etc. shall apply. " [162C E] Chandra Bhan, Gosain, vs The Union of India, , followed. Chandra Bhan Sahas case (supra) applied. Chandra Kumar Bhan Gosanain vsThe State of Gujarat, ; and Chandra Bhan vs The Commissioner of Sales Tax, Punjab, ; distinguished. Chandra Ban Gosain 's Case, [1957] S.C.R. 879, explained.

The petitioner during the assessment year 1976 77 submitted an application before the Lok Sabha seeking approval for the two Proclamations of Emergency issued under article 352 of the Constitution (as it stood at the relevant time) on the grounds: (i) that the proclamation of Emergency was ultra vires the Constitution; and (ii) that in any event since they had been published in the newspapers, the Proclorumions, of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra vires, or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 was passed by Parliament. The petitioner further contended that even though the said Proclomations had been validly issued the President by the Proclamation dated 27th March, 1977 and approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament approving the two resolutions of Emergency as required by clause (2) of Article 352 of tile Constitution as it stood during the relevant period had not been published at the official Gazette of the Government of India. The writ petition filed by the petitioner was dismissed by the High Court following a decision in Danappa Jatti, Vice President acting as President of India and which had become final on the Division Bench Judgment in C.A. No. 418 of 1979 dated 26th August, 1979. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i ) the two Proclamation issued under sub clause (b) of cl. (4) of article 352 was ultra rites the Constitution, and (2). that even assuming that the Pro President had been duly authorised by law and approved without following the procedure established in clauses (1) and (c), there was non compliance with the mandatory requirement of clause (3) of Art 352. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two Pro clamations dated 3th December 1971 and 2nd December 1975 were both in operation at the expiration of the period of five years from the date of issue thereof. [438A B] 2. The provisions of article 122(1) of the Consti tution do not prescribe that a Proclamation of Emergency should be published in ' the official gazette. [444C] 3. In so far as the Governor was concerned it was open to him to publish a notification issued by him under Article 174(2) in the Official Gazette and such publication was considered sufficient. In view of the orders passed by the Houses of parliament approving the Proclamation of emergency as required under clause (1), the two must be deemed to have become ineffective on the expiry of the duration of five months from the issue thereof [444D] (a) The provisions regarding procedure after which a proclamation is issued are complied with. If it were not mandatory if the reasons mentioned therein were recorded in writing, it would have been sufficient compliance with clause (4). Further, there was no provision for compliance with section 103 of the Act. [442G] 4. There is no allegation that the two proclam es of Emergency were validly issued or not and there has been non compliance. [443D] 5. It is true that, under article 71 of the Indian Constitution, the 352 situation prevailing in the country has become a major irrespective of its origin. But that does not mean that the order approving the Proplotamations is invalid on the ground that it is made after following the due procedure prescribed by law. [441C] (b ) The President cannot be said to have contravened article 11(1)(a) of India if he has committed any violation of article 14 of the constitution or if there has already been failure of justice, then there is no justification for making it. [451F G] In the instant case, the two Notifications were validly placed by the President and approved when the two notifications were duly executed. Since the two provisions of Article 122(2)(1) do not require that the resolutions should be publication in the official Gazettesy.

The appellant, who was the manager of a temple, filed an application for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The District Judge decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the premises constituted a temple and set aside the decision of the said authorities. On appeal by the High Court reversed the aforesaid judgment and decree of the Trial Court and found that the subject matter of dispute in the District Court as also in appeal in the High court was more than Rs. 20,000/ and that the judgment of the High Courts having reversed the judgment and decrees of the trial Court he was entitled to leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b). The appellant thereupon filed a petition for leave to appeal to this Court. HELD: 1. The subject matter which has to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property is the private property of the family capable of alienation the High ' Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to its respondents the property was inalienable and was a public temple. [157 G] 2. The assessment order made by such an authority as is enjoined in the Madras Religious Endowments Act, 1938, does not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question res pecting property of value of Rs.20,000 or more and (c) that the appeal did not involve any substantial question of law. [158 B] 3. The question whether the property in dispute was not a private or a public Temple is incapable of valuation as it could have in either case no market value.

The respondents workmen, who had been re employed for inter alia the purpose of employing retired persons should be stopped. The High Court held that the Tribunal has erred in law in making an award in respect of cash allowance for tiffin, because it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiff in its employees. In appeal by special leave : Held, that there is no justification for the contention that tiffs claim against the direction in the award that only 4 cases of reemployment had been brought to the notice of the respondent workman and so, the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage. Chandi Charan Banerjee vs Shib Shankar Banerjee; , referred to. If senior persons are employed after retirement, that is apt to retard or hamper the prospects of promotion to which the junior employees are entitled to look forward. Such re employment would have no material bearing in dealing with the point; and agricultural justice might not have been done without the respondent 's s claim for cash allowance in lieu of tiff. Chand jai Charan Banerjee case , referred, distinguished. Chandji Charan Banerjee & Co. vs Shib Sankar Nath Banerjee; and Workmen of a similar now [1959] S.C.R. 707 and Rajasthan State Public Service Commission vs Shri Om Prakash Jain & Anr. ; , discussed. Joginder Kumar Banerjee vs General Secreatry of the respondents ' Union, ; distinguished. It is well settled that in industrial disputes, the concept of industry has undergone radical changes but a change in the conditions of service as between the parties coupled with the prevailing practice in comparable concerns and in the region may not be reasonable to disturb the existing practices of the employees of the company. Consequently, though the employer had raised a dispute on this point in 1960, the State Government had refused to make a reference on the ground that only four cases of de fences were brought to its notice, and so it did not demand any further facility to the employees by way of giving them cash allowance. The mere fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by him cannot affect their plea that they had become old ones. It was for the appellant that some of the re employments may have been actuated by humanitarian considerations and the appellant could not, therefore, be blamed on that account.

The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. The Union of India also applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money which by section 3 Of the , was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". On application filed by Radha Kissen Agarwalla, the Subordinate Judge held that the amount claimed to be his credit in the Provident Funds account was immune to attachment under section 60(1) (k) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that by sending two cheques to the Reserve Bank of India in performance of the manner of Payment prescribed by Browne, the debt was discharged and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber Browne. HELD: The Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal. But the Union of 'India was a trustee for the subscriber of the money. When the amount lying with the Reserve bank as the agent of the Railway Administration was attached, the Union had itself an interest in maintaining it and the Union created the deposit. The order of attachment of the amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway Adminis tration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the Contract Act.

The respondent workman, a pump manufacturing enterprise issued a notice ending the employment and offering one month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing Orders. The factory management was to offer one month"s salary extra on an ad hoc basis. The workmen protested against the order as victimisation of a Trade Union activist but the Management was heedless, conciliation was fruitless. The dispute between the Union and the Management is ultimately referred to the Labour Court for adjudication. The reference ran thus "Whether the termination of services of Shri L. Michael is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect ?" Both sides stated their cases in their pleadings and the true nature of the conflict emerges from them. The story set out by the employee in his statement before the Labour court was that although he was efficient, appreciated and awarded merit increments, the Management, was antagonized by his active part in the formation of an Employees ' Union, especially because oral warnings by the Regional Manager against his Unionist proclivity were ignored. As such this letter may be treated as a notice for the termination. The workman challenged the termination as "wrongful mala fide, illegal and unjustified". The management asserted that the action being a simple termination without a sting process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. The Management contended: (i) that the warning by the employer was denied and the reference to trade union activities by the workers was more to create a ground for the workman 's claim and has been leveled as a matter of habit and routine, therefore, the action was claimed to be legal and immune to judicial interference; (ii) that even where a management had the power to terminate the services of its employees without reasons but with notice pay only, the colourable exercise of that power invalidated it, and (iii) that since the termination was a colourable exercise Of the powers or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1(i) The appellant 's denial of leaking out office secrets was an after thought pleaded only in the rejoinder and therefore liable to be discredited. When the latter stated the reason which prompted this action for the first time before the labour court, the workman in his reply refuted this case. It is significant that there has not been done. There is also only the ipse dixit of the employer that he was suspecting since 1968 that the appellant was divulging secrets relating to his business. The employer has not dis closed the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968 (which was a ground given by the management and the Court found that it was not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1) 496 of dismissal simpliciter under the provisions of the Standing Orders). It is true that this Court, in appeal, as a rule of practice, is loath to interfere with a finding of fact recorded by the trial court. But if such a finding is based on no evidence, or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence, and is so unreasonable or grossly unjust that no reasonable person would judicially arrive at that conclusion, it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set matters fight. [496 G H] (ii)(a) In the instant case, an employer who believes or suspects that his employee, particularly one holding a position of confidence, has betrayed that confidence can, if the conditions and terms of employment permit terminate his ap pointment and discharge him without any stigma attaching to the discharge. It must rest on some tangible basis and the power has to be exercised by the "employer objectively in good faith" which means honestly with due care and ' prudence.
