In the writ petition it was alleged that after the passing of this Act the notification under section 3 was issued by which the Council had a sole constitution known as Bidhan Sabha for the spread of Hindi as the common language for the whole of India with a view to promote national integrity and in pursuance of this resolution institutions for the implementation and spread of the Hindi nasal, Bhagalpur, East, Assam, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh as provided in Article 351 of the Constitution. It was also alleged that the Samiti was formed on 3.11.83 at Gauhati with a late Gopinath Bardaloi, the first Chief Minister of Assam under the 1935 Act as its President. In 1948 the case of the Bidhan was taken up for considering the question of temporary injunction, the Governor of Assam purported to act under clause 1(ii) of Article 230 of the Constitu tion and promulgated an Ordinance called as the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act 1984, which received the assent by the Governor. The Ordinance was then replaced by the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1951, which came into force on 13.11 9.83. It also challenged the orders contained in Notifi cation Nos. EPG 57/84/25 A and E PG 57/ 84/61 dated 1.10.84 and 19.385 respectively issued by the Education (Personal) Department of the Government of Assam. The grounds on which the order was sought to be quashed are: (1) That there was mismanagement, delay in examinations and results and it was because of that management only under this Act was taken over by the first respondent State with the approval of the Governor and published in the Assam Gazette Extraordinary dated 15.12.84; (2) That the procedure stated in this section was followed and as only one person opposed the Constitution amendment was passed, on 17.7.83 from this date the Chief Minister ceased to be the Ex officio President and since then according to the petitioner he had nothing to do with the Samiti or its ideals and who were supposed to run the affairs of the Samiti.

The appellants were the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal. They were the reversioners of the late Ram Kishori Lai Sao, a resident of Asansol in Bengal, who died in September 1927. The suit was instituted for a declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10 1940 executed by Sumitra Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on the reversion. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court affirmed the decree of the trial court. It was contended before this Court on behalf of the appellants, inter alia, (i) that the properties given to Kamala Devi constituted a reasonable portion of the estate, which there were no compelling reasons for the High Court in interfering with that order and (ii) that it could not be operative beyond the life of Sumitra separately. It is further contended that in view of the provisions of section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act the appellants could not operate beyond the expiry of the validity of the gift and the adoption of which was a subsequent act. Held, that the gift made by Kamala Devi to her daughter by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala Devi did not amount to a valid gift within the meaning of section 124 of the , and as such could not have been relied on for the purpose of making the gift. The marriage of the daughter was a religious duty and the promise to make a gift to the daughter as her marriage portion created a moral or religious obligation in fulfilment of which it was competent for the father to execute a deed. It would be open to a widow to make an effective gift in favour of her daughter subsequent to the marriage, if the conditions laid down were fulfilled. The question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the time of the gifts or not, and, if under the law it was a moral obligation on the family to make such a provision as and by way of a marriage portion and such obligation continues until it is fulfilled by a reasonable provision being made therefor, the fact that one of the sons has become indebted cannot take away the power of the father in making such a gift. In Churaman Sahu vs Go pi Sahu, [1904] A.C. 119, referred to.

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, and was declared duly elected. The respondent filed an election petition in the High Court against the respondent alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices, detailed in the petition an(l 'W ' In the Statement of facts, it was stated that a few ( Mahtab before Tej Singh had come to his printing press and informed him that he (Tej Singh) would be sending some work for printing. Soon thereafter, the witness was approached by Darshan Singh and Mukhtiar Singh, Roshan Lal who admitted that Bhum Raj was the only candidate who could defeat the Congress. The High Court rejected the contention on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters and that no document was brought to show that any expenses were incurred by him in connection with the said posters. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court rightly held that Tej Singh having actually paid the posters for the poster which were filed at his own instance and Roop Lal was certainly not collected from the printing, of the poster. [418 B] The respondent had proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej 's initially paid the money for the entire amount but later on admitted that the appellant had withdrawn he had been clearly admitted by him as above. It is also clear to us that in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to the respondent cannot be ruled out.

The appellant was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. The said Devinder Sharma was defeated in the legislative assembly election to 1982. On 891, the appellant filed an application for contempt against the respondent, which was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon him. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appellant. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the application and discharged the Rule nisi. It is apparent from the facts stated above that the allegations are made by the petitioner, if proved would consitute a criminal contempt. As no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High COurt in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt, section 19(1) is inapplicable and the appeal is incompetent.[892H; 893A B] In the instant case, it was not disputed that it was a case of criminal contempt as defined in section 2(c) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. The scope and ambit of this judgment will, therefore, be confined to criminal contempt because when the High court acquits a contemnor after hearing the parties and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Courts do not exercise its jurisdiction or power to punish punish for Contempt. [893A A] Concerakanta Mishra vs Mr Justice Gatikrushna Mishra; , Right of Appeal is a creature of the statute and the question whether there is a right of appeal or not will have to be considered on an interpretation of the provision of the statue and not on the ground of porpriety or any other consideration. [888C] In considering a question whether the alleged contemnor is guilty of contempt or not, the court whoars the parties, and considers the materials produced before it and, if necessary examines witnesses and thereafter passes an order either acquitting or punishing him for contempt.

The appellant was the daughter and grand sons of one Ladha Ibrahim Sheth. The lessee paid a premium of Rs. 999 for the lease, and also agreed to pay all taxes to his heirs who were entitled under the lease for non payment of rent. The sale deed provided that in default of payment of the rent, the tenant 's rights would come to an end. On the same day Ladha Rahil sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7999. The appellant filed a suit against L and the High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court on appeal by special leave. Held: (per kha chaudra Aiyar, J.) A notice in writing as required by section III(g) was not a condition precedent to a forfeiture and the right of re entry would be a result of an oral communication made by a written one without without way disturbing the mind of a chancery judge. A landlord asking for a notice at his instance is not entitled to make any claim in writing telling him that such a lease had been determined. That a suit may have become infructuous on a subsequent occasion, particularly when he was warned by the Court of appeal on a previous occasion. The well recognised principle of equity and good conscience applies equally to leases executed prior to 1929 or even after the coming into force of the , or to leases made before 1st April 1930, unless the lessor gives an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage of the breach. If the purpose for the rule as to notice is to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine the lease and to avail himself of the tenant"s breach of covenant it could as effectively be achieved by an oral intimation as by a decision without in any way disturbing such mind of another chancery Judge. That does not mean that what has been enacted in sub section (g) of section 111 prior to its amendment in 1929, was merely a new rule laid down by the legislature and is not based on any principle of justice, equity or good conscience and cannot govern leases made prior to the coming in force of tho , or under a statutory recognition of a principle of Justice equity. The supplementary rule applies equally with it as well as with it it cannot be said that this sub section enacts or enunciates any general principle of law of equity. It is not safe to say that the court must and will always insist upon certain things when the Act does not require them, and the facts of some unforeseen case may make the court wish it had kept a free hand. The rule consistently followed in considering all matters relating to forfeiture has been laid down in section 114 of the . The general principle to which the legislature has now given effect by the amendment to section 111(g)(b) was that if at the time relief is asked for the position has been altered so that relief cannot be granted without causing injury to third parties will be refused, but if that position is not altered so it may be done there would no real discretion and the court should make the order and give the relief.

Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 was amended by Act 35 of 1969. This section was as follows: "7E. Certain persons occupying lands for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law or in any contract, custom or usage, or in terms, decree or order of Court, any person in occupation of the land of another at the commencement of this Act, shall be deemed to be a tenant, notwithstanding anything tO the contrary provi sions contained in section 52 or any other provision of the . or any law, custom, or usage or in lnical judgment, decree, or order or Court, or any person who on the 11th day of April, 1957 was in occupation thereof for not more than two years within a period of twelve years immediately preceding the commencement o fication of the Act, and was cultivating the nilam at the inception of this com pany. Subsequent to these evictions the appellant surrendered lease hold rights but continued in possession to be de verted subject to the decision of the suit. In terms of Section 7A, it became incumbent on the owner of the area to occupation any person entitled to lease that land or his authorised agent or a receiver appointed by a court describing the payment as modavaram or nashtavaram etc. which were only in the nature of licence and fell short of a leasehold right. The appellant contended before the Courts below that his clients respondents were prepared to pay to him a sum of Rs.50,000 as ex gratia payment in full and final settlement of whatever claims the appellant may have towards the value of the rubber trees standing in plots but, the courts below held that the appellant had come into possession of the lands by trespass; that he was himself the owner and that after his clients surrender lease hold right to the landlord, but had not actually transferred pos session; and that the Government released the amount from Court without furnishing any security. The respondents filed writ appeals in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. For a proper understanding of the scope and intendment of Section7D, it is necessary to examine the setting and tie c the context in which the said section occurs in the Act. [114E F] 2. In computing the period of occupation of a person for the purpose of clause (c), the period during which the predecessor in interest or predecessors in interest of such person was or were in occupation, shall also be taken into account. Explanation II for the purposes of this Section, a person shall be 2 deemed to have been in continuous occupation notwithstanding any order of court for delivery of possession to another person or any Court Record of dispos session. [115B C] 3. The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to persons whose posses sion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the land on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come to lease from person whom they bonafide believed to be Competent to grant leases or have come into posses tion with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of agreements like varam etc., on which were merely in the character of licences and fell Short short of lease right. It was not within the contemplation of the Legisla tion to confer the benefit of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The expression "in possesess" occurring in Section 7E must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation".

The appellants, who were members of a registered association formed themselves into an Association for collecting the quota of cloth to be allotted to them and sell it on profit wholesale and retail. The Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because of a reference, the Cloth Control Officer allotted the consignment to the Association. The association was dissolved before the expiry of six years from the date of the passing of the Madhya Pradesh State Companies Act, 1935. The appellants were not given a notice of demand by any one of them for repayment. Thereafter the suits were filed in the Court of Additional District Judge who dealt with the suit in the first instance passed a preliminary decree in favour of the appellant appellants. The decree directed Nagar Mal to render accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1946 to June 26, 1946, and it further directed that leaving out 106 bales of Gwalior cloth which was allotted to the family members who would give the Association an option of taking over the consignment; if the Association did not exercise the option, the consignment would be taken over by Nagar Mal. The preliminary objection raised in the High Court was that the suit was not maintainable because no formal Articles of Association were written nor Se it registered, and was it formed in pursuance of a charter from the Durbar. Held, further, that section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies (Act. I of 1935) is prohibitory in nature and cannot be excluded from consideration even though the bar of that provision has been raised at this late stage. It is not confined to affording a party a protection, of which he may avail himself or not as he pleases after he may have been guilty of a breach of law, and does not include only to afford a party protection against his alleged illegal transaction but to establish the existence of an illegal contract which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked. The doctrine of legitimate expectation is founded on certain principle basics applicable in a civilised society governed by statute and it is well settled that a public body cannot be allowed to derive its aid from any extraneous considerations, not wholly irrelevant or extraneous considerations or extraneous consideration such as irrelevant considerations or irrational considerations should be made for the benefit of the public interest. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co., ([1867) L. R. 52 I. A. 126 and V. G. Rangaswami vs Kuppusami, (1924) L L.R. 52 1), referred to.

Respondents, who are respondents in two special leave petitions, moved the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 for quashing the order taking cognizance of an offence against them. The High Court quashed the proceedings on the ground that: (1) the learned Magistrate acted contrary to the provisions of Section 210(1) of the Cr. P.C.; (2) since the investigation was in progress in relation to the same offences, the learned Magis trate would be required to stay the proceedings; and (3) the trial Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance against the accused. Hence this appeal by special leave. PG NO 469 PG NO 468 Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy and object of the Wild Life laws have a long history and are the result of an increasing awareness of the compelling need to restore the serious ecological imbalances introduced by the depradations inflicted on nature by man, which is based on the fundamental concept that nature is "a series of complex biotic communities of which a man is an inter dependant part" and that it should not be given to a part to tresspass and diminish the whole. [465B C] 1.2 There was no eye witness in this case and there is no identification of the petitioner in any manner whatsoever to sustain the allegation even prima facie for the offence alleged. Therefore, even if the jurisdictional police purported to register a case for an alleged offence against the Act, Section 210 (1), would not be attracted having regard to the position that cognizance of such an offence can only be taken on the complaint of the Officer mentioned in Section.

The petitioner was convicted and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment under the and also to a fine of Rs. 10,000/ . The High Court dismissed his appeal in limine. In the special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the appellant that : (1) Setting aside the conviction order in a Special Leave Petition or of an appeal against acquittal or acquittal did not spell out the details of bail and so the magistrate ordered that a surety hl a sum of Rs 10,00/ be produced which he in actual impact was a double denial of bail benefit. Dismissing the special Leave petition, ^ HELD: (1)(a) Every liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on one 's own bond with or without sureties may not strictly arise. Even so, the guidelines which prevail with the Supreme Court when granting suspension of sentence must, in a broad sense, have relevance to what the Code indicates except where special circumstances call for a different course. Moreover, the advocate who participated many of them did covered the wider area of release under the Code, whether with orwithout sureties, and that is why he should be released on bail, or on his own recognizance unless it is shown that there was substantial risk it is appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release. If a Magistrate is Satisfied after making an enquiry into the condition and background of the accused that the accused has his roots in the community and is nor likely to abscond, he can safely release the accused on order to appear or on its own recognizment. [441 D G] (b) The legal literature, Indian and Anglo American, on bail jurisprudence lends countenance to the contention that bait loosely used, is comprehensive enough to cover release on ones own bond without sureties but it is necessary to attain if possible to a degree of precision which a person reading in bad faith cannot misunderstand. There are many considerations which deter an accused from running away from justice and risk of financial loss is only one of them and that too not a major one. Bail Project shows that even without monetary bail it has been possible to secure the presence of the convict at the trial in quite a large number of cases. Moreover.

The question in dispute before the Income tax authorities was whether the business called 'Castle ' at Bombay was a branch of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to 'Cart ' in computation of capital invested for the purpose of section 15C. The respondent preferred an application under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for an order directing the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. The Tribunal rejected the application but granted a certificate to appeal to the Supreme Court. Held: (i) Under the Income Tax Act, it is for the tribunal to decide all questions of fact; the High court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the Tribunal. The refusal of the Tribu nal, on the view that a question of law does not arise out of an order of this Court is not conclusive. (ii) Non inclusion of the income of 'C&T] In the present case it is not open to the assessee to contend that the constitution and ownership of the two businesses "were the same. The High Court had, therefore, misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. (iii) But the refusal of this Tribunal on the ground that a certain question of fact does not require the Tribunal 's jurisdiction to decide is not decisive. Non inclusion must be a relevant circumstance, and its effect has to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assistant Commis sion had relied.

The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition filed by the appellant challenging the validity of the later order was amended in the amended petition. It was amended by amending the petition that after the disposal of the writ petition, the Secretary of the Department was directed to file his personal affidavit. In the Representation Petition filed by him the Minister concerned stated that he had deviated from the normal procedure while passing the impugned order. The High Court ordered that the Minister should file his affidavit. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order of the High Court adding the Minister as a party to the writ Petition, HELD: 1. The direction for impleading of the Minister in a petition was given by the High 'Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, this Court does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal insofar as it has directed that the Secretary be impleaded as a necessary party. [97 A E] 2. In view of the fact that the Chairman was also directed to constitute an inter fular party, the High COurt erred in directing that the Chief Minister be impleaded in one petition. The other part of the order whereby the Minister con cerned was directed by the 'High Court with a direction to apprise it the Minister who was also ordered to file the personal affidavit is set aside; The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala Cantonment for realisation of arrears of rent due under a lease in favour of the respondent under section 259 of the Act on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of 'rent on the basis of a lease In favour of by the respondent. The magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the Respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge, Ambala contending that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of monthly rent due Under section 259 and also under section 258 Of the Act. The Sessions judge accepted the view of the trial court and held that it was not necessary for the Magistrate to recover arrears ofrent due under the lease. On further appeal by special leave the appellant contended: 1) that the magistrate acting under section259 of the, acts as a persona designata and therefore his order is not revisable under sections 435/439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and since the Magistrate was acting under that section he had no power to realise arrears of "rent due" under section 260; (2) that there was no case where the Act did not provide for recovery of rent by the Board. HELD: Per Wanchoo and Sikri, JJ.). The powers conferred on the Board by section 259 are not unguided or uncanalised but they are subject to judicial review which cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. Section 258 expressly authorised the Board to recover all arrears of land revenue and "other payments" under the Rules by resorting to section 259. [344 C] 2 : (a) The provisions of the . must be construed strictly in accordance with the plain meaning that implied on reading a statute it is clear that there are no words used by the legislature to limit or restrict them so as to make it mandatory for all the purposes for which the legislature has been empowered. [345 A C] (b) Section 259 does not bar the right of the Board as an owner or holder of land and buildings to take action for recovery on land and building provided such rent is claimable by a Board under the Act or the Rules, but under the leases there is no provision whatsoever in the Act which expressly made rent claimable or recoverable by either of the two authorities specified therein. [346 F] (c) Section 258 does not debar the right to recover rent on land, buildings and buildings only if such rent was recoverable by a board under the , or the rules framed thereunder. [347 C] The Board has the power to dispose of lands, if any, which is in excess of the amount payable by it under the provisions of that Act and the Rules which empower the Boardto let out the land or buildings upon the ground contained therein are entirely outside the section and the right cannot be taken away by that section.

The respondent company terminated the services of the appellant company on 12.7.73 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and whose services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The appellant 's claim for termination of his services by the respondent company was turned down by the Labour Court but the High Court held that the appel lant is required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. Some of the documents relate to matters of publicity in the area of the area and the action taken to ameliorate stocks. The Labour Court further held that there was apparent error on the face of record which was apparent on the ques tion of the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant ' s pantled his case before the Labour court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [474E] Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Company vs Burmah Ram Shell Management and Staff; ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J. Dechane distributors vs State 476 Kerala and others (1974 11 LLJ 9), referred to. 2.1 The object of this enactment and the employees covered by the provi sions also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of 'workman under the Industrial lice Act as they stood in 1973 when he was his service. [473E F] Burmahs Oil Storage and Distribution Company v Burmah Trading & Staff; , ; D B.S Nagraj V Labour Officer , Kamal and Others, 1973 11 LLJ. 971 referred to 3.2 It is seen from the facts found that the appellant was employed to do canvassing andpromotion sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study the market condition. He was also required to suggest about the advertisement in markets and melas, advertise ments including the need for posters, holder and cinema slide. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could not be termed as either manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical in nature. The supervising work of other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promotion in the areas of his operation. Such a person cannot be termed "workman" is also the ratio of the decision of this Court in Burmah Oil Storage And Distribution Company V Burmah Petroleum Management and Serv ices; and D. S. Nagaraj vs Labour Offi cer, Kamal & Ors., 1973 FJ.R. (41) P 440, considered. 4.3 The management to pay some compensation is necessary to meet the ends of justice. [418F] 3.4 The appellant was employee employed to carry out the duties of local sales men and local travelling salesmen appointed in the Area of his opera tion as well but it was only incidental for his main work of canvassing, promotion in, normally would come within its definition i.e. manual, unskilled,/or clerical nature and that the provisions of the U.P. Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1970 defines "sales promotion employees" as meaning a person employed or engaged in any establishment for hire or reward to do any work relating to promotions of sales or business or both. This Act is to apply in the first instance to every establishment engaged in pharmaceuticals industry. It enables the Central Government by notification to apply the pro ceedings to any other establishment engaged In any notified industry.

The appellant State Government issued a notification under section 182 of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959 ( 'the Code ' ') for evicting the appellant company from the land in question. The appellant Company then filed suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction against the appellant Company. The Trial Court dismissed the suit, but it was made consequent on the failure of the Company to pay rent agreed upon between the Government and the Company subsequent to the unconditional withdrawal by the Company of its Civil Appeal No. 299 of 1967 which was pending in this Court. This appeal has been brought before this court by the company against an earlier judgement of the High Court dated 30.6. 1931 in First Appeal No 1 of 1961 whereby the High 'Court confirmed the judgment of the Trial Court and dismissing the Company 's appeal, holding that the land admeasuring 496.05 acres was held by the appellant State in terms of the lease granted by the State and the company was not a `pakka ' tenant ' and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. The company entered into a contract for lease with the Gwalior State Government (Sanitary Engineering Department) for a period of one year in Samvat, 1999. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed suit Nos. 14 and 16 of 1960 before the Additional Collector cum District Magistrate, Gwalior, on 14.10.1977 for declaration that the appellant was not the `phakka ' s tenant ', and did neither enjoy the rights of a Gair maurusi ' nor were the lands included in Ryotwari village. The trial court dismissed the Suit, but the High Courts allowed the appeal preferred by the respondent company. Aggrieved by the Order of the Additional District Magistrate dated 1.101977 passed on the reference made to it by the Additional Superintend ent of the Revenue, appellant Company filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD:1. The High Court had found in the earlier proceeding that the Land in question was held as 'a person holding land from the State Government and it has never been an ordinary terms as defined in the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (for short the Code). [181B] 2. Under sub section (1) of section 180 of the Code it is provided that a lessee may be ejected from his land by order of a Revenue Officer on one or more of the following grounds namely: (i) that he has failed to pay the rent for a Period of three months from the date on which it became due; or (ii) that, he has used such land for purpose other than for which it was granted; or that he had contravened any of the terms and conditions of the grant: Provided that no order for ejectment of a Government lessee under this sub section shall be passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard in his defence". [181C E] In the instant case, the finding of the trial court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. The finding of High Court to the effect that the Company was not holding the land as a "pakta" s tenant has become by the unconditional withdrawn withdrawal of the appeal from this Court only in 1971.

In their writ petitions filed by the landholders challenging the validity of sections 40, 41 and 42 of the Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act 15 of 1965. The High Court held that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 which provided for payment of compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent was in consistent with article 3 1 A, proviso 2, and is on that account unconstitutional. On appeal to this Court it was urged that when the principal Act was enacted it became law in force as defined in section 2(5a). HELD : (i) The expression "law in force" must be "construed only in the constitutional sense and not in the sense of its actual operativeness". What the expression " law in ' force occurring in section 1(3) must be 'destrued ' only in it the constitutional way. [595 E] (ii) The law relating to ceiling limit viz., IV of the principal, Act was never made operative by a notification and was repealed by Act 15 Of 1965 which came into force on July 1, 1949. [596 H] (iii)(a) By virtue of section 45 of the Principal Act "the interests of the person to whom the surplus lands relate and of all land holders mediately or immediately under whom the lands were being held stand extinguished and the lands vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances". This is clearly compulsory acquisition of land within the meaning of article 31(2) of the Constitution and the compensation determined merely at fifteen per cent times the market price may not prima facie be regarded as determination of compensation according to the principles specified by the Act. But article 31A which applies to the statute in question provides by the first clause that "Notwithstanding anything contained in Article 13 no law providing for the acquisition by the State of any land in an estate under the personal cultivation of the holder, compensation shall not be less than the marketvalue thereof." [595 C] (b) The argument that section47 incorporated by . Act 13 Of 1965 is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitu tion and therefore the power to bring into force the provisions of the Travancore Act was exercisable by the successor State.

The widow of her husband 's property had a son named Mathurbhai who died in 1924 leaving behind him his widow and a daughter Rukmini. Shankarbhai, the widow of the widows, filed a suit claiming possession of the properties during their life time but later on left with no issue. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that there was a severance of joint status by an informal partition between Mathurbhai and Kashibhai but he dismissed the Suit on the view that the widow 's estate was in this case completely extinguished by adverse possession exercised by the defendants, she had in fact exercised no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of reversions. In appeal the High Court held that there could not be any difficulty in properly deciding the question whether a gift made by widow prior to surrendering her husband estate could be challenged by the reversioner during the period of the widow "s life", and that on a surrender by the Hindu widow of 's husband ' 's properties without any justifiable necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse Possession against her the interest created was to be deemed severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrenders must take it subject to such prior interest. Held, that the question for determination was whether there could be any doubt that prior rights derived from the widow were not only for the protection of the material interest of her deceased husband ' s relations but also for the surrender which she had herself made; and the reversionary right to challenge it was no part of the estate in favour Of the reversioner. Tolarammal vs The Madras High Court, 57, relied on. Held further, that there is no warrant in Hindu law for the proposition that in case of alienation by a Hindu widow 'of her husbands property without any valid justification or in this ease of alienation, by a stranger acquired title against her, the interest create was to he deemed to be severed from her inheritance and that she could sue for possession at once. The right of the reversioner to challenge its decision is no part Of the widow"s estate at all and, therefore, could not rank as an heir so long as the widow remained alive. The words "in whichever sense otherwise appears in the law of limitation include the rights which have accrued during the life time of the testator or her husband.

On February 11, 1984 the Cotton Mills Company (the Company) was acquired by Mangturam Jaipuria and his family in 1946. The shares were transferred to the State Government of Uttar Pradesh. There were serious labour troubles in its factory and its work virtually became paralysed. In 1970, the Company filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 against the erstwhile Company claiming oppression and mismanagement of the Polytex Company by him. It was alleged that the appointment of Shri Sitaram Jaipro as Managing Director of Swadeshi Polytex Ltd., be and is hereby terminated prior to the expiry of his term in exercise of the powers conferred by article 110 of the Constitution of India. The Board of Directors of the Company after hearing all parties passed a resolution under section 169 of the Act directing the holding of the meeting of the company and that meeting shall be held in accordance with the order of the High Court notwithstanding any order of injunction etc. issued by any court or authority in India or to be issued hereafter. The appellants challenged the validity of the proceedings before the High Courts on the following grounds: (1) Section 295A of the is a charging order under English Law and it cannot therefore be said that the attachment of shares under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act, 1901 takes away the right of the Cotton Mill Company to exercise its voting rights in respect of the shores in question; (2) The power of the Board of directors to deal with the property comprised in the appointment (both property subject to a floating charge and property subject upto a fixed charge), except subject to the charge, are paralyzed" which was relied on by the appellants is not of much use. (3) The attachment of the shares in the Polyester Company held by the Cotton mills Company had not deprived the Cotton Company of its right of voting in respect thereof; and (4) The company could not therefore join the other requisitionists in issuing the notice under section 17 of the Pre vary Act calling upon the Polyiumtex Company to call an extraordinary general meeting. (5) The Board had not been empowered either to withdraw or modify the resolution passed by the Central Government whereby it had taken over the management of Sideshow Cotton Mills along with five other industrial units belonging to the Cotton Bank Company. The High Court held that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collector in respect Of the shares held by it, the attachment cannot be taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice. Dismissing the appeal ^ HELD: (i) It is not disputed that if the 10 lakhs shares held on February 11 and March 13, 1977 were omitted from consideration, the remaining requisitionists would not have sufficient voting strength to issue a notice under s 169 of that Act. [ 869 A B] (ii) Section 116A provides that Rules 2 to 4 of Order XL of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 shall apply in relation to a Receiver appointed under that section. A Receiver whose name is entered in the Register of Members cannot exercise any of those rights unless in a proceeding to which the company concerned is a party and an order is made therein.

The petitioners, who were plaintiffs in a suit for declaration that they were the owners of the suit land along with some others, filed a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala was not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering their possession. The suit was contested by the defendants. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the suit was simply one of title to the suit property, it was not necessary to decide whether the suit lands were shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlatted, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Aggrieved by the said finding, the Gram Panchayats filed a revision petition before the High Court which came to the conclusion that the issues involved in this case were not triable by a Civil Court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The defendants preferred an appeal before the Additional Senior Subordinate Judge and contended that the suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayats had expressly claimed that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat land deh and that that the plaintiffs had no right or title in it. This question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Act and not by the Civil Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contention of the Panchayat before the trial court was that the Collector had only stated in the plaint that the Land in question was 'Gali Sheh re aam ' or a throughfare belonging to the Gram Sabha which was being used by the plaintiff as an approach to his house for about 30 years and had prayed for an injunc tion restraining the defendants from interfering with their right. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question is shamlat Dev deh or does not appear to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act or in respect of any matter which the Commissioner, or the Commissioner is empowered by or under the Punjab Act to determine. [835D E] 1.2 Section 2(g) of the Himachal Pradesh Village Common Land (Regulation ) Act,1961 defines the expression " Shamlat deh" as under: "2(g), 'shamlat deh". includes (1) lands described in the revenue records as shamilat deh excluding abadi deh; (ii) shamlat tikkas; (iii) shamil gikkas. [861A] Bhagu and Ors., vs Ram Sarup & Ors., [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366, distinguished.

The appellant Board had been giving supply of electricity to the consumers. The Electricity Board charged consumption charges from different consumers for non payment of bills within stipulated period. The supply was duly made with a consequential liability to pay for each day 's consumption, the so called security deposit was not a deposit in the real sense for the consumers to claim the benefit of interest Act. The appellant Board contended before it that it did not have power to charge penal interest on the cash security deposits as the Board compels industrial consumers to secure against default in payment of electricity bills. The quantum of demand was substantially reduced by the Board and by the other consumers, the excess energy was reduced in a sum equal to 3% and the maximum rate payable for supply of energy. It was contended for the appellant Board that there was no law obligation to pay interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms of Clause 20 (a) & (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. The respondent Board, on consideration of facts placed before it and after hearing the parties, held that the supply of power to the appellant was in the nature of cash for one month and bank or insurance guarantee for two months. It, therefore, prayed for allowing interest at the rate of 12% p.a. from the date of deposit at the rates of 3 per cent. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals the Court, HELD: 1.1 There is nothing to indicate under the scheme of the Electricity Act or Schedule VI of the Supply Act that interest must be paid on the security deposit. [278C] 1.2 The true nature of transaction in these cases is one of advance payment of charges for consumption of electricity estimated for a period of approximately three months. In one sense, the consumption security deposit represents only a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer. [279E] 2.2 There was nothing to show that under the Scheme of the Act and Schedule VI, interest must also be paid if there are special reasons why interest should not be allowed namely: (a)(i) where money or other property has been deposited as security for the performance of an obligation imposed by law or contract from the previous date of the deposit; (ii) where cash security is required to deposit with the Electricity Board a sum in cash equivalent to estimated three months consumption charges.

The first petitioner, a Telecommunication Research Centre under the Telecommunication research Centre was engaged in the research and development work concerning the telecommunication equipment for the use of the Depart ment and in advising the P&T Board on relevant technical matters relating to the introduction of new equipment and technology in the existing public communication net work. The recruitment to the different cadres in the Telecommuni cation Research Centre is now being made under the Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I (Telecommunications Re search Centre) Rules, 1962 framed by the President under the provi so to Article 309 of the Constitution of India. During the period between 1956 & 1962 and further till 1965 all the Class I posts of the Scientific and technical arduca ical officers Grade I were being filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission, (the petitioners belong to this category; (b) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the P &T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India, there was consensus on the question of granting of Special Pay to the direct recruits as in the case of transferred officers as can be seen from the letter written by the Association on the petitioners. (c) That the petition ers (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to the TeleCommi neation Research Organisation for a limited purpose are not entitled to any Special Pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telecommunications Service who are working in the telecommuni nies Research Centre discharge same functions as the petitioners and are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is stated that the total number of officers who are thus getting Special Pay was of the order of 275 while only about 25 officers, who were direct recruits working in that Organisation are not given special pay to the others holding the same posts. A number of representations had been made and all in vain. It appears that at the official meeting held in May 1979 with Shri J.A. Dave Secretary, Communications, Gov ernment of India there was dis crimination on account of the displacement of some of some officers from different cadres to the transferred officials who are being recruited, while on the other hand the officers drawn from the ITS cadre, when posted in TRC are required to perform duties, which is not in their general line. In view of the aforesaid categorical statement of the petitioners that the offi cers who are likely to be affected by the decision were not impleaded as parties by name to these petitions, we disposed of them with the observation that the first question should be left open to be decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal. On appeal this Court in the Writ Petitions of the peti tions assailing the grant of Special pay at Rs. 300 would be open to the Central Government and if so it should be raised before the Central Adminis trative Tribunal. Allowing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: It is seen from a perusal of the answer that the Govern ment had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred proce cution officials and that the transfers officials had to be paid extra amount by way of Special Tax Pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same. [1010G] The first question relating to grant of special pay requires 1011 to be settled by this Court is whether the petitioners are not competent and are not able to discharge their duties. All the direct candi recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Uncom situa tion Research Centre. They do the same job as the transferred Officials. [1001C] The second question relating tO grant of promotional opportunities to the petitioners according to the Recruitment Rules is left open for being agitated before the appropriate Tribunal. No costs. P.S. Petitions allowed.

The Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 as in force immediately before the commencement of the 1965 Act is extended to the rest of the State. The C.P. and Berar Act was repealed. As a result, the Act now extends to the whole of the state. Chapter I contains only three sections : Section 2 deals with the extent, commencement and application of the Act and section 3 is the definition section. Chapter II contains only one sections : section 2 deals in respect of an order, matter or change referred to in the said proviso. Under section 4 every employer shall submit for approval to the Commissioner, of Labour in the prescribed manner standing orders regulating the relations between him and his employees; and punishment including warning, censure, fine, suspension or dismissal for misconduct pending enquiry into alleged misconduct and the acts or omissions which constitute misconduct. The appellants were employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him in respect thereof. The respondent contended that the charge was not proper; that the Head Office of the appellant had no authority to deal with his case under Standing Orders, that no evidence was allowed or filed on behalf of the employer and that the finding was based only on his statement and in particular his cross examination. He further urged that the findings of the Inquiry Officer were perverse, that the order of dismissal was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Court directed reinstatement of the third respondent with all back wages.

The suit property in dispute belonged to the appellants and in which a cinema was running, they were served notices on them claiming their right to contin ue in possession after 31.7.1971 as tenants from month to month. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed before Munsif Ranchi a case purporting to be an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The respondents contested the application contending that the application under s.12 was not maintainable since even on assuming the argument of the respondents to be correct, the appellants should succeed. The Trial Judge accepted the appellant 's case that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company and the legal represen tatives of late S.N. Ganguli, the original lessee continued as tenants under the lease after due attornment and were liable to eviction after expiry of the lease period on 31. 7.1971. The respondents however, differed on several questions of fact which, in view of the findings of the Trial Court and appellate Court, were not necessary to be detailed. The parties led full evidence both oral and documentary. On an elaborate trial the learned Munsif accepted the appellants ' case that the respondents are the successors In interest of late Seth Coal Company and the property was owned by Managing Committee of R.M. Ganguli who on his death was succeeded by his legal representative and came to a finding that they are the heirs and successors respectively. The Court accordingly directed the respond ents to vacate the premises. On appeal, the Judicial Commissioner agreed with the findings arrived at by the trial court on merits and concluded in paragraph 48 of thejudg ment accordingly. The Judicial Commissioner accordingly modified the decision of the learned Trial Court in so far as the learned 879 Munsif had directed that his order would be executed and the respondents would be evicted from the premises on their failure to vacate within the time allowed. On the second appeal, it was contended for the appellants that: (1) The appellants ' application under sec. 12 of Bihar Buildings(Lease, rent and Evic tration Control Act 1947 before the Civil Court was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise; (2) The respondent 's application under Section 12 was not barred as it only because even on the assuming the appeal of the appellants one month 's notice under section 10 of the Act from the tenant, the application of the appellant was not entertained before the Munsif, and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1 (a) It is the same court before which both a suit under section 11 and an application for eviction are to be filed. The jurisdiction of the Court is concerned. [975C] Madho Bibi vs Hazari Mal Marwari, AIR 1929 Patna 47; Lakshmi Narain Singh vs Ram Lakhan Lal, AIR 1930 Pat. 481; Lachhoo vs Munnilal Babu Lal Lal, ILR 1935 Allaha bad; Lach ener vs Munni Lal Babu Lal, , AIR 1930 Patna 472 and Ram Prakash vs Bhagwan Das, AIR 1934 Pat. 474; referred to. (b) The power is vested in the Controller. But as regards the question of dealing with eviction of tenants under section II and extension of period of lease under section I, the civil court is the proper forum. In the present case it is the Civil court Ranchi which is the appropriate Court either for filing a suit for eviction under section ll or making an application unders Sec tion 12.

% The appellant a registered Society, filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the Court of the District Judge, Jaipur City. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as Secretary, by another lawyer claiming to have been elected as the Secretary. The trial court allowed the suit to be withdrawn. According to the case of the appellant Hari Narain Swami was not elected as a mem bress and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. Since no notice was given of his application for withdrawal of the same, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was elect ed on 4.9.74 and according ly, the appellant was elected from the office of sti ties. According, a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by Hari Narain vide his application dated 24.11.73. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The High Court dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant in the following circumstances: (1) That the application under Section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Proce dure, for restoration of the Suit is maintainable; (2) That a dispute relating to the election of Secretary of the society had arisen between the parties which ultimately went before the Registrar of Cooperative Societies who decided the matter in favour of Laxman Dasr Swami and against Hari Narain Goswami. (3) That Although the trial Court had vacated its previous order regarding satisfaction on the ground that it was obtained by the judgment debtor 's fraud on the court, the errors in the judgment of the trial com pany Court were serious; and (4) that the sole right to file a fresh suit cannot be exercised. Allowing this appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The principle is correctly discussed in the judg ment in Sadho Saran Rai & Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483, referred to. (b) A court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The principle was correctly settled in Sadhho Saran 's cases. That the factum of the consent can be investigated in summary proceedings but the reality of the permission cannot be so investigated. [237E F] (c) A Court has inherent powers to correct Its own proceedings When it is satis fied that in view of the High Court, while confirming the order, said that in the exercise of inherent power under section 15 1, a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it, and that the party had actually consented to it. But if the case is factually correct that Hari Narain machine was not its elected secretary and was, therefore, not authorised to withdraw t the suit on several grounds, the prayer for withdrawal was not made on behalf of the appel lant at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the Court being misled. [ 237D E] 2(a). The principle has been followed in this country for more than a century. In Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalil Pvt.

The appellant was charged along with the accused Nos. 2, 3, 5 and 6 with having on or about July 11, 1953, transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes of the Denomination of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi Joshi for Rs.1,800 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate 's Court confirmed the conviction and sentences imposed upon the appellant by both the courts. Held, that the Ordinance in question was not in operation during the period of emergency but would cease to be in force on July 11. 1953, when it was promulgated on April 1, 1946, which was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed except with the result that it continued in operation until it became repealed. In view of the provisions contained in sections 72 and 74 of the Constitution of India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, the Ordinance having been promulgated during the periods between June 27, 1940 and April 1 1946, the new notes continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India, though the position in Jammu and Kashmir was that until it Was repealed by the promulgation of section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act (LXII of 1947), the Ordinance continued in operations even after April 1. The Ordinance having lapsed automatically came to an end on the expiry of January 12, 1946.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death, for the murder of one S and the other under section 307 I. P.C. Consultation with the deceased was found dead by a rifle fired from a rifle recovered from him. The deceased S was produced before the Additional Sessions Judge who enhanced the sentence to imprisonment for life. The appellants contended that there was no indefeasible principle or policy evolved by this Court in Rajendra Prasad 's case which laid down the guidelines for imposing death penalty, and that the sentence imposed upon them was neither discriminatory nor excessive, nor excessive or disproportionate or unduly harsh for such an act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law of punishment under section302 I.p.C (as amended) is nothing but a mandatory rule of universal application. The fact that death penalty and the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused are constitutionally valid does not detract from such a provision. [1069H 1070A] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Rajasthan, ; referred to. The reliance placed upon section 354(3) of the Code is not warranted. The decision cannot, therefore, be construed as laying down any policy of general applicability. A decision on a question of sentence depending upon the facts and circumstances of a particular case can never be regarded as binding precedent, much less 'law declared ' within the meaning of article 141 of the Constitution so as to bind all Courts in the country. [ 1069G H] 2. The purpose of sentencing is to impose maximum punishment for murder and the courts have to choose between a sentence of death and a sentence for life; while under section 354 (3) Cr. Pc., 1973, the court is enjoined with a duty to record 'special reasons ' in case the extreme penalty is awarded. But the question whether the death sentence should be awarded or not must depend upon the circumstances obtaining in such case. When a sentence is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High Court under section 366(1) of Cr.P., and the accused also has right of appeal to the High court under 5. It would, therefore be manifest that it is neither feasible nor legally permissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence of ' death on a conviction for murder under section inflicted 302 I P. C.

The appellant was compulsorily retired by the Commissioner of Income Tax. The contention that there had been an enquiry in 1949, by Shri R. N. Srivastava, Deputy Director Investigation or against the punishing authority was turned down by the High Court and he was reinstated with consequential benefits of pay ment. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended: (i) That the findings of fact namely that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental rules and was also barred by rules of natural justice; (ii) That there had already been an inquiry in 1949 by Shri A. K. Bose, Deputy Directors Investigation or who held the enquiry, were pursuing the appellant for some unknown reason which was not mentioned anywhere. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The plea that the appellant has been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous inquiry. Therefore, the two authorities cited, namely The State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N., Roy Biswas and R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State do not help the appellant. [585D E] (ii). Without considering the other material whether any evidence which the appellant tried to produce was really wrongly excluded and at what stage and for what reasons. All these were questions of fact which should be initially raised in the departmental trial. After that, if there was any patent error a writ petition lay. [587E F] (iii) It is true that the High Courts have considered at some length all relevant questions raised. [584F G] (iv). The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that it would vitiate the whole departmental trial, which can affect the final decision, it could not be material. In the case before this Court, it has not even been shown how the witnesses whose production was said to have been disallowed could help the appellants ' case on specific charges.

The appellants who were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh contended before the Sales Tax authorities that they were not the last purchaser but the M.M.T.C. was the last buyer within the state, and therefore, the M/s. V.S.S., was liable to pay the tax. The Sales Tax Authorities came to the conclusion that the contracts between the appel lants and their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis were integrally connected with the contract entered into by them with the M Public E tee Company. Accordingly, they held that these contracts were linked and was con tractally connected. The High Court took the view that there existed a bond between the ac cused and the M;M. T.C., on board the ship. In the Special Leave Petition to this Court it was contended that there were six contracts and they had been the case of the appellants that the contract was different, and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. On behalf of the State, it was submitted that there 'the contracts between them and the foreign buyers were two separate and independent con tract of sale; that the High Court erred in holding that all contracts between they were related, and that even if the M was the one who was the exporter within the States of Andhra P.K., the M being the last vanted State, was liable for payment of the tax under the Sales tax Law. Alternatively it was argued that there had been a breach of contract between the appellants and the G.M.,T.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" As the respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings, the reference was heard ex parte. The appellant also moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent inter alia contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of this extended period of probation, his service was terminated by letters dated 12 10 1974 and December 8, 1973 with effectfrom August 19, 1974; but he was not found suitable for the post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court granted an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for set aside the exparte award and sought permission to participated in the proceeding which motion, motion was also granted. On examination of evidence both oral and documentary, it was held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper nor unjustified and that the claim of the Appellant was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The termination would constitute retrenchment within the meaning section 2(oo) and in absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25F, termination was held to be invalid. [528H; 532A] (b) It does not bring about a cessation of service of the workman and the workman continues to be in service. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25 F. [525G] (c) Section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a workman is not in employment for a period of 12 calendar months, but has rendered service for a periods of 240 days within the period of twelve calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date, i.e., the date on which calculation is to be made has actually worked under that employer for not more than 240 days. [544G] 2(a). Section 25F provides a deeming fiction in that where a workmen is in service for for a certain period he shall be deemed to be In continuous service, for a minimum period of one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. It is not necessary for the purposes of sub section (2) (a) that the workman should be in continuous services for a more than one years despite the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for 240 days in a period or six months. Therefore, both on principle and precedent it must be held that section 25B comprehends sick and non sick industries would receive a set back by this impermissible assumption. [ GondG] 4(b). It is enough that he had worked for 240 day in a year of 12 months and, indisputably, therefore, his case falls within Section 25 B (2)(a) and he shall he deemed to have been in continuous serv ice for a continuous period of two years for the pur poses of Chapter V.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of certain misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The appellant challenged the authority of the ' Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submit that the procedure followed by the Enquiry Officer in making the inquiry was irregular. Held, that the protection under article 311 (2) of the Constitution applies as much to a temporary public servant and one could only be discharged at any time during the period of probation. In the present case the enquiry was for ascertaining whether the appellant who was a temporary employee should be continued in service or should be discharged under the terms of his employment, and even if a probationer in an enquiry on charges of misconduct was found to have committed the misdemeanour charged against him. Section 2 (2)(a) of Punjab State Act, 1948, defines by way of punishment that it includes punishment for disorder, but does not include punitive action including dismissal or removal from service when the appellant 's appointment was terminated. The order of termination of employment did not cast a stigma on his competence nor imposed penalty upon him. There was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order terminating his services for unsatisfactory work and conduct, because, it put a stigma for his ability to be confirmed, and the appellant had been given no such opportunity as provided by article 311 of the Constitu tion. State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das, ; , followed.

% The question that arose for consideration related to the interpretation of clause (b) of sub section (2) of Section 133 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, which was answered by this Court in L.V.D. vs State of Jammu & Kashmir, ; , whereby it was held that the Commission shall be consulted on the suitability of the candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers, and if the Governor has been consulted, appointed another person as Professor in accordance with its requirement, he may make regulations specifying the matters in which either generally or in any particular class of cases, it shall not be necessary for the Commission to be consulted. The question involved was whether section 133(2)(b) was attracted, because the two rules which had been replaced by the rules made under clauses (a) and (b), were "not at all attracted" in the matter of making promotions in the same service". Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: 1. The second requirement is that the recommendation for selection should be made on the basis of marks obtained by the candidates. [875H; 874A A] 2.1 Since it has been specifically stated by this Commission that it consulted the Commission under section 133 of ' the Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea in regard to the principles to be followed in making the promotion, to the posts of Professors, has not been done. [874E] 2(a) The High Court erred in holding that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. With this finding, the rest of the case for decision by the Bench concerned. [861C] (b ) On the facts, which have been brought on the record, it is difficult to sustain the view that a Commission was not consulted either in regard thereto nor was it permissible for the appellants to advance their arguments with reference to article 16 of the Con stitution. [871H; 876A B] 2.(a) It would thus appear that the High Court was wrong in holding on the facts which have already been brought and brought on record that the State Government at first framed rules for selections, appointments to be made to posts of persons from different service, and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another. [ 876A] 2 (b). The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise is a matter which will have to consider at this stage, whether that section has been correctly interpreted and whether the Public Service Commission for the State of J&K was consulted in accordance 'with its requirements. [877C] 3.1 (a). The decision of this Court is quite correct and no other interpretation is really permissible on the plain language of the clause. [ 871B C] L.

HELD : The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred upon a citizen under article 19(1) of the Constitution. Article 194(3) which provides for powers, privileges and immunities of the House of Commons of the British Parliament of the United Kingdom and of its members and committees at the commencement of this Constitution lays down that " until so defined, they shall be those of the Houses of Indian Legislature of the State of Bihar and until then they shall 'be those of these Assembly of the Indian Dominion of India. " The question for decision was whether by virtue of article 194(4) of our Constitution it was open to the House by a resolution of the Council of Privileges to decide what was a breach or not. Held, that the law made by the Legislature in respect of the powers, privilege and immunities enjoyed by the House thereof were competent. The impugned resolution of 356 Business was void on the ground that it violated article 19 (1) (a) of ' the Constitution and was not saved under article 2(2). It was reasonable to infer from its language the decision that a law imposing any restriction on the right to make speech within the meaning of cl. (4) was therefore void. Held further, that section 194 (3) of I1) did not violate article 19 as it contravened article 19 and was valid. Sri Tipper vs The State of Madras ; , applied. Per Subba Rao J: Article 194 (2) which authorises the House to decide the true effect of the Speaker 's directions in regard to the procedure of the Legislature contained in cls. (1), (2), and (3), which deal with powers, immunities, privileges etc., of a House of Parliament and of the members and the committees of a house of such legislatures, was valid as it did not infringe article 19, and that the impugned resolution did not contravene article 194 as it purported to do. The House of Lords, upon many occasions, had declared the publication of its proceedings without the authority of the Assembly to be a breach of privilege but that by reason of article 212 (1 ) it was not necessary for the Parliament to make any law defining the powers privileges, privileges or immunities just as the Australian Parliament had not made any under section 49 Of the Indian Constitution corresponding to article 194 (4). The impugned order did not offend article 19 because it purported merely to regulate the procedure for removal of the member and committees but also authorised imposition of a duty on them which might have been passed by the Speaker.

The Respondent College which is an institution which grew out of a school established in 1856 was taken over by the Government in pursuance of the unanimous resolution of the Managing Committee of February, 1970 and in pursuance thereof, the transfer to the Govern ment was of all the assets of the college but without any liability. The managing committee continued to be liable for the outstanding liabilities, if any, of the College for which Government is not liable. The College after taking over was administered as a Government College. It was taken by the State in pursuance 0.E.S. (Orissa Education Service) Rules, 1971 that a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the Colleges and the Governor of the State. In the meantime, the Transfer to the Government was of the assets which were material for the purpose. The services of those who were not found suitable by the P.S.,C. (Public Services Service Commis sion) shall also be terminated with effect from the date of taking over and vesting them in the Government service, and that all the Respond ents were qualified to be referred to the P .S.C. for determination of their suitability to hold posts in Class I or II as the case may be. The appointments letters were, however, offered to. the Respondents under the terms and conditions of take over which have been already extracted.
