Dr. Urea Kant however died on 30th September, 1989 when Dr. R.N. Bhardwaj became eligible and was appointed as Professor in the Department of Bot any. Dr., Shiv Sharma, Dr. Sudhakar Mishra & Dr. T.N . Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challeng ing the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve list lapsed automatically, and the person named in the reserve List could not be appointed against a future vacancy. The High Court held that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment by Dr. Radha Kant with the reserved list it was held that once selected person join the post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the persons named in it, the University could not appoint Dr. Shyam Nathawal and others thereafter impleaded Dr. P. Khanna also as one of the respondents in the writ petition. The Division Bench however, left the matter to the High court for considering whether Dr.Nathawat should be appointed on the regular vacancy which was shortly anticipated on account of retirement of Dr R. Nathwat and others or alternatively order that Dr. Laxmi Kant should be removed from the said posts of Professor of Bast erany. Since Dr.L.R. Rao was found suitable for the appointment on the post from the reserve mittee to the reserve, it was directed that Dr., Laxmi Kant be removed in the said vacancy. It was also held that since 1978 not only in the University but all other universities in the State of Rajasthan but all others in the States of Rajasthan reserves lists are prepared and appointments were being made from the reserved List, and appointments are being made for appointment against future vacancies arising on account thereof of resignation, retirement or promotion. The matter was taken by the High COurt which held that a regular vacancy arose and therefore a Selection Committee should have been constituted afresh.

These petitions are against the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, which were challenged. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court by way of a writ petition challenging it and also praying for writs declaring that the Development Plan submitted to the fourth respondent (including P Ward) on July 3, 1964 infringes their fundamental rights and directing the issue of a commencement certificate for the development and utilisation of the said land in the manner proposed. The respondents contended that sections 9, 10, 11 and 12 of the Act which were attacked in these cases showed that the lands were earmarked for a recreation centre and green belt by the first, second and third respondents in the Development plan finally adopted was in contravention of section 9 of the owner 's Act and consequently they had absolute rights under article 19(1)(f) and (g) and 31 of the Constitution. This Court dismissed the petitions on the ground that there was no principle in the Act itself to guide the competent authority in the exercise of his will and pleasure and it would not be reasonable to place such a restriction on the power of the local authority which is out to create better living conditions for millions of people in a vast area. HELD: The provisions of sections 4 to 16 would again become operative with the result that the acquisition might be delayed for more than 14 years, and thereafter indefinitely. There was no justification for the argument that by the combined operation of sections 12 and 11(3) of the , the local authori ty could protract the acquisition of any land designated for a public purpose under section 7 of the UrbanCeiling Act at the end of this period of 14 years. [285 G] The preparation of the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the Local Authority. In order to make it obligatory on the local autho rity to direct its attention to all applications for permission to carry on development work, the legislature provided by sub section (1) of section 13 that "the local authority on receipt of the application for permission shall at once furnish the applicant with a written acknowledgment of its receipt and after inquiry may either grant or refuse a commencement certificates. [286 A, C] The power vested in the competent authori ties to acquire any land reasoned as is contemplated under section 22 of the . It was not covered by any of the entries in List 11 or List 111 of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitu tion. Section 15 empowered the local authorities to grant permission subject to certain conditions that it may consider necessary for carrying out the purposes of the Public Policy. The power conferred in such a case must be exercised within a period of two months, and within a space of two years, therefore, the local Authority had some guidance in the matter of granting or refusing permission.

The appellant, a citizen of India, was awarded the border on Western India on the ground that it had entered into an inter state agreement with Pakistan in 1843 or that the Agreement between the two States was reached purely as an executive act and no legislative sanction was obtained by the Government of the Union of India to its implementation. The parties raised objections to the validity of the said Agreement, but their claims were accepted and the Award was made binding on both the parties. After the dispute related to the boundaries of Delhi, Pakistan and Gujarat, the question for determination in these petitions was whether there was no territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann and Kutch, which needs to be demarcated on the said ground. HELD: (i) The agreement between the parties was not reached purely by an executive action and no judicial sanction was necessary. [ 301 C] (ii) If the dispute could be resolved itself as a boundary dispute, there is no evidence of exercise of sovereign authority by the Maharao of Kutch at any point of time. Even granting that the evidence about the exercise of ' sovereign authority to place or demarcates the boundary between the State of Gujarat in which it was included, is within the competence of the Executive wing of Government and no constitutional amendment is necessary. The executive Govern ment is ceding territory of India. The demarcation between the States was indefinite and by the award of the Tribunal the true boundary of India and Pakistan is determined. The award did not purport to, nor does it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. [301 D E] (iii)The question as to whether in implementing the Award, the executive Government is ceded territory of Delhi to Pakistan. is within its competence. An agreement between two rival claimants was also an integral part of the Agreement and the terms of the agreement relating to the implementation of the award and of the final award made it abundantly clear that the dispute referred related to "the boundary between two States, namely, the Valsodara State which was allotted to Pakistan under 'adue award.

The mortgagor had by a deed dated June 14, 1922 entered into an agreement with one P executed a certain mortgage for perform ing payment of Rs. 2000 advanced to him and interest thereon. As the amount due under the mortgage were not paid within twelve years from April 14, 1925, the mortgagee filed a suit on July 12, 1946 in the Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad for recovery of the amount mentioned therein by way of interest for peaceful realisation of the annual interest at the rate of Rs 1/8/ per mensem and also an endorsement in that behalf was made on the mortgage deed. A suit to enforce payment of money charged upon immoveable property might be filed within twelve months from the date when the money sued for becomes due. The plaintiff contended, relying upon certain payments towards the mortgage dues made by the mortgagor, that the mortgagee did receive the amount as royalty from the tenants under mining leases in Mauza Bahaldih in the month of Aswin and Simitanr under his own arrangement and prayed for a decree for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. He also relied upon several payments towards interest which was signed by P, the mortgagor. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was not barred by limitation because the mortgage 'was partly simple and partly usufructuary ' and even though the plaintiff could not rely on part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying upon the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 7, 1937, by the auction purchaser who purchased the mortgagor 's rights in Bahaldhih lands at the Court auction and that the only claim for execution of the mortgage was within limitation. The High Court also held that as the plaintiff had in her plaint not relied upon dispossession as a ground for extension of the period Of limitation, that claim should have been allowed to be made out by the trial court. On appeal by certificate: Held, that P a mortgagor who has lost all interest in the mortgaged property cannot by payment of interest or principal within the meaning of section 20 bind the person on whom the interest has devolved. But the mortgagor is deprived of his security by or in consequence of wrongful act or default of the mortgagor or any person claiming under a title superior to that of the former mortgagor.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories and are charged at the rate of Rs. 5 per month. A charge of Rs, 2 per month was levied for the transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants contended that these amounts were realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of the arguments, it was pointed out that when the company prepared to grant free transport facilities to the supervisory staff there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to them and that the Commissioner had dismissed the appeals filed by the employees and holding that the transport vehicle provided to the employees by the appellant would be a public service vehicle. The High Court also held that the Transport vehicles provided to them by the company would be 'public service vehicle ' in any sense of the term. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1. Under section 3(1) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 "private service vehicles" means any omnibus constructed or adapted to carry more than nine persons excluding the driver and ordinarily used by or on behalf of the owner of such vehicle for the purpose of carrying persons for or in connection with his trade or business or otherwise than for hire or reward. But does not create any difficulty because having regard to the preamble of the Act it is not necessary for us to go into such meticulous details, because the legal position proceeds to be clear enough. As the Counsel for the appellants has already undertaken not to charge any amount from the employees for providing transport facilities, the point has now become more or less academic.

The appellants, who were the residents of a locality, filed a petition under Article 226 challenging the validity of the order of the State Government conceding inter alia that they were the owners of a permanent cinema license granted to them by the licensing authority in exercise of its power conferred by section 5(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that there was a mosque and a temple in the vicinity where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed, and even though their objections were upheld by the District Magistrate, they were not heard in the appeal preferred by the third respondent and therefore the order granting no objection certificate is violative of the principles of natural justice. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants did not file any objection at that stage "no objection" certificate was granted to the third respond ent. Thereafter when the second respondent applied for a cinema licence, the appellants made applications for the first time. Both the applications were rejected on the grounds inter alia (a) that there were different stages through which an application for no objection certificates was filed and (b) that the appellants were not acting bona fide in vindication of their own rights but they were a fence or a cloak for the owners or owners of Paras Cinema, the holders of permanent cinema licence in the locality. [799C E] 2. The contention of the appellants is that before granting renewal of such license the State government in the appellant appeal filed by the second Respondent had not heard them and therefore they are being proceeded against ex parte. [800C] 3. There was only one point raised in this appeal, which clearly H.P. Cinemas Regulation Act, 1953 could be said to have been complied with and that no objection Certificate was granted on that short ground. When an application is received it is to be advertised in the manner prescribed inviting the public to file objections. After considering the objections the licensing Authority has to decide whether to grant or refuse a permit the applicant or may refuse to grant the same. If after taking into consideration the objections, the no objection certification certificate is granted, there ends the matter subject, of course, to any properly constituted legal proceedings, conceivably a writ petition under article 226. But sub section (3) Of section 5 of the Act is unambiguous when it provides for an appeal only at the instance of a person aggrieved by the decision of the licensing author ler refusing licence. A fortiori, every objector to renewal is not entitled to file an appeal if licence is granted rejected rejecting his objections. Nor in an appeal by the aggrieved person within the meaning of section 5 (3).

The agreement to sell was not an acceptance of the offer. The agreement stipulated that the defendant agreed to assign the mining lease and gave them the right to win and remove the iron ore, subject to the plaintiff 's paving. On November 1, 1957, the plaintiffs filed a suit (O.S. No. 46 of 1957) against the defendant claiming specific performance of the contract. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no concluded contract between the parties and that it was not necessary to give consent of the Central Government and that as the government concerned could not be compelled to accord the necessary sanction, the contract to assign mining lease could not therefore be specifically performed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) The plaint in O.S No. 47 of 1957 was not a suit for specific performance; (ii) The acceptance should Pr=& the institution of the suit. HELD: (1) Under section 2(6), 3 and 7 there could be no finality either oral or in writing. Mere mental assent of the plaintiffs to the defendants proposal is not sufficient. [584 D] (2)(a) Under sections 2(7), 3 & 7, the Contract Act if given should Pr =& the Institution of the suits. But this rule cannot apply under section 8, 4 and 5 (b). The special purpose i.e., taking shares must be complied with; but when the defendants chose not to accept the offer they are bound to do so before. [585 C] The general purpose of sections 2 (6) & 7 along with the writ of summons was to enforce the plaintiffs ' right under the contract dated August 3, 1957. In re: Pellatt 's Case ; followed. (b) If the defendants desired to set up a new case that the contract was concluded in November 1957 they should have amended their pleadings accordingly. [58 C] In re : Pellat 's case , referred to.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K.G Sugar Ltd. and the former Secretary of the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937. A complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of r. 3 of the Order read with section 7 of the , on the ground that they have failed to pay the sellers the price of the sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The complaint was investigated and the appellants were objecting to the investigation. In their application for directions by the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution the appellants contended: (1) Sub rule ( 3) of rr. 3 & 4 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955 could not have been validly issued under section 3 Of the Act because (i) the said section did not authorise the Magistrate to investigate the case; and (ii) sub rule 3 of r.(3) being a general mandate. Held: (i). The power conferred on the Government under section 11 of the Essential Commodities Act cannot be challenged as invalid. [677 F H] (2) It is well within the competence of Parliament to enact the ,and hence the power conferred upon the Government,under section 3 of that Act could not be questioned as invalid merely because there was an agreement in writing to the contrary between the parties and the Criminal Court had no jurisdiction to investigate that complaint. [674 B C] (3)(i) The second contention raised by the appellants that sub r. (3), which was a specific mandate, could not operate against the Magistrate also was unsustainable on the mere ground that he was deemed to have been altered in view of article 372 of the Constitu tion which provides that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [679 G] (ii). The word 'crops ' in section 2(a) includes Sugarcane and the third contention was unsustainable in view Of Entry 33 of List III of the 7th Schedule which empowers Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs. It is not disputed that the Central Government had declared by law that it was expedient in public interest that it should exercise control over foodstuffs and that therefore power conferred under section 2 (a) could be exercised in the instant case. [676 A B] Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , distinguished.

% The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy for encouraging industrialisation, by an order dated 12th January 1977, the Government of India sanctioned this incentives and concessions to entrepreneurs for starting new industries in Mysore State. This allowance was made available by the Government on 30th June 1969. By another order dated 11th August 1975, the procedure was prescribed for obtaining the concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th February 1977, a Division Bench of the High Court issued an Order in which it stated that the reasons for making the said order were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Govern ment earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limit or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. On 13th March, 1977, another Order was issued by which it was provided that a cash refund shall be allowed on all Sales Tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first 5 years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concessions being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce. By an order of 11th February, 1977 inter alia, provided as under: "Consequent upon the directions of the Governor of Mysore, the Governor was pleased to sanction the following incentives and concession concessions to the entrepreneurs for start new industries In the Mysore State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed only on all sales tax paid by an old industry on the raw materials purchase purchased by It for the 1 5 years immediately from the day the industry went into production as set out in said Order. " On 12st January, 1977 another order was issued which recited that the Government, namely, the Govern mate of Karnataka was committed to a policy of rapid industrialisation and that, in pursuance thereof, the State Government had on 30 11 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industry in the MysoreState. The material part of the said Order ran thus: "consequently, the Preservement of the aforesaid incentives and facilities to the investors for commencing new industries shall be limited to 10% of the cost of fixed assets per year, thus not exceeding the total of 50 per cent over a period of five years for which the concession is available". The order dated December 12th, 1977 was issued on 11th January,1977, inter alia provided that the concession of refund will "exclude certain words used out of context. However, in view of this, it would not be proper to hold the Government to the promises or the assurances it had given under clause 2 read with para 2 read together thereof".

A 1 to A 7 were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. It was in evidence that all the accused persons belonged to opposite factions, and there was long standing enmity between the parties. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The deceased was undergoing life imprisonment for the murder of one of the persons belonging to the group of the accused. He had come on parole; On the day of occurrence at about 7.00 A.M., when he was passing near the field of A I, he was attacked by the accused party and his daughter in a nearby land owner. The trial court acquitted A 7. For convicting the appellants under Sections 148 and 149 IP. C. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. Section 149 and 34 I. P.C deal with a combina tion of persons who become liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences. [879 G] 2. Section 141 does not bar in convicting an accused under 7 for the offence committed by him. The non applicability of Section i49 I. p. C is, therefore, no bar in conviction against the appellants. [851 A B] 3. Section 147 and 34 are on bail under orders of this Court. It cannot be said that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The appellants acted in the furtherance of their common intention of killing the de ceased. The injuries caused by the deceased with their respective weapons, therefore the appellants acted under Section 302 read along with section 34 I P.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam. On 25th December 1965, he sold a house for Rs. 16,500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The Income Tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment for the assessment year 1966 67 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice: 48,500. The assessee submitted a revised return on the basis that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45(2) and taking the view that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent for invoking the applicability of that provision. The Assistant Commissioner rejected the contention. On appeal, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal held that in order to bring a case within section 52(2), it was not necessary that there should be under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assessee. The Revenue filed an appeal with this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The object and purpose of sub section (2) is to avoid or reduce the liability of the assesses to tax on capital gains. But since the actual consideration received by the assesee was not declared or disclosed and in most of the cases, if not all, it would not be possible for the Income tax officer to determine precisely what is actual consideration receive by the assesses or in other words how much m ore consideration is received by him and permit the Revenue to take the fair Market value of capital asset as on that date. [639 F] 2.1 In the present case, it was never the contention of the Revenue that the property was sold by the assesssee to his mother in law, and five or more of his parents for a consideration which was more than the sum of Rs.16,500 shown to be the consideration for the property in the Instrument of Transfer and there was understatement or concealment of the consideration in regard to the transfer. It was common ground between the parties and that was a finding of fact reached by the Income 8 Tax Authorities, that thetransfer of the Property by the appellant was a perfectly honest and bonafide transaction where the consideration did not exceed 15% of the value so declared. [650 G] 2:2 The object of sub s (2), as explicated from the speech of the Finance Minister, was not to strike at honest and bona fide transactions where the considerations in respect thereof were correctly disclosed or declared by him, but to bring within the net of taxation those transactions where consideration in the respect of transfer was correctly declared or declared or disclose by him. [643 E F] 3.

The appellant was charged in the Court of Presidency Magistrate, Bombay as follows: That you on 3 12 1968 at 8.m. at Bandra in contravention of provisions of section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption and thereby committed an offence under section 16(1) (a) (1) of that Act and within my cognizance. " The two witnesses produced to support this charge were D. P. Tambe, a businessman, said that he had gone to "a shop to make purchases", without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. Under cross examination it was alleged: "Black Tils can be used for human habitation. " It is not correct to say they are used only for Pooja and not as human food. On these facts, the appellant must get the benefit of that doubt. As already indicated above, the use` article sold was not entirely irrelevant. The accused told me that he will write on the cash memo the purpose for which black Tils were sold". To almost every question under cross examination D did not remember who made the cash Memo and whether anyone signed it in his presence, but stated that he took the signatures of the packet, whereas no signature of the witness was obtained on the counterfoil of the cash memos. It is clear from the evidence that when the case of the appellant supported by his cash memo, it could not be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the Food Inspector that they can be use as food also. On a consideration of all these facts and circumstances the judgment of the High Court in convicting the accused under section 21(1 ) (a)(1) was set aside and the conviction and sentence were confirmed on the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appellant must pay the benefit thereof. As rightly indicated above that this is not so widely known a fact that we could take judicial notice of it. It was enough if an article of adultered food is either manufactured for sale, or stored, or sold or distributed in contravention thereof or any provision of the Act or of any rule made there under. However, it became necessary to examine the evidence of the only witness produced to corroborate the food Inspector. [330 E G] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration; , referred to.

% The plaintiff, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31.8.1967 on the ground that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17.6.1969 asking for a declaration that he order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it has not been com plaint within three year from that date, as contemplated under Article 49 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench, reliance was placed on a decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; , and in support of the contention that it was not filed within 3 years from that day. It was further submitted that the suit was barred by limitation. Rejecting the contentions raised, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 113 is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies. The fate of the appeal rests upon the finding as to when the right to sue first accrued. All the three courts have accepted the position that on 1.3.1966 when the order of dismiss al was made by the Collec tor, the right stood merged into the order dated May 7, 1949 merged in the appellate order of the State Govern ment and the High Court was, therefore, right in its view that it would not be correct to say that the order in question could not be the subject matter of an application under Article 226 of the Constitution for that would be giving retro spective effect to that Article. [52G H] 2.

The appellant, who was one of the defendants in a suit for partition, filed an application before the trial court under article 133(1) Of the Constitution for his half share in all the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father as his successor and several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father were not binding on him and so his share in the properties covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his claim, but on appeal the High Court reversed his decision of the trial Court. It held that the decree sought to be appealed from was one one of affirmance and there was no substantial question of law raised by the proposed appeal: Held, that where a variation is made in favour of intending appellant it is not necessary to take the decree as a whole and enquire whether it is a decree of affirmence or not. In applying the test of the value of the subject matter of the dispute what we have to consider is the true nature and character of the appellate decree, which conclusively determines the rights of parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in suit, and it is also true that a party aggrieved by a decree may appeal only against a part of it and is not bound to file an appeal against the whole of the decree; but so it is necessary that the matter in respect of which there has been a variation should be the subject of the proposed appeals to this Court. The principle underlying article 133 can, therefore, be applied only when there is a conflict between the two provisions. Where, however, in a case where preliminary decrees are passed, but the normal rule is one decree is passed in one suit and so it would be reasonable to hold that the word 'decision ' must likewise mean the entire decision of that court and not a part thereof. If an appellate decree affirms the decree of the lower court it is only the Punjab High Court and the majority decision of this Court which have taken a contrary view.

The appellants in the appeal and the special leave petitions raise a preliminary objection that sections 115, Code of Civil Procedure and section 115 were not maintainable. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed under section 115, C.P.C., on the ground that it was not maintainable since the five cases before this Court must be considered in the context of their individual facts, but that it had jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in respect of cases arising out of original suits of a value less than Rs. 20,000/ and above, and that no such revision petition was maintainable before the High Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 An order passed by a District Judge is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High court under section 5, Code, Civil Procedure. The proviso to section 115 of the C. P.C. only provides for an appeal and a revision in cases falling under Section 24 and Section 25 respectively. Cases in which the District judge and the High Courts respectively exercise revisional power, revisional powers are specifically mentioned. [40E, G] 1:2 In cases arising from original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by the District Court, the High Judge alone is competent to exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 C.p.C.; but in the main two questions arise : (1) Whether the High 843 possesses revisional jurisdic tion under section115, Code with respect to cases decided before the 20th September 1972; and (2) Whether an order of the District Judge under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act dismissing a revision petition would lie. [41E G] 2:3 An examination of the various provisions of the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act indicates that it is a self sufficient code so far as the present enquiry is concerned. For the purpose of correcting decrees or orders made by a Court of Small Causes, the Act provides for appeals and revisions in cases failing under Section 25 are specifically mention. The legislature clearly intended that a decree or order made by the court of Small Cause should be final subject only to correction by the remedies provided under the Provincial Civil Courts Act.

The respondents, who owned Khasra No. 383 area 14 bighas 16 biswas situate in village Madrampura on the outskirts of Jaipur City, filed a petition before the Rajasthan High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated February 8 , 1984 issued by the State Government under S.5 (21) of the Act for the acquisi tion of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust, Jaipur for a public purpose namely for implementation of a development scheme viz. Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The said notice was duly served on the respondents and they in compliance therewith appeared before the Special Officer , Town Planning Department, Jaipur and filed their reply dated September 8, 1975. In the reply, the respondents while denying the existence of a public pur posation for the purpose of expansion of their business activities to the State of Rajasthan contended that the petition under article 226 of the Constitution is in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon and the ad interim ad interim injunction secured by them on the basis of such petition from the learned Single Judge on March 13, 1984 when there was total lack of inherent jurisdiction on the part of (1) ; , 602 which the Calcutta high Court to entertain such a petition constitutes a flagrant abuse of the process of the court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under S.(2) of S.52 of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 arose within the State at Jaipur Bench. [605C D] 2. Even though the power of the High Courts under article226 of the constitution are wide and the judges must ever be vigilant to protect the citizen against arbitrary executive action , nonetheless ,the Judges have a constructive role and therefore there is always the need to use such extensive powers with due circumspection. There has to be in the larger public interest an clement of self ordained restraint. [06E F] 3.1 Since the respondents having failed in their effort to get the land released from acquisition, they took up the matter with the State Govt. They made an application to the Government on February 10, 1977 seeking exemption of the notified land under section 20 of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act , 1976 stating that they required the land for construction of a Three Star Hotel Hotel. The State Government in their special leave petition has explained that the notification under section 52(1) was effective the moment it was published in the official Gazette as thereupon the notified Land became vested in the State government free from all encumbrances. [ 602F G] 3.(i)(ii) It is not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special officer , Town planning Department, Bangalore under S(2) for the grant of an appropriate writ , direction or order under article 227 of the Constitu tion for quashing the notification issued by State Government. [ 603G] 4.(ii) The High Court has no territorial jurisdiction to issue a rule ni dure on the petition filed by the respondents under Article 226 of .

The respondents filed a suit for eviction and for arrears of rent and damages alleging that the appellant was inducted as a tenant by the respondent in 1974 under a co operative housing scheme of the State Bank of India for which, the loan advanced. The building in question was assessed to house and water tax on 1st October 1971 and as such, the building was not covered by the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972. The appellant also claimed that the building in suit was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2)(i) of the new Rent Act, and that it was covered by a new Rent Acts. The Additional District Judge negatived all other pleas except the finding about the arrears of land rent. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the findings on all other points except the findings regarding arrears of landlord rent but dismissed the revision petition in part. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the building had been constructed substantiallyout of funds obtaining from the source mentioned in proviso to s.2(2), and (ii) as such the view taken by the High court that the property was exempted from the operation of the old Rent Act on two grounds, namely; (a) that the land had been cleared upto 6th April 1977, and there was no default in the payment of rent, and therefore the new Act had no application to the building during that period. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The Court had to decide the case on the basis of cause of action that accrued prior to the date of filing the suit and not on a new cause of actions, but this question need not detain as it is covered by decision of this Court in Pasupati Venkateswrlu vs Motor and General Traders. [338C D] 1(b) The stage before which amendment was allowed would be an opportunity for deciding the case in accordance with justice under the law. The question in the present case was whether by seeking the benefit of section 39, the new rent Act there is a change in the cause of ' action. In A.K. Gupta & Sons vs Damodar Valley Corporation this Court dealing with the cause to be decided by the trial court.

The appellant company entered into three contracts with the respondent for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings stores and other works at Ranchi. The contracts were referred to arbitration by one Col. A. W. section Smith and later to an arbitrator for being filed as provided in the Act. At the earlier stages the parties entered into the agreement and compromised the matter in accordance with the provisions of 1940. After a detailed trial, the Subordinate Judge passed a decree in terms of the award except as to a part which he held himself to be in excess of the claim. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court. The questions that fell for consideration were whether there was a valid agreement of reference to arbitration binding on the Government and whether a decree could be passed on the unstamped copy of the Award filed in the Court and whether any decree could have been passed thereon, and, if it did not fall within section 175(3) the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date. Held, that the agreement dated February 6, 1948 between the parties was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor and in consequence there was valid reference to it all contracts made in the exercise of the executive authority of the Federation or of a province. The order was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private tribunal and it could not be brought within item 2 of the Government 's Indian Act, but in consequence thereof no decree could he passed thereon. The law was no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated by the Official Gazette but there is nothing in section itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person and when that is established the requirements of the section must be held to be satisfied. In the present case the award in court was tendered to the Government for its acceptance and in pursuance thereof the appellant had made alterations and modifications in the agreement on the basis that it was the Government that was a party thereto.

The respondent, a Municipal Engineer in the State of Punjab was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the appellant State. On various dates in that year, he placed orders for purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the said orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received in the department against the respondent pertaining to the purchase of the sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In pursuance of that investigation, the respondent retired from service and was prosecuted for offences punishable under sub section(1) & (2), Prevention of Platioin 's Corruption Act. The prosecution against the accused was challenged by the Respondent in a Criminal miscellaneous before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Crl. No. 5837 M/85 on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement, and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea raised by the respondent found favour with the High court which relying on an earlier decision of that Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; quashed the First Information Reports by its order dated February 12, 1986 relying on the decision of this Court in the case of Des RajSinghal and held that the said Rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said rule and therefore the High Courts committed an error of law in taking the said view. The High Court accordingly quashed the first Information Report, quashed the second information report as against Kailash Nath and directed the State Government to decide afresh the petition filed by Mangal Singh Minhas for quashing of the First F.I.R., as also Crl. Appeal Nos. 423 24 of 1988 and Crl. (Criminal) No. 2993 and Crl . Misc. Application No. 988 and CrlP. (C.) No. 4488 of 1986.

Section 23 A of the Income tax Act, 1922, provided that where the income tax Officer is satisfied that in respect of any previous year the profits and gains distributed as dividends by any company up to the end of the sixth month after its accounts for that previous year are laid before the company in general meeting are less than sixty per cent of the assessable income of the company of that previous years, as reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the company, he shall make with the previous approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner an order in writing that the undistributed portion of the chargeable income would be deemed to have been distributed as dividend amongst the shareholders as at the date of the respective general meetings. The Income tax Officer served a notice after obtaining the approval of his Inspecting Assistant Commis sioner, of Income tax, calling upon the respondent company to show cause why an order under section 23 A be not passed against it and after considering the objections raised by the Company ordered on March 31, 1953, that the accumulated portion of assessable income should be deemed as distributed to its shareholders as per section 23A of the Act. The appellant contended inter alia, (i) that this provision was unconstitu tional or ultra vires; (ii) that section 23 Of the Act introduced by the Finance Act did not define the expression "company in which the public were substantially interested" and (iii) that the Explanation to sub sec tion (1) of section 23(A) was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in whichthe public are substantially interested. Held: (i): Where the controlling interest i.e., a minimum of fifty one per cent or more of the voting power is held by a single individual or a group of individuals acting in concert hold fifty one percent or more or less of the shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend, it would mean not twenty five per cent either of the total voting power but power exercisable in respect thereof. The Explanation raised a conclusive presumption that the company was one in which a public are materially interested, having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty One per cent/ more of that voting power was held by persons entitled to ordinary shares outside the controlling group and the shares yielding a fixed percentage of it has to be excluded. The expression "twenty five per centum of the share 'of the shareholders" would mean a third vote, for each share, ordinary and preference alike and twenty five percent of that .ac ture is directed primarily against the accumulation of undistributed dividends to avoid payment of non corporate rates of super tax. But shareholders who are entitled to shares in such shares must be taken into account. There is obviously no person who could hold 75 7 per cent share or more Of the ordinary shares. In the present case, as already observed there was a real control ,of one shareholder or a groups of shareholders acting in com panyising concert held 50% or more per cent.

The appellants were the selling agents of a textile mill. They were del credere agents and guarantee payment to the first appellant of all sales made and on the other side, guarantee delivery was given to the purchasers with whom they dealt direct. In pursuance of all these orders and rules made under the Essential Supplies Act, 1946 the first appel lant despatched 13 bales on 28th February 1947 and sent them to Dharsi Moolji. As for payment it looks to Dwarkadas Khetan & Company the price of the goods specified in the ready sale note was Rs. 14,000. The loss was not made over within a week; but the Sales were allowed to take delivery of these 13 bales. Under section 5(1)(a) which required every manufacturer to submit " true and accurate information relating to his undertakings ' to the Textile Commissioner C.S.T., Bombay, in compliance with this order, the first respondent sent the 13 bales to the Mills concerned on 28st February 1947. The first appellant thereafter wrote to the appellants requesting that his goods should be sent to "our godown", whether the " we " refer to Dwarwadas" " godowns or for jointly shared between the Mills and the second appellant was not clear. On receipt of this advice slip the first res pondent handed over the 13 consignments on 28rd February, 1947 to the company and the appellants were handed over to the Company. Immediately thereafter they brought a fresh demand to the same day by saying that unless be received the money for them from the Mills as provided in section 5 (1) (a) of the Act, the goods had actually left the Mills premises and that they were in the Dady Seth Seth Seth godown under the control of Dwarkadash Khetan. The appellants further stated that they had actually received the amount for the bales from Dharsi Dunji and had not received anything from the company to the latter. They accordingly asked the Company to prepare a delivery order and deliver them, but did not comply with the requirements of the form because the form required information regarding physical delivery to the quota holder or his agent and as Dwarkad as Khetan was not the agent of the quotaholder, the statement was inaccurate and misleading The Magistrate found that the mills had established their case and so convicted all the appellants. The High Court on appeal held that the prosecution had established its case and acquitted the appellants, but confirmed the convictions. Held: Where a man lives abroad over a period of years and leaves his house and furniture in charge of an agent who has the keys of the house and immedi ate access to and physical control over the furniture, it would be difficult to say that there had been anything beyond a technical and unintentional breach of the law. Dwarkadhatas Khetan could not, in the circumstances given above, be described without any straining of language as the person to whom the goods were actually delivered. It was true the legal possession would continue to reside in the owner but the actual physical possession would surely be that of the agent. And so with a del create agent, because such a person is the agent, of the seller only up to a point.

The appellant, a Senior Lecturer in the Government College was charged with offences under section 161 Indian Penal Code with which he was charged. The Special judge who tried both these accused found them guilty of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 read with s.5(1) (d). The High Court took the view that even an Examiner was a public servant and therefore could not be regarded as a public Servant within the meaning of Sec.21 of the Penal Code. Dismissing the appeal to this Court ^ HELD: 1. Where on the evidence produced by the prosecution, comes to the conclusion that Saxena taking advantage of his own position as an employee in the Chief Commissioner 's Office and Ram Narain 's ignorance and anxiety to get the license, had induced him to part with the money on (I) ; , , , it is not possible to put the case of a University Examiner in the place of a publicist which is one of the ways mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's case. When he was acting as an examiner it could not he said that there had been any abuse by him of his position as a Public servant. [329 H; 319 A B] 2. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the High Court such a construction would also keep the offence within the limitation and the object of the Act. [322 F G] 3. The use of the word 'corrupt ' in Sec.161 Indian Penal code does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of receivers One may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position, as a 'public servant '. [326 H; 327 A] 4. There are two ways of looking at the clause on is that the words 'cor BHAGWATI ' stand by themselves and as soon as it is established that a public ' servant has by such means obtained any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage he will be guilty of offence. But, the abuse by corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in the Narayanan Nambiar"s case is clearly implied. [324 A] 5. The word 'otherwise ' refers to other than corrupt or unlawful by which a public person may abuse his position. There is three ways of looked at the clon on is the words "corrupt or illegal" mean ing 'actually ' and 'otherwise" mentioned in Sec.(1)

% The petitioners in each of these applications under Article 32 of the Constitution are a workman engaged on terms of casual labour for periods ranging varying between 10 140 and 16 years, in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway. All the writ petitions having been disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein are similar. The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and have applied discriminatory rates of wages. They have asked for a direction to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked him for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondent. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondent contesting the claim of the petitioners. According to the respondents five out of the forty four petitioners in this group of writ petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasi. One of them has been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to be all the rights and privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. The respondents have placed reliance on the definition of "Project" which means: "a project should be taken as construction of new lines, major projects, restoration of dismantled lines and major important open line works, line doubling, widening of tunnels etc". which are completed within a definite time limit". According to them five out four out of forty four writ petitioners in the group of Writ Petitions had undergone Medical examination and they were granted permanent temporary status on completion of 120 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement. That status is acquired on completion Of 360 days by casual labour in Project Works as provided in the scheme formulated under orders of this Court, though such status were acquirable by project casual labour on completion thereof within a specific time limit. The writ petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs.

The Forward Markets Commission, came into force on January 21, 1956. There was no dispute that these contracts were in accordance with the bye laws of the Association as they stood at the date when the contracts were entered into. The terms and conditions of forward contracts in cotton including "hedge contracts" and the manner of their implementation were governed by certain bye laws framed under section 11 of the Forward Markets Regulations Act, 1952. The appellants had entered into "hedges Contract" in respect of forward contract in February and May 1956. Clause (f) was that the appellants could not, on a proper construction of the Bye law, be validly vested with the power to make bye laws under section 12 of the Act by the mere fact that they entered into contracts in regard to another per sons ' basis, and that the conditions of the forward contract were governed in certain byelaws of the association. Sub section (3) was added to the effect that "all hedge Contracts outstaining at the time it came into existence shall be deemed to be closed out at such rates as shall be fixed by the Forward Marketing Commission and the provisions of Clauses (3), (4) and (6) of bye law 52 A in so far as they applied to hedge and on call contracts". On January 21 1956, the Central Government notified a new bye law 51 AA to be substituted in place of the earlier bye law 49 AA. The notification was issued pursuant to the decision of this Court in [S.R. Chari vs Union of India] (1962) 2 S.C.R 689 and the appellants contended that as the power of the Central Govern ment to make a bye law retrospectively had been delegated to it by the new bye laws, they were not in either case subordinate legislation under section II or 12 as the case might be, of the act and hence the Central Govt. could not issue a direction to the respondents to do so. Held:(1) The notification dated January 24, 1956, by the Central Gov ernment was illegal and the appellant had no power under section 3 (i) of the , to make such a bye laws having retrospective effect. (2) Section 12 of A of the as amended by Act 52 AA which came into operation on January 1, 1956 in so much as it purports to operate retrospectively did not confer any such power on the Central government by necessary implication. The specific mention of the rules made under the , could not be overlooked by the phrase "under the Act" and consequently the new sub bye law enacted on January 19, 1956 which came to an end with effect from August 8, 1957 must be held to be invalid. (3)(a) to (e) and also that the notification dated December 21,1957 issued in exercise of the power conferred under section 26 was brought into force retrospectively. The words "by or under this Act" shall have no reference to the rules framed under the Act which are made under section 10 of the .

The assessee, a shareholder of a company called the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd., claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357 B, Rs. 28,125/ , for the years 1358 B.S., Rs. 29,250/ and Rs. 21,822/ . for the assessment year 1358 E, the assessee claimed that on the facts and circumstances of the case, the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to land acquisition compensation received by it, was a receipt of income in the hands of the assessee and taxable as the income of the asses from other sources, was liable to be grossed up. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the whole amount for each year was income in 'the hands of assessee, but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal further observed that as the entire amount for the first year was taxable as pondent and that, therefore, there was no question referred to the High Court. In reference under section 66(1) of ' the Indian Incometax Act, the High court held that part of the 'amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the assessee for the grant of long term leases after 31st March 1948, was not taxable as dividend, but the income from other source. The High Court further observed : " It is agreed between the parties that the answers in the negative on all the questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964 pending in this Court". In these appeals, by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that distribution of dividend out of capital gains was taxable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. There could be no doubt that the High 'Court had jurisdiction to decide on the questions whether any amount of salami was capital gain, and whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisition was capital gains. [35C E] 2. The second question as to whether any sum of salmi was capital expenditure or was not capital gain.

The respondents were the ex contractors in the State of Kerala. They challenged before the High Court the jurisdiction of the court in C.C. Nos. 145 and 148 Cr. P.C., 1973 for short 'the Code ' by way of writ petitions in the High Courts questioning the jurisdiction, jurisdiction of court in the said Special Leave Petition, on the ground that sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under Section 2(f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 and thus it is not forest produce, and that these appeals by special leave were heard together. The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The State Acts regulate preservation of forest and forest produce to supplement the Central Act. The Kerala Act prescribes procedure for preservation of the forest and regulates possession of theforest produce failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil either was found in transit or in possession of manufacturers, it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under Section 5 1(1)(or contravention thereof. As the jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that Sandal Wood oil is not ' Forests ' as defined in Section 2 (f) of Kerala Forest act, 1961 for short `the Act ', the High court quashed the complaint holding that SandAlwar Wood Oil was not wood oil ' as contemplated by Section 2, (f). Hence these appeals. Setting aside the judgment and allowing the appeal of the accused, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word wood oil used in the Kerala Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [505A] 1.2 The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose of the Act and the literal interpretation giving narrow meaning to the word wood Oil ' should be excluded.

Certain injuries were caused to two brothers who had been tried by the Sessions Judge, Ganganagar for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The Sessions Judge disbelieved the whole evidence and convicted both of them. On appeal to the High Court the order of acquittal was reversed and they were convicted under s.302 read with s.34 I.P.C. and sentenced by the High court. Held, that in the present case the evidence on record is of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the accused could properly be drawn. The second point on which the judgment of the High COurt was challenged was the lack of compelling reasons for setting aside the judgment Of acquittal. This Court has held that the High Courts should not set aside an order of conviction unless there are " substantial and compelling reason ' for doing so. In the present ease the evidence in the case is of a such quality, which no legitimate conclusion could be drawn, because ordinarily a dying declaration of the kind which the prosecution had relied upon was by itself insufficient for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. The learned Sessions Judge was not wrong in accepting the testimony of these witnesses in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations nor could the statement of the deceased alleged to have been made in the circumstances of this case be considered sufficient to support the conviction of the appellant. The third point on Which the judgment was assailed is the lack Of compelling reasons; for setting quash the sentence. Held further, that although this Court will not interfere with the findings of the trial Court because its conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the Accused differ from that of the above High Court, yet where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused was guilty this Court would set aside the conviction. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Stephen Seneviratne vs The King (1649) A.I.R. ; , referred to.

An industrial dispute having arisen between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at Jamshedpur, the appellant, a company representing the said workmen represented by their union. The dispute was referred to the Tribunal under section 10(2) of the . In terms of an agreement between the Government of Bihar and the workmen of all its establishments the appellant claimed a sum of Rs. 11/1/ per month as overtime to office staff with effect from April 1, 1963. The workmen, however, did not produce any evi dence to show that they were being paid due for overtime work in respect of those demands. Eventually, on May 21, 1964, the Government referred five disputes to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. On October 23, 1963 the Government refer ence was made to the tribunal which held that the constitution of the said Indoxco Labour Union came to be amended from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment it, "the references referred to are those set out in the agreement and state 554 and were between the management of the appellant 's factory at Ranchi and their workmen represented through the Indox co Labour Union ". The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the com pany was not justified in making its award operative not only to the said workman at its Jamshedpur factory but also to the workmen at its other establishments and granted 1/4 times the ordinary rate beyond its normal hours. ^ HELD: (i) Article XII of the Constitution deals with alteration of rules and cl. (e) thereof provides that copies of all new rules and amendments or revisions of .rules shall be submitted to the Registrar within 15 days from the amendment and until the Registrar is satisfied that the amendments are in accordance with the rules of the union, and on such satisfaction registers them in a register kept for that purpose and notifies that fact to the union 's secretary, the amendments do not become effective. [352 F G] (ii) The contention that an obligation to grant special leave to attend the meetings of the executive committee of the Unions, the meetings o f the executive com por tant of the Union cannot be accepted. A demand for special leave has nothing to do with any disparities or inequalities social or economic. [353 A B] (iii) When conciliation proceedings are likely to get thwarte if the workmen 's representatives are not there to discuss the disputes and put forward their point of view before conciliation officers and wherever possible to arrive at a settlement or compromise, it would amount to interference in the administration of the respond ent company and his autonomy. [351 E] (iv) In respect of the workmen in question the Tribunal had fixed the rate for overtime worked at 1 1/2 times the normal rate of wages. It did not specify on how many occasions the executive Committee meetings of .the union and other meetings would be held when the company would be obliged to give special leave with pay to the Union 's representative.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In 1946 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership on June 29, 1939. The firm was dissolved by two partners of the firm Gajjan Mal. The assessee was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm alone was entitled to relief under section 25(3) or in the alternative under section (4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, and as the assessee was not carrying on business within the meaning of sub sections (3) and (4), he was entitled only to relief thereunder. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub ss(3)(a) or (4). In appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. On further appeal by certificate granted by the High Court. HELD: The Indian Income Tax Act (Amendment) 7 of 1939 was brought into force on April 1, 1939 and it could not be said that the assessee commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution of the partnership from April 1. The partnership therefore came into being at the precise point of time at which the Indian income tax (Amendment to Act 7 of Vanaspati) Act 7 Of 1939 came into force and it can not be held that the business of Messrs. Hakam Mal Tani Mal, Tanimal Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Gopi Mal Sahib Sud Kuthrala son from the 1st of April, 1939, was carried on by that firm.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shim dissection, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. The said order was rescinded on April 25, 1967, and the matter was adjourned to April 25. 1967. On April 25 the Secretary to the Regional transport Authority called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the issue of the permit the respondents preferred appeals to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal on the ground that the Secretary had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under r. 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permits. The appeal of the respondents were allowed by the State transport Appellate Tribunal by majority on January 29, 1969. Respondents 4 to 13 preferred appeals against the said order to the District Judge, who dissented. An appeal filed by the appellant before the Revenue Appellate Tribunal was dismissed which led to the unsuccessful writ application in the High Court and hence this appeal by special leave. The point that arose for consideration was whether any appeal lay under section 64 of the Act to the state Transport Appellate tribunal against the issue Of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Motor Transport Authority granting the permit, HELD: 1. Section 64 has to be read with rule 178 of the Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to the various authorities Appeal is a creature of the statute.

The appellant was the sitting member of Parliament and, among others, an independent candidate. The election symbol of the appellant was elephant and the election symbol was Merchants and on 7 February 1967 a candidate named Basharaj Shastri secured 1,49,943 votes while the appellant secured 34,274 votes. The Swatantra candidate Sri Naseem secured 36,272 votes while respondent Smt. Kamla Chaudhury secured 33,988 votes. In support of the allegations the appellant relied on exhibit 28 the news report in the newspaper 'Hindustan ' published on 8 February 1967 and also on Exhibit 23 the news item, in the newspapers described 'Vir Arjun ' published at Hapur under the date 7 February, 1967. The appellant contended that the publication was not in accordance with section 123(3A) nor was it published in the Hindustan 's Times. He further urged that the editorial constituted communal propaganda against the appellant and that the speech of the candidate who attacked him was a communal propagatory speech and as such his election symbol could not be said to have been acted upon by respondent in the publication. The High Court dismissed the petition. HELD: (1) There is no violation of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act. [900G] (2) It is not shown that the original pamphlet was published or published at a newspaper under the name 'Hindustan Times ' but the appellant did not say who had assaulted or chased and whom he believed to have committed such corrupt practice. The offending statement in exhibit 22 do not make any reflection on the moral or mental character of the appel lant. [901A B] (3) A pamphlet is not a communal document which may be used as evidence in support of such an allegation unless it is shown that there was some disturbance which would attract penal consequences and a corrupt practice can be alleged to have arisen. The first and second occurrence on which the appellant based its case is that at the meeting held on 7 2 1967 the respondent was not called upon to state as to whether there was a meeting on 6 2 1967. There was no evidence that the assault was by the workers of the respondent or that the supporters of the first respondent threatened the Scheduled Caste and Harijan voters, and prevented them from going to the polling station to cast their votes. It is impossible to ignore that when appeals are made by candidates there is an element of 'partisan feeling and there is 'extravagance of expression attacking one another and "it would be unreasonable to ignore the question as to what the effect of the pamphlet would be on the mind of the ordinary voter who reads reads the pamphlet. [1000B C] (4) The appellant failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri caused communal propaga tion against the first appellant and others.

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of a final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh since deceased, the predecessor in interest of the appellants filed an applica tion under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale, which was opposed by the judgment debtors. The application was resisted on the ground that as the application was filed more than one year after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the Limitation Act. The District Judge held that in view of the provision of Explanation I1 of section 47, of which was inserted in the Code by Section 20 of the C.P.C., an application under Order XXII Rule 95 of the code will be governed by Article 136 of the , and, as held by the learned Single Judge of the High Court, Article 136 stands impliedly repealed by Section 47 read with article 136 of . The District judge on appeal affirmed the order of the District Judge. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the judgment creditor that having filed more or less one year within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134, no application for delivery of possession could be made within three years from the date of dismissal of the second application for settingaside the sale. On the other hand the contention of the Judgment debtor in view thereof was that even though the sale was confirmed and became absolute under Order XX Rule 92 it was subject to the disposal of the application for set aside the Sale on the basis of which the appeal is filed, and that as held in Chandra Mani Mani vs Kumar Kamalanagar & Ors., AIR 1934 Patna 77, an applicati tion under order XXI Rule 95 will be regulated by Article 138 read with Article 136 ; that an application for deliv ery of possession can be made only after the decree was put into execution within the Period of limitation prescribed by article 136; and that even if an application is made and disposed of, the sale will become absolute after the disposal Of such application, even though, the application is not one as contemplated by Rule 92, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the CPC. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. Article 134 will apply to an applicat ion under Order 21 Rule 95 if it is held that Article 136 would apply to a suit for possession of immovable property which is purchased in the course of execution of the decree. [362C] 2. When an applicationfor setting aside sale is made, the order passed by the executing court either allowing or dismissing the application will be final and effective subject to an appeal that may be made under the provisions of the com pensation Code. [359F] 3.

The appellant, an election worker, filed a petition claiming a declaration that the appellant 's election was void on the ground of corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of People Act 1951. A Single Judge of the High Court declared the election of the appellant to be void on account of the corrupt practices alleged in the petition and held that both these acts amounted to corrupt practices. The pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily "Malayala Manorama" was marked as exhibit P 1, and two photographs of the wall poster were marked as exhibits exhibit P I and two photograph of the same wall were marked and their negatives were marked. The High Court also found that the pamphlets contained the repre sentation of the newspaper containing a news item in daily " MalayalaManorama". Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the first respondent being a Marxist leader, he has not stated as to why it will create such an impression among the electorate; and (ii) the evidence of P.W. 1 that exhibit P1 was printed and distributed with a view to create a false impression among his elector ate that he was a murderer, was wrong and untrue. Dismissing the appeal by Special Leave, this Court HELD: The first respondent and his workers would not have failed to do so had the posters been pasted at the time alleged by them. The appellant ' case both in his written statement as well as in the Court is that the wall Corpo ndy leader who was arrested in that connection was responsible for the murder and he was arrested. There is no doubt that the contents of this poster directly named the first respond ent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the said poster was affixed prior to the election by the workers of the appellants with his knowledge and consent as alleged in their petition, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the incor pation within the mischief of Section 100(1) of Act. [776A B] 2:1 An election worker may claim that he has a right to know the version contained in the statement on which the respondent relies so as to take it into consideration the allegations made in the written statement, and a full and comprehensive reading of such other evidence, or facts, or, as well, as in any event, has to he pleaded either that the statement in that meaning is not defamatory or that it is then true of the respondent. Once however, the Court of Appeal held as follows: (1) The deposition of this witness in chief makes a general statement as follows; "Personally against me propaganda on behalf othe first respondent . .
