Darar PW 8 states in his examination in chief that he had seen copies of exhibit PI being distributed in 7th Division and he also alleged therein that he did not know who pasted exhibit P19 although in examination in at chief he has categorically stated as follows "Personly against me. . . 1 . . . I am an illiterate person, the first Respondent is a Maraxist leader.

The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No. 5 from its erstwhile owner, by a development plan of Greater Bombay, consequent upon the development of a plot on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay, bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land owners were entitled to be members of various ecological action groups, appeared in the appeal and opposed the same contending inter alia that (i) the whole of the said land should be kept reserved for a green belt or recreational ground in the interest of general public; and (ii) the entire land should remain reserved for recreation. The Municipal Corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the saidland under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing operation. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent re filed an appeal before the State Government under Section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act 1966, for setting aside the order granting sanction of the building on the said plot. The appellants challenged the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and granted sanction to the plan submitted by the Respondent No. 2 without hearing them as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the scheme on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. The respondent No .2 set aside the orders of the Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation rejecting the said plan after hearing the appellants as also, the Municipal Commis sioner and directed sanction of building on certain terms which will he referred to earlier in this Judgment. The Respondent No . 2 set aside, the order of the Commisisoner rejecting the application for approval of the proposed development plan submitted on behalf of the respondent company without hearing the parties as also in the High Court or before this Court. The petitioners, who were rate paiders of the M.C.C., and claim to be member of various environmental action groups appeared in appeal and contested the same by contending that the whole land should he kept reserved. It was further contended that in granting exemption on the ground of availability of 75,000 sq. of open site for the purpose of gardens it is a fraud on the Urban Land Ceiling Act. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The ground for rejecting the plan is not tenable and the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal. This contention was advanced before the Respondent Corporation by the petitioners (appellants) that the respondent had misunderstood the provisions of Section 46. It is further submitted that grant exemption on a ground of available 75,200 sq. yds.

The respondents were pro posed ofute, under Sec. 28 read with Items l(a), 1(b) and 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act 1971. After hearing the parties, the Industrial Court held that the existing industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. The Union, therefore filed two special civil applications before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Tribunal. The High Court dismissed both the applications. In the appeal by Special Leave it was contended on behalf of the employers that the industrial undertakings of the respondents had never closed or even at any rates have resumed work in full, and that no new hand will be recruited. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 26 of the ID Act prohibits an employer in a public utility service from locking out any of his workmen without giving notice as provided therein. 23 prohibits an employee from declaring a lockout or has closed down the business. [68B C] 1.2 There is no intention to close the industrial activity. Even if the suspension of work is ordered it would constitute lock out. On the other hand closure implies closing of the industrial process as a 68 consequence of which workmen are rendered jobless. 22(2) of the I.D Act prohibits any employer in public utility services from locked out any or of his workman without giving Notice as provided thereunder. 23 prohibit an employer from declaring any lock out in any of the eventualities mentioned therein. Lockout out has been defined in Sec. 2(L) of tho Industrial Disputes Act, 1974 to mean the closing of a place of business, or the suspension or of work or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him. In lockout the employer refuses to continue. to employ the workmen employed by them even though the business activity was not closed down. The terms of the undertaking of Dr. P.D. Meghani as recorded in this judgment. Both the appeals are disposed of accordingly.

The appellant company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects set out in el. III of the memorandum of association were mentioned therein and in cl. 11 it provided: "In relation to the purchases made by the company as stated above no appreciable sales of shares were made during the period 29th July, 1924 to 30th June, 1942, the sales made in the year ended 30th December, 1942. The assessee Company contended that its books of account showed him as a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties under a misapprehension and as such it was not a "49 dealer but merely an investor". Along with the return filed by the assessee company in which it stated that "the return of total income which was submitted by the Company 's letter of 25th May 1943 was prepared in conformity with the ruling of the Income tax Officer in 1940 41 assessment that the company was to be assessed as a "dealer" in investments and properties but this contention was negatived by the Income Tax authorities and upto the assessment year 1939 40, the assessee Company withdrew its return and filed a revised return on March 7, 1944 contending that it was a " 49 dealer" and that it never carried on any business in the purchase or sale of shares, security and immovable property during the assessment years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal and upheld the order of the Tribunal. On further appeal by the Department before the Income_tax Appellate Tribunal the High Court held that in the case of the assessee not only the memorandum 'of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case fell within the scope of its jurisdiction. In respect of assessment years 1940 41 and 1942 43 the Tribunal held that since that return was submitted the Central Board of Revenue had decided that the Company was an Investment Holding Company, and therefore an amended Return of total Income under section 22(1) of the Indian Income tax Act is submitted herewith on which the assessment for 1943 44 may be based. On the question whether the assessee was a dealer or an investor according as it incurred losses or made profits and (2) whether the profits and losses arising from the sale of share, securities etc. could be taxed as business profits. HELD: (i) As far as the question of "whether there were any materials on the record to support the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the assessee ' company was a tenant" or an investment was itself a question of law and could not be properly framed "as to whether there was material to support its finding". The final conclusion of the tribunal can, therefore, he challenged under section 66(1 ) of the Act. The appeal must accordingly be allowed and the judgment of the High court dated March 2, 1966 set aside and directed the Appellate Assistant Tribunal to submit a fresh statement of the case. [53 D] (ii) It was not correct to say that the question as to what were the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investment is a mixed question of fact and law; in dealing with it. the High Courts may have due regard for the view taken by the Tribunal but its decision would not be lettered by that view. [51 E, 51 G, 52 A].

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. The charge against him related to the first charge of bribery, dismissal from service and in respect of other charges he framed two charges separately. After enquiry into the allegations the Enquiry Officer submitted his report on October 20, 1953, that he had made false returns to the District Court and that to cover his defaults he had altered the records of the court so as to be consistent with those returns. The appellant filed his explanation in answer to the charge on June 22, 1953. The enquiry was then held by the Enquiry officer. After according to the findings of the Enquiry Offi cer, the appellant was dismissed from service. The Government issued a notice to the appellant on August 12, 1954, to show cause why he should not be dismissed or removed from service, and he should be dismissed from serv ice. On September 29, 1954 the appellant filed in the High Court a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954 on the grounds: (1) that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953 which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22,1953 with effect from October 1, 1953 the enquiry into 'the conduct of government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above might be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same, and (2) that the proceedings in the Madras High Court subsequent thereto were without jurisdiction since it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion. Held, that when r. 4 of the Andhra CIVIL Services Rules differed in some respects from the corresponding Rule of the Madras Civil Service Rules, there is no valid reason for departing from the procedure laid down in the Indian Civil Service. The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government. Such an order is neither one of dismissal nor of removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution.

A private limited company was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co. a private Limited Company with its registered office in Bombay, died on May 13, 1945, having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The said Memorandum having been signed by the heirs to the estate, the Company and one Morarka, the executor agreed to sell the remaining 2224 shares of the Company to Morarkhaka and pursuant thereto the relevant share certificates with transfer deeds duly executed were delivered to the legatees in respect of those shares and no question arises in this appeal. While computing the income of the company for the assessment years 1946 47 and 1947 48, the Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed, but after processing the amount under section 18(5) included it in the total income of Anderson as "assessee". The Income Tax Officer then issued a notice to 'James &erson the estate of Maniram 's an incorporated company with its Registered office in the Bombay died on July 7, 1949. On March 26, 1953, the said Income tax officer passed an order under section 23A of the Income Tax Act (as it then stood) that certain undistributed parts of the assessable income of 'the company shall be deemed to have been distributed as dividends amongst the shareholders as at the dates, viz., May 26, 1947 and December 22, 1947 of the General meetings of the Board of Directors of the dissolved Company. On October 12, 1953 the Incometax Officer issued a second notice under section 34(1)(b) of the Act addressed to "Jamis Anderson Administrator to the Estate of late Shri Henry Gannon" reciting that he had reason to believe that Anderson 's income assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949 was escaped assessment and that he proposed to re assess the escaped income, and for that purpose called upon Anderson to make a return of his total income and the total world income assessable for the years ending March 31, 1949". The High Court answered the first question in the negative and declined to answer the second question. With special leave the Commissioner appealed to this Court.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. After passing the Indian Independence Act 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947 and thereafter entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government thought fit. The Ruler later compulsorily leased the lands to the appellant from January 1, 1948. On December 15, 1947, he entered into another agreement with it whereby he was ceded to the Government on January 22, 1951, and thereafter he entered an agree ment with the Dominion Of India to be extended with the prevailing State of Madhya Pradesh. The question whether the villages mentioned in Schedule A and B of the petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution fell within the category of Estates or Alienated lands. Held, that the appellant was not a "ex Ruler" for purposes of the Act and as such he was entitled to be registered as an ex Ruler under the Indian . There is nothing in article 366(22) which requires a court to recognise such a person as a Ruler for purposes outside the Constitution. The appellant had no right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in his villages. The burden of proving this fact was on him to prove this fact. He must prove this even which he never attempted to discharge. State of Madras vs Kover Limited, ; , referred to. Accordingly, in view of the provisions of article 363(1) of the constitution any dispute arising out of the Merger Agreement or the Instrument of accession is beyond the competence of the courts to enquire into.

The respondent, a Garden Curator in the Office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong was transferred to Pauri by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, B.P. JEEVAN REDDY on January 29, 1991 by the Postmaster General, Government of India. As many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including respondent, he filed a writ petition before the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the order of his transfer. The learned Single Member of the High Court quashed the order transferring the case on the grounds: (1) while ordering his transfer, there is no doubt, the authority has not kept in mind the guidelines issued by the Government on the subject; and (2) the guidelines are applicable to the case of the respondent. Further, "in the matter of considering transfer of an individual officer, the Office Memorandum dated 3.4.1986, educational dislocation of the children and health ground, if all present, deserve special consideration not to pass the order". Aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment, the Union of India has preferred this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: ( 1 ) The guidelines requiring the two spouses to be posted at one pi" as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. [435G] (2)(a) Before ordering the transfer, the authorities must keep in mind all the guidelines contained in Government O.M. dated 3rd April 1986, educational qualifica tion and norms which the High court observes while exercising the said jurisdiction apply equally to the Tribunal created under Article 323 A. and find it all the more surprising that the learned Single Judge who passed the impugned order is a former Judge of the Court and is thus aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdic tion.) The Administrative Tribunal is not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the authority competent to transfer. [441E F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; ; Bank of Mysore vs Jagjit singh Mehta, [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306; Bank of U.P vs Jagjit Sing Singh Mehta [1992 ] 1 S .C. 306 and Bank of Indian vs JagjitSingh Mehta, referred to. (b) The guidelines are in the nature of guidelines. They do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order is vitiated by mala fides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the manner of ordering the transfers, there are no doubt; the authority must keep In mind the guideline issued by Government on 2nd April 1986. The guidelines say that as faras possible, husband and wife must be posted to one pi". [441G H] Bank Ltd.

The accused persons were tried under sections 147 and 148 I.P.C., for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of one Jawahar, as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the learned Trial Judge but on appeal, the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A 1to 3. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar had been proved beyond doubt and as such the offence committed by them came within the parameters of section 325 read with 34, I. P.C. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of perma nent and arms and no finding was called for against A4 and therefore had mistakenly been passed which could not have done so. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the accused to cause grievous hurt and as said under section 325 I. p.C.; is to cause simple hurt and As such, the offence com punent committed by ted accused came within th parameters of Section 325 read along with 34 IPC. [3B C] 2.

The respondent firm was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970. The loan amount of Rs.80,000 was admittedly advanced by way of loan by the Bank after its nationalisation. The respondent firm owns certain motor vehicles which are mentioned in A and schedule to the plaint of the suit. The firm was carrying on business at Madras as fleet owners and gasolene carriers. It had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, the father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent NO. 2 Sunkavali Rajlaxmi. The case of the Bank was that in addition to the hypothecation of the A and Schedule properties made in its favour to secure repayment of the aforesaid amounts of loan, the other partner, the respondent created an equitable mortgage in favour of the bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of E schedule properties of the plaint. In the suit the Bank prayed for the sale of the said properties for the recovery of the amounts claimed by it on account of the loan together with interest due thereon. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statements denying the creation of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees while denying the existence of the mortgages contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank were bound by the alienations and transfers made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The dispute was whether the Banking companies Act of 1949 was a `special Indian ' or not; and the High Court upheld the contention relying upon section 4(e) of the Act, but rejected the contention based on section 4 (e) which provides for scaling down of the debt of an agriculturist. Accepting the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act IV of 1938 are not applicable to the appellant Bank and, therefore, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the bank by the respondents. [970B] 2.1 Courts have not intended to refer to any law made by any legislature of our country but only a law made under the sovereign philosophy of the British Parliament [970C D] 3.2 The intention of the Legislature is very clear in that the provision of section 4 of the Banking company Act would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian law, whether it is created in pursuance of or by or under the special Indian laws. But there is nothing repugnant in the language and the words `special ' must be understood in their natural meaning so as to convey a clear meaning, still a different interpretation or meaning should be given to them because of the setting. In other words, while the setting of the words may sometimes be necessary for the interpretation of the word of the statute, but that has not been ruled by this Court to be the only and the surest method of interpretation. [969D E] Surinder Singh vs S. Agarwalla, ILR , Shankar Murthy vs State of A.P, AIR 1983 Andhra Pradesh 348 referred to. 2.3 The expression `special one ' in section 4 42(e), is not exhaustive but a broad and technical interpretation of such words would be given not to them as an enactment of the Government of India Act.

The Central Government, by a Notification dated July 30, 1958, fixed the ex factory price per maund of sugar produced in Punjab Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. The notification further stipulated that "the prices for the consumer only should be fixed". The Central Government issued an order on August 27, 1955 fixing ex factory prices of sugar to be supplied by each factory for export and levy an additional excise duty at the rate of Rs. 17 per maund on any factory failing to deliver its quota of sugar for export. It was contended that the notification was ultra vires as it fixes ex factory rates only for factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and NorthBihar and, therefore, it was void and unconstitutional. Held, that the object of the Act was to provide for control of the production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in, essential commodities in the interests of general public, so that the prices might be fixed at the stage where the consumer is the purchaser. The Government must not only fix ex factory Price but also wholesale and retail price. It could not therefore be said that the impugned notification did not subserve the purposes of the legislation nor did it provide for a fair and equitable distribution of sugar in the country at a price. Similarly, there was no discrimination after the control of sugar prices in these three regions and the contention that the factories in the other areas were left free to sell at any price fell well within the terms of the notification. The impugned notification was bad because it fixes 'ex factory prices only for manufacturers of sugar at lower rates is not correct. Under cl. 5, the Central Government might fix the retail price, i.e., the price for the consumers, fails, and under cl. (c) there could be no discrimination in effect by the fixation of prices in those three regions. The contention that there was discrimination is purely theoretical and does not merit a moment 's consideration.

Section 19(6) of the provides that notwithstanding the expiry of the period of operation under sub section (3), the award shall continue to be binding on the parties until a period of two months has elapsed from the date on which notice is given by any party bound by it to the other party or parties intimating its intention to terminate the award '. The question for consideration was whether the increase in dearness allowance justified While fixing the basic wages and the rate of dearness allowance payable, the Tribunal took into account the scales of dearness pay and capacity required to be taken into consideration in determining the amount, namely, (1) at that stage, the Court might not be in full possession of all material circumstances to make up its mind and (ii) the order is only an ex parte one made in the absence of the respondent. Held, that in regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement was the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of living index in the year 1957. The Act did not therefore provide any restriction on the right of appeal to any party from the decision of any tribunal, but it conferred a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal from the order of any Tribunal in the territory of India. Pritam Singh vs The State of Madras ; and Bengal Lai Sarkar vs Its Workers ' Union, [1950] S.C.R. 491, referred to. It was not correct to contend that if the cost of working index in 1954 was taken as the basis, there was a fall in the rate during 1957 and in fact it rose to 4006 in May 1957 with the result that there was an increase in the dearness allowance on the basis of the rise in the cost in living index. There could be no justification for interfering with that award except in respect of matters covered in the above. Pritam Sing Singh vs State of Rajasthan, ; , relied on.

The appellant was the Mahant of a private religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. This Mutt is situated at Uravakonda in the district of Anantapur. It appears that on the 6th September, 1939, the Board of Hindu Religious Endowments constituted under the Madras Act 11 of 1927 framed a scheme under section 63 of the said Act for the proper administration of the Mutt and its endowments. The predecessor in office of the appellant then filed suit No. 21 Of 1939 on the file of the District Judge Anantapur for getting the said Scheme set aside. His suit substantially failed because the District Court was persuaded to make only a few minor modifications in the scheme subject to which the scheme was confirmed and that decision was taken in appeal by the predecessor of the appel lant to the High Court of Madras, (A.S. No. 269 of 1945). During the pendency of the appeal, the appellant 's predecessor died and the appellant brought himself on the record as legal representative of his deceased predecessor. The appellant came on the question whether the scheme in fact had not been implemented till then. Held, that the scheme did not bring out the fact that the provisions of the earlier Act were inconsistent with the provisions Of section 103(d) and (b) of the latter Act and the scheme framed under it was valid at that time. R.S., in the light of the other provisions of section 103 (a), and (g) clearly brought out the facts that where the Legislature wanted the conti nuance of the action taken under the provisions o the earlier statute only if the said action was consistent with the relevant pro visions of the former Act, it had so provided. The scheme having been framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law, his property rights had been taken away.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. While he was working with the approval of the authorities for almost 4 years his appointment after 1986 had not been approved by the educational authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1983, and that the appellant would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation holding that the appel lant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989; that the services as such teacher were continuous for aperiod of over six months and that he had continued till 18.7.1986 with breaks in between and the appellant 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue till replaced by the candidate from tho Select List, and his case therefore will not come within the preview of the Validation Act; and that for regularisation the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the validation Act on the above view. Aggrieved by the High Courts decision, the appellant filed this appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government is expected to function as a model employer. [995A] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, A.I.R 1987 S.C. 478, followed. Rattan Lal & Lal vs state of Haryana , Tolaram Dass & Ors.

The High Court dismissed the petition and hence this appeal by special leave. HELD: (i) Under that rule the persons entitled to daily allowance are divided into two categories and a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti belonging to Category II is entitled to Rs. 6/ per diem when a Member of the Panchayat Samiti does not have to spend money out of his own pocket for the discharge of his duties. The conveyance allowance had to be restricted to 1 /4th and not to Rs 4/ per month when a Chair man performs a journey in connection with his official duties outside the district.[427 B] (iii) Under R. 3 it was observed that the mileage allowance is payable only for journey undertaken outside the District while, while in respect of daily allowances, the fact that the right of to receive it accrues only when the journey is outside the districts was made manifest by laying down that the receipt of this daily allowance is to be subject to the provisions of r. 7. The fact that in the year 1965, it was considered desirable that the Chairman of the a Panchayat Samitis should not draw travelling allowances and daily allowances while performing duties within the District and should only he entitled to theseallowances when required to travel outside the states. The appellant was tenant of the tenanted premises purchased by the respondent for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later. They filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damage to it. The dispute having been compromised, the landlord filed a fresh suit with permission of the Rent Controller and the Civil Judge allowed the defendant 's suit, which was confirmed by the Additional District Judge. On second appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the first appellate court, on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying eviction under sec. 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act 10 of 1952. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The construction of tin shed could not be held to have materially altered the accommodation. [978C] 1.2 In the absence of any legislative defi cition of the aforesaid words it would be useful to refer to the meaning given to these words in dictionaries. Concise Oxford Dictionary defines the word 'essentially as change in character, position "Materially" as an adverbimpor tant essentially concerned with matter not with form. [979G] 1:3. The expression 'materially altered ' means "a substantial change in the character, form and the structure of the building without destroying its identity". It is not possible to give exhaustive list of construction which do not constitute material alterations, as the determination of this question depended on facts of each case. In arriving at the question whether the constructions are sub stantial in nature and they alter, the form, front and structure of tho premises. The construction that amounted to material alteration was a mixed question of fact and law. [980F G] 1 :4. The High Court committed error in interfering with the findings of the First Appeal Court. There is no merit in the submission. [981G] 2:1. In the circumstances, the constru c tion of tin sheds could not have materially changed the form or structure of building as it can easily be removed without causing any damage to the premises, or its value or might not amount to an unreasonable use of leased premises, yet con struction may fall within the expression ' material alteration '. [976C] 2 :2. The nature of constructions, whether they are permanent or temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alteration '

The appellant Company filed a suit in the Court of Additional District Judge, Indore against the appellant company claiming damages on account of non delivery of certain goods. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the Company and it came to know about the decree decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte decree. The respondent firm filed a revision application before the High Court under section 115 C.P.C., which allowed the revision, set aside and reversed the judgment of the Trial Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. A summons by post to the registered office of the company, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on the company itself. But the first part of clause (b) has got to be understood with reference to the other provisions of the Code. In Rule 17 of Order 5 it has been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the summons or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the corporation and make a report to that effect." [1033B C] 2. The meaning of clause 'b) had got to he understood in the background of the provisions of Order stated In order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons, it has gotto be understood in their background of provisions of Court in 2 Order 5, Rule 17 C. P.C." [1031D] 3. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. If the serving peon or bailiff is not able to serve the summons on the Secretary or any Director or section other Principal Officer of the Corporation because either he refuses to signed the summons, or is no scope for saying that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so. [1032B C; 1035A] 4.

The respondent filed a complaint in the Magistrate against the respondents on the basis of a police report that he was in possession of the land in dispute and that the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements, and then after an full enquiry as provided by section 145. The Magistrate passed the final order on February 17, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession thereof. Against this order the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the proceedings in view of a finding that there was an apprehension of breach of peace and therefore he was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order in the final report also. The High Court allowed the petition and remanded the case to the Magistrate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 145(5) it is for the magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach of the peace and once he records his satisfaction in the main order, the High court in revision cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise of materials on the ground of which the satisfaction of the Magistrate is based. [96E F] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal ; , R. H. Bhutani vs Pandit J. Desai & Ors., A.I.R. 1981 S.C.[910, referred to. In the instant case there was no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under sub section (5) of section 145 nor was such a case set up by any party before the Magistrate or before the High Courts. [95A] Hariram & Ors vs Banwari lal & Ors, A.l.R, ; Ramarao vs Shivram & ors., A Cr. No. 356/79 dt. 1 12 1979; R.H. Bhondutani v Shri J.J. Desai and Ors. ,[1977] 3 S.L.R.(Supp) 352; Hari Ram Ram & Anr.

The assessee was a public company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn and for the purpose of that business it purchases cotton and occasionally sells it. Its profits were computed by applying the formula evolved by the Indian Income tax laws and as such excess profits as were liable to tax. The Department did not accept the correctness of the figures and the Income Tax Officer made certain adjustments, but, on appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the intermediaries were benamidars for the purposes of section 42(1) and therefore, they could be taxed only if they were remitted to British India and that, in fact, little or no profits were made by it in those transactions which did not affect the chargeability of the appellant to tax on the profits made by them. The assessee then moved the High Court under section 66(2) of the Act for an order requiring the Tribunal to refer those questions to the court and that the High court having rejected the applications, he appealed to this Court. HELD : (1) It was not a pure question of law. [709 E] (a) When the finding is one of fact and is itself an inference from other facts, it is open to challenge under section 64(1). The principle that the inference from facts would be a question of fact or of law according as the point for determination was one of pure fact or mixed question of Law and fact. [ 705 A] (b) When a finding on a question is open by the court, it will be an idle formality to direct the Tribunal not refer the question for the decision of the Court. The facts relating to this matter are that during the periods of assessment with which the appeals were concerned, the appellant opened branches in the States of Travancore Cochin, Pudukkottah and Mysore, and sold yarn to its consti tors (1)[1964] S.C.R. 729. (c) The point in dispute was whether the profits were liable 'on income or profits when they have arisen or accrued. [777 D] (d) The nature of the transactions is that it is a pure and mixed question on a mixed question. It is wholly illegitimate in view of section 14(2)(c), which recognises a finding On a question Of law, such as construction of a statute or document of title, the decision is open open to review by the Court only on the ground that it Is not supported either by evidence or perverse but also on the basis that it was not the proper conclusion to come on the facts. [773 E F] (2) Where the finding in the words of the statute to endeavor to secure for 'a finding on pure question Of fact is open ' to attack, under section66(1), as erroneous in law when there is no evidence to support it or if it is perverse. The nature and character of a particular income will depend upon the facts found, and the intention appears from the terms of the definition. Therefore, where there is evidence to consider, the Court has power to substitute its own judgment for that finding but not in the latter. [763 E G] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co., ; , referred to. (3) The Tribunal had no power to make a reference on the question whether the conclusions were arrived at by it or conclusions drawn therefrom, and there is nothing unusual in its finding that they were arrived upon by it, nor can it be said to have been argued in the High Courts.

The assessee was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets, other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49 the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager, Shri J.P. Vaish, who had been given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish in July 1947. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish. He also found that no general practice of giving commission at the rate of 25 % existed in the assessee 's line of business, but there was some collateral reason. On an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the said charge of conduct after the deceased Vaish, the General manager. Tiffs post carried a remuneration of Rs., 18,000 plus Rs. 6,000 and therefore the commission paid by Shri Vaish was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business but there were some collateral reasons. But considering the practice in similar business concerns, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner expressed the view that the rate paid to one of the Directors existed in his line of activity of business. At the time when it was old and dilapidated, the firm was converted into a company and the post carried by the General Managers was abolished and one of its Directors who managed the affairs of the Company was given Rs. 18,500 per annum as remuneration and Rs. six,000 per annum was increased to Rs. 37,732 in that year. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the assessee it was contended on behalf Of the respondent that the entire amount of Rs 75, 464,465 paid to an employee was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business of the assesses within the meaning of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. HELD : Although the practice of similar business concern, the Income tax Department expressed the opinion that the rates of commission paid were not fixed on account of business considerations but there being some collateral ground the allowance was restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) Of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. The appellant claimed that he was not authorised in accordance with his own liking. The case was adjourned to January 21, 1957 for filing a compromise or hearing and on that date a further application was filed praying that the agreement filed in respect of his case should not be accepted and that he and his agents should be heard before the disposal of the case. This application was dismissed by the Tribunal in accordance of its order dated February 26, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting his application for a writ because the Union which had espoused his cause was being repre sented by its Secretary, Fateh Singh. HELD : (i) The Tribunal committed no error in refusing the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his own choice in preference to Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union. As a last resort, learned counsel for the appellant wanted to urge that the Secretary had no authority to compromise is a question of fact which cannot be allowed to be raised at this stage. [202 D] (ii) The terms of the compromise of the dispute regarding the appellant and his dismissal were that he would not get reemployment but by way of "humanitarian considerations the company agreed without prejudice to pay an ex gratia amount of Rs. 1,000/ . . [203 C E] Central Provinces Transport Service Ltd. vs Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, , referred to. (iii) The award of the Tribunal was correct and that it had been established that there was nothing that would justify this Court in interfering with the order of the High Court rejecting the appellant. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the defendants on the allegation that defendant No. I was the tenant inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No 2 and further stated that he looked after the affairs of the house property and acted for and on behalf of the family just as other members of the joint Hindu family looked after other affairs including the business belonging to the family. The appellants contended that (i) the deceased belonged to a joint Hindu Family and other members; and (ii) in view of r. 5, O. XLI, r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it was not necessary to bring on record any other person and (iii) in the alternative defendants Nos. 1, 3 and 11 formed a joint family, even though time had been given to them for filing an affidavit stating such a fact. Held, that the appeal could not have been taken to be an appeal under the Code or under the Letters Patent of the High Court. The provisions of 0. XLI r. 33 were applicable to appeals filed by all the parties jointly and there was nothing common in their provisions which make the provisions of one interfere in any way with those of the other. State of Punjab vs Nathu Ram, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 636, applied. Baij Nath vs Ram Bharose, [1952] 53 I.A. 84, relied on.

The appellant tenant was a tenant of a building in Delhi, having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument has arisen). At the time of the lease the appellant had not been extended to Delhi although later, on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord had been receiving rent from the tenant until the time he filed a petition for eviction (1967)), the statute which regulated the right to eviction being the Delhi Rent Control Act 1958 (59 of 1958) (for short, the Rent Act). The eviction petition set out two grounds out in many specified in section 14 of the Rent Acts viz; (a)unauthorized sub letting of a portion of the premises and possession by alternative accommodation. But, in the High Court the appellant tenant fell back on certain defences grounded on ss.106 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act on the score that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections; (b)una Jaisri Prasad vs Smt. Shashi Aggarwal & Anr., [1970] 3 SCR 471, followed. In appeal before this Court it was contended for the appellant landlord that the lease has expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g); although there is some confusion in this order about the determination of the leasehold being under section III(g) or outside it, the thrust of the holding is found in these concluding words: "However, as held by the Supreme Court in Narender, Lokmanya Lodhi vs manifestation Bai & Ors. ; the provisions in section 111 (g) as to notice in writing as a preliminary to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease are not technical in character, in that they require such termination by fifteen days ' notice expiring with the end of the month of the tenancy; (c) the tenant remonstrated against this new plea being permitted in appeal but the Court construed the statement in the pro forma in column 18 B, that no service has been effected upon the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the ground that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux or by forfeiture following the breach by the tenant; (d) the building had not yet been fully operational at all and the appellant did not send a copy of the termination notice as required by those Sections; (e) the provisions of the 1958 Act had not, therefore, apply to the lease in question and that this was the essence of the matter if such transfusion is permissible, and in the absence of a specific statutory provision, the rules of justice, equity and good conscience govern the situation, and this element was amply fulfilled by the filing of the eviction petition itself. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The tenant remlegged against this old plea being allowed by this Court on the footing that it had decided in Namdeo vs Jagdish Chandra & Ors., [1971] 2 MLJ 596, to the effect that settlement by forfeiture under section 11 of the 1956 Act would not be binding on him and in consonance with the principles of justice equity, equity, and good justice; and fair conscience. The requirement as to written notice provided in the section therefore cannot be said to be based on any general rule of equity or whether it is merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the 1956 section by the legislature and is not based on anything to rule of justice or what is the true nature and character of the rule. [910C, F G] 2.

The Governor of Assam in exercise of the powers conferred by cl. (c) of the proviso to clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution gave a 15 days ' notice to the public servant to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. He was also informed that he would be required to appear before the Governor and a reasonable opportunity had been given to him for showing cause against the proposed action. The Governor on the basis of materials before him held an enquiry under proviso (c), to clause 2, article 311(2) as it existed during its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963 which came into force on October 6, 1963. He accordingly dismissed his services with immediate effect. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the decision of the Governor under cl. 5 of the said proviso was wrong and should be upheld. HELD: The satisfaction recorded by the Governor in an order passed under cl.(c) to clause II of el. (3) of Article 311 is recorded in the following words: " It is not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity of showing cause, against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him, and this view was based on the language used earlier in the unamended article and on the interpretation placed on that unamended Article by this Court. [486 H] Khem Chand vs The Union of India & Ors., ; applied. Khemchand vs The State of Punjab, ; Khem Chand v The Union Government of India and Ors. ; followed. Khem Chand V. Union of lndia,[1969] Vol.VI Assam Law Reports 192; referred to.

The assessee disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10 lakhs but claimed set off in its return the assessee, a subsidiary concern, from out of which it claimed set up de claim for set off of capital loss of Rs 3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. The Income Tax Officer disallowed this claim on the ground that when in the assessment order the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of his appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. As no further appeal was carried by the assessee with the first appellate order, the matter had become final. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that both the Income tax Officer as also the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had found that the loss sustained by the compu tant during the previous year rele vant to the assessment years 1957 58 and the same should be set off against the capital gains in the asses see 's assessment year, and accordingly allowed the assessee 's claim, but held that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional inasmuch in nature and that the claim for setting off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income Tax Offi cer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. That having not been done, the claim was not admissible. The High Court also found that there is no genuine gains; it held that even if the answer to the question is in the negative, whether any loss could be said to have been determined for the assessment period 1957 58, which could be carried forward to subsequent years would be carried off against capital gain in the assess ment year 1965 66. It therefore upheld the order of t he Tribunal and dismissed the appeal by the Revenue. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The benefit conferred under Section24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of Sec tion 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claimed of set off was admissible in our view. [1167 E] (b) On a bare reading of the provi sions of Section 74(1)(b} and section 80 together it is clear that on a plain reading of those provisions, and without reference to anything more the assessment proceedings would be neces sary. [1108 F] 1.(a) A close analysis of section 75(1) (b)) shows that the benefit conferred by Section 24 of 1922 Rules continued to he given effect to under the said 1961 Act, and notwithstanding anything to more, this appeal can be disposed of.

The Union of India and the Direc tor, Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P), Ministry of Defence had preferred this appeal against the decision of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad Bench. The three units, viz., Defence Science Service Rules, 1987, and DQAS, and Rules 13 in DAQAS and Dos, were the same, and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science service Rules. In the year 1979, the Defence Science Services was trifurcated and reconstituted as Defence degree Quality Assurance Service (DQAS). The appellant who was working in DTD &P became a member of DAQS but when the trif ulcation was made, the Service Rules governing the three units had a common Rule which was rat ed in DA QAS, which provided that other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of services of the members of the service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these Rules shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect t he serv ice, be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. At the time the present controversy arose, and as the respondent was recruited initially, to that service and then sent to different units. The service conditions of the employees belonging to the three independent units were thesame, viz; Defence Science and Air, etc. were the identical and governed by the said set of rules, viz, Defence Science In the month 1979, after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the Service, in any of the said three units. All, the service conditions belonging to Defence Science was tri fated and reconstituted into three different services. All the service condition of the person working in the three con stations including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. was the same and were governed by that set of rule viz. Military Science Service (DRDO). In the seniority list, however, the respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal who held the post of Deputy Chief Scientific Officer, who held that the post fell vacant on ad hoc basis after completion of five years of service and thus entitled him to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years, provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age of 58 years within the preced ing five years. The Tribunal also directed reinstatement of the respondent in service within one week of this Order, and further directed that he would continue in service till he attains the age Of 60 years unless of course for some other legal reasons, it became necessary to discontinue his services before that date. In appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, it was contended that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of Service for the members belonging to different unit which he belonged to the newly constituted service, and merely because the superannuationage of the member of the scheme was increased, it could not be held that he was enti tled to the said benefit; that there is no agreement between him and the Union of india nities who belonged to another unit, viz DAQE was entitled to the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circum stances of the case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 In spite of the decision by the Tribunal as also pending this appeal, when no stay was granted, the Union Government retired the respondent at the age, of 58, years. [864A] 1.2 The respondent was already working in either of the three plants were deemed to belong to the respective newly constituted Service. This being so, their service conditions would have to run parallel and no discrim ination can be made between them by an unilateral action.

The appellant was elected from the constituency of a Municipal Council. The first of these was to effect that the appellant had published all the phmphlets mentioned in the petition and distributed them amongst the voters and the appellant, who did great public service in the past, challenged the election of the appellant before the High Court on several grounds set forth in paragraph 3 of the petition. He also alleged that the notice calling for the particulars was issued to the first respondent and his advocate, but he declined to do so, on August 21, 1968, The High Court dismissed the appeal summarily on October 4, 1968. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that having rejected the application, it is not open to the Judge to examine these two persons as court witnesses and that the trial was vitiated in that the two witnesses who were examined as Court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier. Held: (i) The High Courts acted illegally in rejecting the application for issuing summonses to these two candidates on the ground that there was no evidence on which the judge could have come to the conclusion he did, and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the trial Court although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summonses should have been passed. (ii) The words "reason to believe" used in section 21(1) meant "that no person or other person is found with the commission of a corrupt practice". It was, therefore, not open for the High Courts to go into the question as a third party but it was not to be understood that the Court never had the power to summon a witness and to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter particularly of corrupt practices. (iii)The appellant knew exactly what points he had to meet. Evidence was adduced about the publication and distribution of the pamphlet by the appellant and contradicted by the appellants. The trial Judge rightly took into account this evidence and came to the conclu sion that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June, the below mentioned candidates were elected from that date and the petition which was filed on the 24th June was beyond time and should not have been entertained. (iv)The High Court had jurisdiction to call these two witnesses as witnesses under the provisions of section 21 of the Act. (v)Section 21(2) did not prescribe any pre scribed condition for the examination of a person as court witness envisaged by the Code of Civil Procedure.

Section 3 A of the U. P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 which, as it then stood was deleted by a fresh notification on August 1, 1956, validating the said notification as from March 31, 1956. The petitioner company challenged the validity of the Validation Act by filing a writ petition before the High Court who dismissed the same in limine. Thereafter the sale was treated as unauthorised and inoperative, because, the ban imposed by section 3 A was not operative. The State Legislature passed the U .P. Sales tax (Validation) Act, 1958 validating the aforesaid notification asfrom March 31. 1956. Section 3A of the Act provided that a single point taxation (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 3, the State Government may by notification in the official Gazette declare that the turnover in respect of any goods or class of goods shall not be liable to tax except at such single point in the series of sales by successive dealers as the State Govt. may specify and section 4 Of the Act was made applicable only to the dealers who were assessed to sales tax on the sale effected between April 1,1956 and July 31, 1955. The writ petition filed by the petitioner challenging the validity was dismissed by a Full Bench in appeal by special leave granted by this Court. Held, that the validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and it operates retrospectively: it operates retrospective effect only for a period prior to the date on which the notifications were issued. If the impugned notification was valid because it was issued before section 3A was in operation but later it could not be challenged as invalid by reason of article 254(2) of the Constitution. The validity of a law passed under entry 52 in List II is an incidental issue and does not affect the competence of the Legislature. It was finally urged on the basis of sections 8, 14 and rule 23 Of the U P. Act that there is no question of any incompetence to enact the impugned section which imposes a tax retrospectively but it operates prospectively.

Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Where the vice is widespread and the larger felons are often let loose, in prison treatment must, therefore be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation, apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji frequently insisted. In prison treatment should, therefore, be ge Obled to psychologistaling, released of stress es, restoration up of self holdings and cultural felon. It may be marginally extenuatory to mention that modern Indian conditions are drifting into societal permissiveness on the carnal front promoting proneness to pornos in life, what wit libidinous 'brahmacharis ' womanising public men, lascivious dating and mating by unwed students, sex explosion in celluloid and book stalls and corrupt morals reaching a new ' high ' in places. [591 C] 2. The special circumstances of this case constrains the appellant to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [593 E G] 3. It is desirable to superadd to the sentence of imprisonment a few directives to ensure that the carceral period reforms the convict. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, Edibley molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and mostly criminals victimised. It might be marginically extenumental to mention: that modern India conditions are fit reassess mentally, punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative apart frombeing deterrent.[593 F; 596 E] 5. The Special circumstances of the case constray made the current efforts of Governments, Central and State to reform jail regimen we hope, will give a better deal to the caged community. For these reasons, in this case, it is considered desirable to re conduc tuted to superad to the term of imprisonment S a few directions to ensure recovery that the Carceral Period reforms the appellant convict turns a new leaf; one major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a fresh leaf of normal life. [566 F H] 6. The Court must restore the man. A hyper sexed homo sapiens cannot be compassalised by humiliating or harsh treatment, but that is precisely the perversion of unreformed Jail Justice which some criminologists have described as the crime of punishment. This Court has held in Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation deprivation of his personal freedom should be goalvanised and humanetyly restolutely rest sanitaryly rest suitable apart from becoming deterrent. [595 B] 7. The human ingenuity of the poor appellant is very much important a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a newlic leaf.

The respondent was a limited company dealing in land. It maintains its accounts on the mercantile system and by an order dated June 21, 1946 under Rule 75A(1) of Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Defence ofIndia Act, 1939 certain plots of land measuring about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5 requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952 published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the respondent, which was also reduced by the Arbitrator from Rs.513,624 on account of the permanent acquisition of the land and thus enhancing the original amount of compensation by Rs. 5,13, June 24, 1955 on which he directed interest at 5 per cent per annum from January 8 1953, the date of acquisition to the date the payment till the date on the date when the award was made. The State Government appealed to the High Court and during the pendency of the appeal on April 25, 1956 it deposited Rs.736,691 which the assessee was permitted to withdraw on May 9, 1956 on furnishing security. On receipt of the amount the appellant credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57 the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956 the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum Rs. 7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This represented the difference between the sum of RS.737,190 payable to Shri Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd. and others vs Commissioner of Income Tax (Central), Calcutta, which represented the amount of Rs,.12,276 out of that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The income tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesse, on the assumption that the aforesaid income accrued lo him on the day of the award, and therefore a trading receipt of this business carried on by the assessee, and held that no receipts of revenue nature were liable to tax in respect of the additional amount of compensa tion. The Appellate Tribunal held that the compensation received by the respondent related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipts of the business carried out by the assesee, and that a receipt of a revenue nature liable to Tax. On second appeal by the Revenue 's order dated February 22, 1964, at the instance of the Revenue the High court answered the question in favour of the respondent and against the Revenue. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the amount did not accrue to the appellant as its income during the relevant previous year ending March 31. 1956 relevant to the assessment years 1956 57 and the amount paid by the appellant related only to the acquired land which had been the stock m trade of trade of assessee, but was a trading account in trade or commerce; (ii) that it was on the final determination of the quantum of compensation that the right to such income in the nature of compensation would arise or accrue and till then there was no liability in praesenti in respect Of the additional amounts of compensation claimed by the owner of the Land. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1 (i). A mere claim by the assesses after taking possession of the lands at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation. It must not be forgotten that even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by tile Government to theHigh Court, and the High 844 Court may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation.

% The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction from the suit premises, on various grounds including arrears of rent and other reliefs. The plaintiffs appellant tenants contested the suit, in which an objection was taken that no compromise decree was passed by them. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the defendants was dismissed by the Third Additional District Judge Gwalior. In a second miscellaneous appeal before the High Court, the plea taken on behalf of the appellants was not resintegra and as such was amenable to consideration in several decisions of this court. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that paragraph 1 of the compromise petition was an admission in respect of only the first part, namely, the positive aspect of clause (f) and not of the second part, viz., that the landlord has no other reasonably suitable nonresidential accommodation; and that the respondents were denied in para 3 of the written statement. Dismissing the appeal. ^ HELD: 1. Where an order for eviction based on consent of the parties is found to fall in line with that of the section when in paragraph 5 of the judgment, it says "there is nothing in Section 12 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 prohibiting contracting out, such a prohibition would have to be read by implication consistently with the public policy underlying this welfare measure" was approved. [882 F G] 2. In order to get a decree or order for possession against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions of the Act. When the suit is contested, the issue goes to trial. The Court passes a decree for eviction only if it is satisfied on evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance 981 with the requirement of the statute has been established. Even when the trial proceeds ex parte, this is so. If however, parties choose to enter into a compromise due to any reason such as to avoid the risk of protracted litigation expenses, it is open to them to do so. [888 H 883 A] 3. When a suit is resisted the issue went to trial, and the Court passed a decree which shows that the compromise was legal, that is to say, lawful and was in accordance With the plaint. The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decrees under the law. [868 C D] 4. In such a situation, the only thing to be seen is whether the compromise is in violation of the requirement Of the law.[851 B D] 5. A similar argument advanced in the cases of Nagindas Ramdas Ramdas vs Dalpatram Inchharam @ Brijram and Otheres (6) took pains to go into the matter elaborately once more and said at page 552, 587 and distinguished. [89 E F] 6. The object of the provision that order is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3, because grounds for claiming relief are always limited whether the relief be claimed under the general law or a statute. The protection of the tenant is inherent to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction of a tenant except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in Section12(11). [864 F] 7. A contrary argument advanced by the appellants is that paragraph I have no other reasonable suitable non residential accommodation of his own in his occupation in the city or town concerned. It does not give any indication either on the face orin the background, of other material in the ease that the tenants expressly or implied impliedly is agreed to suffer, a decree would be valid. [87885 C D].

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were RS. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs Redemption balance of RS. 91,116/ . The Income tax authorities disallowed an amount of Rs 1188,000 out of this loss in the value of 83 shares held by the company in its investment account. It was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the words "losses and smallness of profit" occurring in section 23A(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, must be confined to losses previously incurred by the assessee company and not to befool themselves in the wild hope that the value should come up again. HELD : The income tax Officer took an erroneous view of the scope of sec. 23A (I). [864 D] Commissioner of Income tax West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd. , referred to. It is impossible to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering these two matters only. Their Lordships are of the opinion that the Statute by the words used while making sure that "lossinges and largeness of profits" are never lost sight of require all matters relevant to the question of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established is one of them. [863 D G] Commissioner for Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., , distinguished. Commissioner of Incometax West Bengal, vs Gangadharjee & Co. , explained and applied.
