The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation, since then he was a degree holder. He got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. The promotion was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition and the High Court dismissed it. Allowing the Petition filed by the Petitioner, this Court HELD: 1.1 Though persons appointed directly and by promotion were integrated into a common class of Assistant Engineers, they could, for purposes of promotion to the cadre of Executive Engineers, be classified on the basis of their educational qualification. The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to be the exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution and must be upheld. [716C F] 1.2 Article 14 and Article 16 of or Article 16 have been separately made in the instant case. [ 767E G] State of H.C. Sharma & Ors., ; , relied on. Goru and Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Anr., ; ; followed. 2.1 The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [76H 767A] 1:2.1 In the absence, of rule, or regulations, the authority cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction. [77C] 3. The proposition in State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao; ; and The Union of India & Ors. vs Dr.(Mrs.) S.B. Kholi; , relied upon.

The petitioners filed applications under Article 32 of the Constitution for a direction to the Union of India and to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts of the country. It was contended by the Union that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. Relying on this decision of this Court in the case S.P. Gupta vs Union of lndia, [1982] 2 SCR 365, it was contended for the petitioners that (1) The petition ought to be disposed of expeditiously with expedition and steps should be taken for determining the sanctioned strength in the subordinate Courts and (2) Any further directions as deemed fit were necessary. Disposing of the petitions and the writ petition, HELD: 1. The primacy of the Chief Justice of India in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. [462E] 2.1. In cases where there is difference of opinion amongst the constitutional functionaries in regard to appointment of a Judge in a High Court, the opinion of none of these constitutional functionaries is entitled primacy but after considering the opinion oth er each of the constitutional functionary and giving it due weight, the Central Government is entitled to come to its own decision as to which opinion it should accept in deciding whether or not to appoint the particular person as a Judge. [463C] 2:2. Further, the view which the four Judges shared, in Gup ta 's case, that the fixation of pay of Judge strength is not justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. [465D] S.S. Gupta v Union of india, ; ; ; S.L. Jain vs Union Territory of Chandigarh and Anr., ; , followed. The matter is not to be considered whether the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. There are preponderant and com pelling considerations why the views of the chief Justices of the States and that of the Government should be afforded a decisive import unless the executive has some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment was otherwise undesirable. [447E] 3:3. The binding decision of the Supreme court in S.B. Gupta 's Case relating to the status and importance of the project or institution of the Judicial Commis sioners is not a decisive test but merely a limited one. That is to be done by a judicial recognition of the standard with a concomitant legal and constitutional obligation for the executive to adopt and apply the standard. [467G] 4:4. The Constitution envisages a method of consultation with the Chief Secretary, the Governor of the State, the Chief Judge of the High Court before the Presi dent of India makes the appointment. On one occasion to meet the stalemate it was pointed out that there had in the meantime been a change in the personnel of the Union Government or the Chief Minister of the Central Reven tional Council and the Supreme Courts.

The respondent C. Bernard while serving as a Relieving Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by him by the Bank on May 15, 1978. The said bill was passed by the bank on May, 16, 1978, but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/s. Shri Manju Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a letter dated August 1,1978 by the Divisional Office calling for his expla nation. The respondent was thereafter served with the charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. However during the pendency of the departmental enquiry he retired from service on January 31, 1979. Not withstanding his retirement he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded the enquiry against the re spondent by the end of 1979. He then gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and thereafter passed the impugned order of discharge on January 14, 1980. The appellant assailed this order before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution which was rejected by a Single Judge of the High COurt. A Division Bench of the said High Court dismissed the writ petition filed against the order of dismissal in the High court. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was urged that since the initial appointment of Shri U.B. Menon was valid, his actions and decisions could not be invalidated by his subsequent retirement; furthermore there was no prejudice caused on him on that account and therefore he could have appointed a non official as an enquiry Officer and therefore his decision could be saved on the de facto doctrine. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he enquire into the conduct of an employee nor did it not cure the defect as to his compensa tion. Where pun ishment is imposed by a person who has no authority do so the very foundation on which the edifice is built collapses and with it fails the entire edifice. It is a case more or less akin to a case tried by a court lacking in inherent jurisdiction. [204G H] 1.2 The impugned order was bad in law. [205E] 2.1 Even if it be assumed that an Enquiry Commis sion Officer need not be an officer of the Bank, even a third party can be appointed as an Inquiry Officer to enquire into tho conduct of An employee. It was for this reason that the appellant had made the claim on the basis of fake receipt; whether he himself was duped or not would be a different matter.

The respondents are owners of the premises and that the construction was old and required urgent and extensive repairs on October 16, 1965. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondents that their application for execution of work in respect of house Nos. 3766 to 3776 had been refused on the grounds : (1) that the proposal was under acquisition and was also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial; (2) that they did not conform to bye laws or the provisions of section 336(2) or any other law in respect thereof for which the plan had been submitted by the respondents did not comply with the Master Plan, and (3) that under the Master Master Plan prepared under the Delhi Development Act, 1957 certain areas includingceded Chawri Bazar would be the Central Business District. The respondents contested the application contending that the permission proposed construction was in contravention of section 339(2)(a) of the Corporation Act inasmuch as there was no such contravention established by them and if that were so the Commissioner had no power to refuse to accord sanction asked for by the Respondents. The High Court dismissed the petition holding, inter alia, (1 ) that though a Zonal Development Plan for each Zone in which two areas have to be divided will have also to be prepared and has not come into operation for the zone concerned, nevertheless till such a Zonal development plan comes into operation, the Master plan will hold the field. The appellant filed an appeal by special leave against the decision of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a). Under section 33(2), where any particular and definite use of land is indicated in a Master Plan simultaneously with the preparation of the Master plans, or as soon as may be then thereafter, no Zonal Development plan for the Zone concerned has been prepared, it cannot be said that when the respondents are attempting to renovate the building they are using the land in the zone otherwise than in conformity with themaster Plan. [168 H] (b) The Master Plan also contains provisions regarding the allotment or reservation of land for roads. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Development Plans, then section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of a land or building otherwise than as in conformitywith the Zonal development Plan will be hit by that section. [170 C] (c) Under section 38(2). no person shall use or permit to be used on such terms and conditions as may he prescribed by regulations made in this behalf any land or a building for the purpose and to the extent for and which it is being used upon the date on which such plan comes within operation. Section 15 provides that the Authority shall sanction the erection of a building or work unless such building or works would contravene any of the provisions. Under section 40, the Commissioner may refuse to grant sanction where not more than three months have elapsed from the date of the notice. [171 D] (d) The grounds on which the sanction of a construction was sought for were that the Master Planning Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi, which has statutory force, had come into effect under the Development Act. Under sub section (2), the owner of any land and building within his own zone has given notice to the Commissioner and also to the Central Government making modifications in the Master Plans or as early as possible. [174 E] The Master plan prepared by a Zonal Planning Authority for each zone is mandatory under section 8(1) to be followed. As a result of this, section 14 would become applicable. [175 G] (e) Section 15 of the Development Corporation Act was a self contained code and was not intended for acquisition of any property other than in accordance with the sanctioned Master Plan. The words "all development" in section 342(2 ) are wide enough to include all development on the land covered by it. Therefore, irrespective of the necessary consequence should be given to it.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and a Minister of industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No, 2 as the Minister in Chamber of Industry and Industries on his being informed by the appellant that he would meet him at the Constitution House and told him that the appellant had asked the matter to be put up by him before a "Special Judge" for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, the Judicial Commissioner reversed this order and convicted both the appellants of the various offences with which they were charged. On an application made before the Judicial Com missioner for leave, the Court held that the statements made to them were not recorded on the night of the 11th April, 1949. Held also that the statement made by the accused No. I was admissible in evidence as there was no doubt that the appellants were asked by this witness to give the bribe money from his home and handed it over to the appellant for being paid to the complainant. The statements made by this accused were inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. There was also an important circumstance for the purpose of establishing the falsity of the allegation made by him that he had brought these moneys from his house which they had been given to him by way of balance and the most natural reaction to the recovery of this large sum of money would have been that he should have definitely denied that these moneys were his and he would have assured for payment of money or illegal gratification to the appellants.

% The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the defendant was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh as a result whereof he physically injured and detained another Gurdial Singh. Another chargesheet was filed against the respondent on 6.11.1982. After the trial, the accused were acquitted by the trial court. The plaintiff appealed against the said decision before the appellate court which was dismissed. In appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directed that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the ground that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. Secondly, it had been asserted on oath before the trial Court and not denied by the respondent that the aforesaid Kahan singh had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order of his dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and that later he was again dismissed. Secondly it was further contended on their behalf that another convicted consta ble Surinder Singh was given the benefit of probation by the criminal court and his case, therefore, is distinguishable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case was an old one. [826G] 2. The suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Court in the manner it has been done. The provisions of law would not be ignored merely on the grounds that in case of a another member the police may have been later punished, is recognised. The power to award a minor punishment of crossing one month must be exercised with great care and caution and should be exercised liberally. [825D] In the instant case, the High court was wrong in dismissing the second appeal in limine.

The appellant was a private limited company. The assessee entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958, the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of B Twill and 2500 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B T Will was with two parties M/s. Raghunath & Sons (P) Ltd. for 500 bales and M/S Mahadeo Ramkumar for 600 bales. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative but the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court; Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh ; , referred to. In reaching this conclusion, the High Court upheld the view taken by the Tribunal. This appeal is by way of special leave granted by this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) In the instant case the question was whether on the facts there were two separate transactions of sale so that tax was payable at both the points under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. [186E] A transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) but only to brand them as speculative transactions so as to put them in a special category for income tax purposes. The Explanation does not invalidate speculative according to explanation 2 if there was no actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips. [187H] (2) In enacting the explanation 2 of Section 24(i) of the Income Tax Act 1961, the legislature did not intend to affect any transaction of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there is no actual or physical delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative proceeding which could be allowed to be set off only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature.

The respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed a petition before the Election Tribunal challenging the rejection of the nomination papers on the ground that the nomination paper which he had put in four papers, amounted to a technical defect and that the inclusion of the later two first and seconders behind the attestation were invalid. Held, that a perusal of sections 33(1) (d), 36(2)(d) of the Representation of the People Act showed that after the attestation it cannot be held that the attestation in the prescribed manner was required in the case of proposers and second petitioners who were not able to write their names, that there were no valid signatures of either a proposer or a seconder in any one of the four nomination papers. The word "subscribe" is not defined but it is equally clear as when the Act is read as " a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that "subs delegating" means to sign something in accordance with prescribed regulations where any such exist But though this is the strict primary meaning of the word, it may sometimes be, e.g., in the attestation of a will or a mortgage and is on the same footing as the II subscribing ' required " in the ease of illiterate persons unable to write his name but it cannot mean " sign " plus something else, namely a particular assent, the element of signing " has to be present; the nomination of the second petitioners was rightly rejected by an election Tribunal in view of section 33(2) (a) of Act as the Returning officer was bound to reject them under section 36(1)(d).

The appellants had in their writ petition contended before the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication of a dispute relating to re instatement of three of the union leaders who had been dismissed by the Company. The Tribunal rejected the plea and held that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls on the presumption that they had abandoned service would constitute a change in the conditions of service applicable to them immediately before the commencement of the said proceedings which prejudeted them, and therefore, the impugned action was illegal and invalid. In appeal by special leave against the award, it was contended: (i) The action of removing the appellants name from its roll did not constitute abandonment of service because of their going on strike in enforcement of their demands; and (ii) the purported action of removal of the names from its Rolls was illegal, and arbitrary. 3. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD : (1) It is well settled that before a workman has abandoned or relinquished service he is always a question of intention, and normally such an intention cannot be attributed to an employee without adequate evi 618 dence in that behalf. [616C] Express Newspapers (P) Limited vs Michael Mark & Anr., [1959] Suppl. 2 SCR p. 421, applied. The requirement of giving up all concern in something ' is always well established and indeed the intention may be inferred from the acts and conduct of the party, and is a question which of fact has to be determined in the light of the surrounding circumstances of each case. [625E] (2) Under common law an inference that an employee has abandoned service or relinquished services is not easily drawn unless from the length of absence and from other surrounding circumstances an inference to that effect can be legitimately drawn and it can be assumed that the employee intended to abandon service. Abandonment or relinquishment of service is always in a question in fact which has to he determined in a light of surrounding circumstances. [524G H] Express Newspaper (P.) Limited vs Ejas, followed. (3) The word 'abandonment of Service ' has been explained as meaning 'to leave wholly and finally; for sake utterly, inductively it must be total and under such circumstances as clearly to indicate an absolute relinquishment.

The respondents were trustees of a public trust. The Trust bad agreed to give to the trustees six months ' purchase money for payment to the appellant and Rs 6 for payment of the mortgage amount, by monthly instalments of Rs 100 each. An action instituted by the mortgagee against the trustees was compromised which was compromised and it was decreed that the trustees did pay Rs. 3,910 due under the mortgage by monthly instalment of Rs. 100 each and in default of three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mort gage property. The trustees applied under 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale and deposited the sum (in default) by monthly installments of Rs . 100 each, and in an application for execution by the mortgage, the mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs. 5,000/ . The appellants therefore applied under O. 21 rule 89 for setting set aside the auction and deposited Rs. 250 being 5 % of the purchase money, and the balance, in default, of three instalment the entire outstanding amount payable shall become payable and recoverable as from the mortgagee property. Before the District Court the trustees contended that (1) the jurisdiction of the Bombay High Court which originally extended over the territory now forming part of the State was ceased when a new High Court was set up in the State of Gujarat, but it was held by this Court in Pijare Karimbhai vs Hariprasad ; , that : (a) the decision of the Calcutta High Court would be regarded as binding since the Bombay City Civil Court had inherited the jurisdiction; and (b) the power and authority in respect of the territory of Gujarat was not barred by section 36, by virtue of section 35 B. HELD: The order passed by the District court restored. [459 B C] (1)(a) When a Judge enters upon his office takes an oath of office that he will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established and that he would duly and faithfully and to the best of his ability, knowledge and judgment perform the duties of office without fear or favour, affection or illwill and that if he finds that the earlier decisions of the High Court. whether of a Division Bench or of a single Judge need to be re considered, he should not embark upon the enquiry sitting as a single judge but should refer the matter 'to a Division bench for hearing and dispose of the case or the questions raised in the case. [446 E F] (b)(c) The High Court acted illegally and with material irregularity in not deciding the question. [463 C D] (2) The judgment of this Court is binding upon the parties to the litigation. It has no existence in law. But it cannot be sustained.

Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950 empowers the appropriate authority to retire a Government servant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service provided that he shall give notice of not less than 3 months before the date on which he wishes to retire. The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He retired from serv ice under Rule 2(1)(b) of Pension Rules on April 21, 1970. He filed writ petition in the High Court contending that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2). The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there Was no in Firmity inRule 2 (ii) of pension Rules. The Union of India appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the Division Bench of the High court Central Government servants retiring at the age of 58 years on three months ' notice. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The object of Rule 2 of Pension rules may also be to heed out unsuitable employees. [800C D] 2. Rule 2046 has no parity with Rule 2 which is a statutory rule and is identical to Fundamental Rule 56(j). A Division Bench came to the conclusion that Rule 2044 having been framed under Article 309 of the Constitu tion and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only govered by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. [O801E F] 3. The Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 cannot and did not add anything to Rule 2.(2) in pension Rules which is the statutory rule. [ 800C D; 800A] 4. Para 620 of the Manual being executive instructions it cannot be modified or amended by executive orders. A valid rule having some lacuna or gap can be supplemented by the execu tive instructions but a statutory Rule which is inconsistent with it cannot therefore be validated with the support of executive instructions.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. It had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechu from October, 1940 to September 1941, and the sales in this case were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 31st March, 1946. The Sale of kats was by M/s Biharilal Balkishan at their shops in Kanpur. The assessee firm did not maintain any books account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/S Employees Malkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". In the course of its assessment, the Income Tax Officer computed the sales of Katech ure under consideration, but on appeal he found that the constitution of the firm during the chargeable accounting period was the same as in 1940 41 and the ac count ments were maintained in their accounts. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this view. In appeal, the assessee contended that there could be no profit or loss during the relevant chargeable accounting periods, although there was no sales effected yet profits accrued to the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. From the definition of "accounting period", it has to be borne in mind, is the twelve months ' proceeding just on the basis of the income tax year and the assessment must be made on the same basis. The chargeable accounting period is the period beginning from 1st September, 1939 ending after amendment on 31st December, 1946, and ending on 31th March, 1944. So if there was any deficiency of profits in any particular period, it must be determined on that basis and after set off carried forward to be set off during the provi sions period. [614 A C] 2. In order to work out the scheme of the Act, there must be proper devetailing of the concept of " accounting period" and after that the deficiency in profits for that year should be computed on that count and after setting off carried tained forward tobe set off for the chargeable provi dure period. It is thus an harmonious construction of 615 the different provisions of the Income tax Act bearing in mind that excess profits are excess of profits which were intended to be mopped up during the war period intended to being taxed separately and differly. [613F G] 3. The concept of 'accounting Period" in the context of the chargeable business period can thus be harmo nised. The law is that the activity that the assessee carried on at Raichur was part of their business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the . [615B C] 4. Where a loss has been made in any charge able accounting period, the amount of loss added to the amount Of the standard profits, does not fall in one chargeable accounting Period and falls in another part of the accounting period i.e.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the aforesaid Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after, a common rank list was prepared by the Kerala Public Services Commission as per the directions given by the learned Single Judge and that these candidates had already been appointed. However some aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petitions filed appeals before the Division Bench of the High Court which allowed the writ petitions and directed the Government to prepare "two lists, namely one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the service Commission has not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines that the petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by Public Service Commis sioner. Accordingly, the petitioner would be entitled 10 to a post, if he has exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the Common List for claiming the post". The writ petitions were dismissed in view of the fact that the K &PSC had advised 239 candidates according to the separate lists for Civil and Mechanical Engineering prepared on the ground that they had qualified in Civil engineering questions. This court answered the question in favour of the petitioners. In these special leave petitions, it was contended by the respondents that preparation of no common list was directed either by the Single Judge or by the Division bench of the K PSC to prepare two separate rank lists one for Civil Engineering graduates and the others for Mechanical Engineering graduate on the view that they would be chosen in terms thereof. Thereafter, the Kerala Government appointed another candidate and appointed another person and appointed a person and also selected him but later. It had been contended that the expression "the common list" prepared by it should be deleted. Allowing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.

In a suit for accounts, the plaintiff respondent No. 1 claimed that he was a partner of a partnership firm and had been converted into a partnership Firm by regular deed, and later converted into another partnership firm, with a regular deed. During his life time the business was under the control of Abdul Samad, but on his death, the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 have effectively taken charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff. The Income Tax Officer passed an order on 26th December 1981 on the basis of the false alleg made by the defendant respondent in para 13 of the plaint that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. The defendant No. 2 challenged the valuation given by him as grossly undervalued and arbitrary, and approached this Court for relief. Upon these questions being raised, this Court had to consider the matter on merits. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the plaintiff has laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department mentioned in para 11 of the Plaint, and it is, therefore preposterous on his part to suggest in paragraph 19 of the suit that it can be tentativeyly valued @ Rs.49 only only. According to him the defence that the suit was governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act and not by section Russell Exchange, this relief could be reasonably valued at a money only. Allowing the appeal, this court, HELD: 1.1 The interpretation put by the appellant on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by the learned counsel help him. It is true that in a suit, for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334; and Shama Pershad Shahi vs Sheopershad Singh XLI, I.C. 95 (Patna), it is not a uniform. The argument that the defendant can give an arbitrary valuation in the plaint, and that the court is bound to accept that" made on behalf thereof before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849 was rejected, after observing that there was some authority for the extreme view as urged in two Calcutta decisions but later a different view was taken by the said Court at page 69: [ 512D E] It is not uniform. [510F G] Smt Tara Devi vs Sri Thakur Radha Krishna Maharaj, and Meenakshesundaram Iyer Chettiar vs Sri Radha Krishna Prasad, , referred to. In the instant case, the defendant 's objection to the valuation was rejected by the trial court "on the ground that the Court was powerless to challenge the valuation put by him on the relief claimed in the suit. " The Full Bench decision of this court governed the case. [511D] Smt. Tara Devi and vs Sri Hari Radha Krishna Swamiar, I .L.R. 6 Patnaamma, approved. Smt Tara Chand vs Shri Thakur Radha Krishan Maharaj, A.I.R , approved. It would be open to the trial Court to take into consideration the statement in the Plaint that the appellant has been ousted from the partnership business. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the plaintiff would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The respondent assessee is a registered establishment carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling drugs for foreign ness. As regards this, it manufactures customers for sale of goods as well as for other sources, by virtue of their registration certificate. Under the licence, the assessee was entitled to exemption from sales tax in respect of sales tax for certain periods. The respondent asses see claimed that these were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption and that a conce cial exemption should be granted to them under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them certificate for three years. The assessee 's claim was accepted by the Govern ment and the Director, Industries, State Government issued an order dated 12.1.1983. In view of this, the Sales Tax Officer, Gwalior held that these rules and instructions were no relevance to the claim put forward under the exemption notification. However, subsequently a Full Bench of the High Court dismissed both the appeals. On appeal by the State, it was contended on behalf of the asses see that the benefit of exemption was not intended to be wider than that of the con tending industrial units granted earlier, but subsequently revoked and reversed the decision of the Single Judge dismissing the writ petitions filed by certain other assesses. It was further contended that, in view of the fact that the tax free under the 1981 1981 notification was only in the nature of an alterna tive to the provision for exemption, and the former was not available to traditional industries because of rule 14 above, the same should be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The question of grant of eligibility certificate by the Industries Department is not an empty formality but before granting a certificate, the Industries De partment has to see whether all the requirements as con tained in the instructions are fulfilled and complied with or not.

The Delhi Higher Judicial Service was the highest grade of a District and Sessions Judge. The High Court by its judgment dated January 16, 1981 dismissed the writ petition filed by the promotees. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (i) Rule 8(1) of the Delhi Higher judicial Service Rules is ultra vires the Constitution inasmuch as it is permissible to create temporary posts in the service and, even substantive vacancies in the Service can be filled by making permanent appointments; and (ii) Articles 14, 16, 17 and 311 of the Constitution are unconstitutional. On behalf of Respondents: the appellants contended that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District & Sessions Judges as well as seniority basis so much so that persons found not fit for promotion were ignored as in the case of Shri C.D. But, the provisions of Rule 16 and 17 are also relevant to the present purpose and have, indeed, an important bearing on the question of reservation of vacancies for direct recruits to the extent of one third of the substantive posts in Service. In addition, on behalf, it has been submitted that under Rule 16, promotees were appointed to temporary posts as Additional learned District & Session Judges after the promotees are so appointed and the seniority over promotees would continue to apply notwithstanding the fact that appointments are made to the service under Rules 16 and17; (iii) Under these circumstances, there is no discrimination in fixing the inter se seniority of members of the Punjab Judicial Service promoted to the Delhi High Court. hut it was urged on behalf the appellants (i ) The main question for determination in the instant case is whether the seniority between direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined by the dates on which direct recruits were appointed and (2) Whether there is any quota rule specially in view of the fact, that working of the said rules over all these years indicate that the rule was not adhered to. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1(a) It would appear from the provisions contained in Rule 8 (1) which governs inter se Seniority of members because it is impermissible to create permanent posts in its service and even substantive vacancy in the 'service can be made within the framework of the Rules and have to be made, if at all, from amongst the promotees and promotees only the quota rule contained in the proviso to Rule 7 must inevitably break down when such appointments are effected.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in three years of assessment. but appeals by Debi Parshad, who was a stranger in respect of his income for the year 1951 52 were rejected. In appeals to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of assessment of the assessee on two grounds (i) that he was a member of an association of persons and, therefore, could not be assessed personally in respect thereof; and (ii) that the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order,.of assess ment made by the Income tax officer. In appeal to the District Court, the decree was reversed by the High Court under section 34(3) of the Act on the view that the income belonged to Debi Parath and he was liable to be assessed at his own request in respect with the income. The question for determination in these appeals is whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the appeals were maintainable before a Single Judge. HELD: (i)(a) A combined reading of section 30(1) and section 31(3), shows that the cases where persons other than the appealing assessee might be affected by orders passed by the Appellate Commissioner. Modification or setting aside 'of assessment made on a firm, joint Hindu family, association of person for a particular year may affect the assessment for the said year on a partner or partners of the firm, member or members of the Hindu Undivided Family (1) ; 394 or the individual, as the case may be. [392 D F] Commissioner of Income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed. (b) The expression 'any person ' in section 34 sub section (3) proviso 2 at p. 346) means that he must be one who would be liable to have been assessed for the whole or part of the income let went into the assessment of that year under appeal or revision. If so construed, it is necessary to pursue the matter further.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by the respondent. As the respondent was unable to pay Court fees under section 7(iv)(b) Of the Madras Madras High Court Fees Act, 1951, on the valuation of Rs. 15,00,000 he claimed to have made a claim for partition and accounts at Rs. 1,000, as provided by section 7 (v) Of ' the Act and was not prepared to pay court fees accordingly, but the suit was decreed in terms of the trial court fee payable under the Act on the plaint filed by the appellant in the High Court. The appellant therefore appealed to this Court. On behalf of the respondent it was contended that if all the material allegations contained in the plaint are fairly construed and taken as a whole it would appear that the plaintiff has been ousted from the enjoyment of the properties in suit and his claim for parti tion in substance is a claim based on title within the meaning of section 7 of the Act. Held, that since the decision of this Court in Krishnaswamy Naidu J cannot attract the finality mentioned in section 5 of the Madras High 's Act, the jurisdiction of the court either to try the suit or to entertain the appeal must be held to be final under section 5 Of the Act though it does not necessarily follow that a right should be given to the plaintiff to amend his plaint and set out specifically the amount at which he values the relief sought for. As a result of this, the decree passed by the High court was in error in holding that the case fell within section 7, sub section (iv)(c) of the ' Act.

% The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) invited objections to the Revised Plans for the construction of "Statesman House" proposed by Statesman Ltd., did not, in fact, prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws. However, the NDMC raised a dispute that the plans for the multi storeyed high rise building were 'external wall ' and as such were liable to be revised under Bye law 16.4.8 and 16.1. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plan on or before 5th May, 1989. The NDMC assailed the decision of the High Court on grounds principally that the sanctioned plan for the constructions of " Englandman House ' did not provide for a "podium/pedestrian walk way" made mandatory by the Zonal Development Plan for Zone D 1 (viz., Connaught Place Area) approved by the Central Government, and that, thereafter, there was no impediment to the sanction. During the course of the hearing, the Standing Counsel for the NDMC sought a clarification from the NDMC 's order dated 18th February, 1987, pointing out that: "However, to our surprise on the final date of arguments, that is, on 31.3.1982; 31.7.1985 and 29.8.85, there would appear prohibition on high rise structures. In the course that the order dated 28.4 1989 finally dis posing of the writ peti tion, the High court after referring to what is considered to be a co operative attitude of the DUAC and other authorities, however, had this to say of the NDMC: " However, to this we surprise on 31st March, 1986, that was on 31 3.3,. ' The High Courts were persuaded to the view that NDMC ' s disinclination to accord sanction to the plan was unjusti fied; that whatever reservations it had had as to the ade quacy of the fire safety measures, as envisaged in the Building designs, were allayed by the Chief Fire Officer 's clearance and held that thereafter there was a no impediment for the sanction; that what reservations the NDMC had as envisaged was not otherwise disputed. 6.2.4 The eligibility of the proposed construction for sanction except on the point of adequacy of "Refuge areas" in the requirement of a "pedest 89 walk way ', and "Podium" is not otherwise dispute. There fore, the Union Territory had raised the question of applicability of Bye law 17.1 as well as its failure to do so would detract from its validity. The respondent NDMC contended that in any event, whatever reservations were cally banned by the Town Improvement Trust Act, 1911, in relation to the Union territory of Delhi and that the proposed build ing did not also provide for "a 'podiya/pedent walk way". 6.5.1 The application for sanction from the Rent Controller was made before the NDMC, which came up for hearing on 22nd March, 1987 and it was observed: "The proposal for sanction of building plans was required to be submitted by 15.4,.90 to 31st August, 1985 and it would not progress beyond a height of 15 metres. The requisite permission from the Urban Land lord to commence the construction work according to the respective bye laws was granted. It was also condi tions that the said buildings are located on external walls "by cantilever projection or in any other manner", abutting a vacant space from which rescue operations are rendered possible.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for partition against the appellant of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The suit was decreed in terms of the compromise on July 25, 1947. The dispute between the parties was whether the Plaintiff was barred by res judicata or by order II, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed a fresh suit for each of the joint family property including the account of all business carried on by them separately to themselves. The plea of res judicata was not accepted by the trial Court but was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the compromise between the plaintiff and the parties did not expressly negative the right for accounts of the motor transport business; (2) the suit was barred under Order II, r. 2, of the C.P.C.; (3) the cause of action in the subsequent suit was different from the cause because of the decision of the previous Suit No 39 of 1945 which he deliberately relinquished. Held that a consent decree is as binding upon the parties thereto as a decree passed by invitum. The compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, misunderstanding or mistake, the decree passed thereon has the binding force of resjudicata. Order II rule 2(3) clearly lays down that if a person Omits, except with the leave of the court, to sue for all reliefs to which he is entitled, he shall not afterwards sue for any relief so omitted.

The appellant was the owner of certain salt works. After the coming into force of the Bombay Salt Works Act, 1948, the entire area of the Salt Works was open, and on the sea side the market area had filled in so as to prevent sea water flooding the salt pans. The cage for determining whether what is done at this Salt Works in connection with the conversion of sea water into salt came within the definition of the word " factory " under Cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act, HELD : Dismissing the appeal, (per Gajendragadkar, Sarkar and Mudholkar, JJ.) 1. The High Court was right in holding that the process of converting sea water from salt carried on the appellant 's Salt Works comes within the expression " premises " in the definition Of the word ' factory " and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within that definition of manufacturing process. [599A C] 2. The appellant having been rightly convicted by the High Court, there is no force in his contention that the salt works as such do not come within the term " 'factory " in cl. (k) of s.2. [602B D] Kent vs Astley, , explained. 3. The process of conversion of the sea water to salt carried out on the appel lant 's Bengal Salt Works and described above. comes within section 2(k)of the Act. [600D F] 4. Under the Bombay Act there is nothing in the Act which makes it uniformly compulsory for every occupier of a factory to comply with any requirement of the , Act, which apply to the factory he is working and that therefore the Salt works would come within within the wide terms prescribed by section LXXIII of the Factories Act. Since the various factories and the Mills which were covered by the Factory Act of 1833 were such which could function only in buildings, they came within its definition. [ 634B F] 5. The word " premises" includes precincts. it has been urged clearly indicated that the word premises ' is not confined to buildings alone but is a term which enlarges the scope of the words " premises". It does not enter the Salt work as defined in cl (k). [601C D] 6. 'The appellant engaged on these salt works are dealing with the sea Water in a particular manner and so on these works would fall within the scope Of section 2 (k), of the Central Act. The fact that the meal which was ground was not intended for the purpose of sale but was meant only for feeding the stock from the farm, is sufficient to show that salt works were carried out in the Salt Estate and described below. [625E G] 7.

The respondent entered the service of a Princely State in 1935 as Instructor in tailoring and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. One Shri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty who was also an Instructors in tail rolling Department filed a writ petition in the High Court claiming that in any case, he could not be discriminated against and treated differently from K. N. Chetty who is junior to him in the parent department as emolumentsery Instructors were to take effect on that date irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit Officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him, K.N. Chetty, who was junior to the respondent, and was identically situated, was accorded the same treatment. " On April 21, 1965, the respondent was again posted on deputation as Instructor ( oh provisional basis) in tailoresoring and recommended for their absorption with effect from November 28, 1949 which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. His specific grievance was that he could be absorbed as Tail Appointment Instructor from the date of his appointment as such as had been ordered in the case of Sri K. V. Rajalakshmiah Setty vs State of Mysore ; , followed in the matter of absorption and appointment, while his junior K. Gopalaswamy Chetty, whose case was identical in all respects, and six other officers who were similarly situated, were absorbed on that deputation. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the Department of Technical Education with effect From November 28 by which he had become Assistant Engineers from the dates of occurrence of vacancies, according to seniority. In 1953, the State Government passed orders reverting him to his parent department and ordered absorption of the Respondent in the department of Technical education in the grade of Rs. 150 with retrospective effect from the said date, in the vacancy in which he worked, subject to these conditions. (a) that he would not be entitled to the benefit of revision of scales of pay that had been effected in 1957 & 1961 by way of increments or weightage, and (b) that the State Govt. did not accept the representation. On April 23, 1965 the respondent filed a Writ Petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the Andhra Pradesh High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State to fix his seniority, also on the basis that he had already become Assistant Engineer from the earlier date of joining duty on deputation, and give him the benefits of revisions of pay. The petition was opposed by the appellant relying on the decision in K.V. Rajavalaksh acquisitions. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no principle of policy or service rule on the ground of which they could ' claim such promotions as of right. ' [259 A B] (2) The acceptance of the respondents ' contentions does not lead to any untoward results such as were apprehended in Rajalakshappa Chetty 's cases, and indeed it has not been shown that this was so called "reversion" which was not ordered owing to any fault of the petitioner.

An application for appointment of a foreigner as guardian of a child for a period exceeding one year in terms of the letter addressed by one Laxmi Kant Pandey, an Advocate practising in this Court complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents, alleging that not only Indian children of tender age under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. The Court issued notice to the Union of India on January 8, 1982 and considered the matter in accordance with the law and norms which should be followed in determining whether a child should be allowed to be adopted by foreign parents and if so, the procedure to be followed for that purpose, with the object of ensuring the welfare of the child. The net effect of this provision, if the Bill were enacted into law, would be that in view of clause 17 no institution or organisation can make any arrangement for the adoption of an Indian child by Foreign parents unless such institution or Organisation is licensed as a social welfare institution and under Clause 21 it would be unlawful to pay or give to any person any payment or reward for or in consideration of the grant by that person of any consent required in connection with the adoption .of a child or the transfer by that foreigner of the care and custody of such child with a view to its adoption or the making by that Person of any arrangements for such adoption. " The Union Government, instead of examining the home study report for some other purpose, by an order dated January 8. 1982, framed a scheme under which the national Council of Social Welfare would be to examine the home Study Report and submit it to the Court for its consideration. The Committee of the State has accepted this scheme and issued instructions on behalf of the Union Government in regard to adoption of Indian children by foreign Institutions making the application for guardianship, but no such direction is given. In doing so, this court directed that every application of a foreign parent for taking a child in adoption shall be routed through a recognised social or child welfare agency licensed by the Government of India or the Government or any other independent, reputed and publicly or legally recognised social agency should also undertake while forwarding the application to the social or Child Welfare Agency in India, that it will ensure adoption of the school and the children admitted therein. In view of this direction in a letter addressed to the National Commission forrievance (CWN) calling upon the Union Ministry of Social welfare and keeping in view the interests of the foreign parents who have taken a child, the Court may issue notice to Union of States, the Indian Council of Child Welfare and the Indian Councils of Social Education to appear in answer to the writ petition.

The appellant, a Commercial Tax officer in 1954, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954 and later as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on 7 S 1975. On promotion as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial Tax he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28,1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) (i). His service book showed that he had an excellent record of service. The several promotions gained by him were unknown in 1969 and 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax Officers it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner as follows: " This Commercial Tax office is a very intelligent and capable officer who kept the entire district under his control in perfect discipline." However, there was one dark spot. In 1969, when he felt that the charges for which he was promoted were not substantiated in the enquiry made by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption he accepted the report of the Director of Vigilance, Anti Corruption and Anti Evic tion. Charges were framed against him in respect of allegations substantiated, obtained his explanation and sent its report thereon. The Full Board of Revenue then reported that the charge to be dropped was nowhere noted in the personal file of the appellant. The Government, after considering the report, reduced the charges to writing writing for further remarks . Thereafter he filed a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the finding of the Full Board and the order of November 29, 1974 of the Government were to be reviewed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The post of a Deputy Commissioner is a Selection post. Under Rule 36(b) (1) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for Commercial Taxes Service: "All promotions shall be made on grounds of merit and ability" seniority being considered only when merit and suitability are approximately equal. So, what do we have ? There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of appellant in 1969. The basis of the entry 79 was knocked out by the order dated November 29 1974 of A Government, and the effect of the entries was blotted out by promotion of the appellant as Deputy Collector. After his promotion as Dy Commissioner there was no entry in his service Book to his discredit or hinting even remotely that he bad outlived his utility as a Govt servant. servant. The only question of eligibility involved is whether the failure to note the result of the enquiry in the ville order of the Govern ment retiring the appellant from service. [80G H] 1.2 In the face of the promotion of just a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order that of the Govt retiring the Appellant from serv ice. The learned Counsel for the State argued that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the employee including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 [80A] 1 .3 In the instant case the appellant was promoted for a period of nearly 20 years after his promo tion in September 1965.

The appellants were the operators who were permitted to be taken over by the said route as stage carriages on their coming into force. The appellants challenged the validity of certain scheme which had been published in the newspapers as well as approved schemes published under section 68 C of the , on the ground that they violated article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petitions on the view (1) that the Regional Transport Authority as well the approved schemes were fully in conformity with the requirements of section 68C and therefore, it was malicious to allege that the decision by the Corporation to frame the schemes was vitiated by mala fides of the Chief Minister; (2) that it was not in fact the Corporation which formed the opinion indicated in section 68 D(1); (3) that section 68 F(1) was repugnant to section 68 which provides for the delegation of legislative powers to the State Transport Authority, where the power is specified by sub section (7), but there is some other authority which functions as the Regional 's authori ty for the purposes of the article, such an authority may be that which would be comprehended by section 68F(1). HELD: The High court had rightly held that the schemes were vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 69 C and the Rules made thereunder. [353 E] (2)(a) Merely because the Regional Regional Transport authority of that area cannot grant permits under Ch. IV of the Act, he does not cease to be a licencee or a person who has been allotted a permit by the State Government as required by section 66 of the it. The provisions of Chapter IV A of the Road Transport Corporation Act, 1950, do not confer on the Regional Authority the power to issue a permit. The power to grant permits is not reserved to the Provincial Government but only to the Central Government. Section 68 F, which deals with delegation of powers by legislature in a State, does not confer any unlimited or uncontrolled powers upon the Provincial Legislature under Ch.(7) of the said Act and also to provide for delegation of such power. [355 H; 356 A C] (b). The Regional Transport Commit tee is empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking " notwithstanding anything in Chapter IV" and that the section rendered the provisions Of Rule 141 of the Motor Vehicles Rules inapplicable to cases covered by section 69 F(i). In a State where there is no Regional Transport Tribunal at all [vide e.g. proviso to section 44(1), but, there is out whether any authority which function as the regional Transport Authority for the purpose of the Art can relate to a matter which under section 58 C, it is left to the unfettered discretion and judg ment of the Corporation where that is the State Govern ment.[353 B D] (c) The scheme framed by the Regional Road Transport Authority was not a rigid or hard and fast rule, but the order passed by it did not indicate any definite intention of the Government. [354 E F] State vs Bengal Immunity Company Ltd., ; , relied on.

The appellant is a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954 in the return for the year the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,999 28 10 0 and deposited the tax of Rs. 9 6 on the said amount in the treasury. The Commercial Tax Officer by notice fixed August 4, 1955, for hearing the assessee in respect of its return. Under section 5(2)(a) (ii), the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish a declaration form duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry the Commercial Tax officer adjourned the matter on the ground that the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The assessee then flied an application to the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, West Bengal, for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order lo prove that they had issued the declaration forms to them and filed an application before the Commissioner for revision against the order. The Commissioner dismissed the application on the view that it was not able to comply with section 5 (2)(1)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, [730 E F] The provisions of r. 27A are also not helpful to the appellant. Under these rules the assessing authority is required to take evidence on oath etc. Thereafter the condition prescribed is strictly construed and in any case if so construed, a dealer is not precluded in a case where the proviso cannot be strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purposes mentioned in the section. The application is dismissed by the Commissioner on appeal. In appeal by certificate under article 133(1)(i) of tile Constitution the appellant contended: (a) the condition under which exemption can be granted was not mandatory but only directory and, therefore, it would lead to the position that if the declaration form is furnished, well and good; and (b) since in the instant case the clause in question became redundant and frustrated, HELD : (1) The object of section 5 is self evident. while they are obviously intended to give exemption to a dealer in respect Of sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks also to prevent fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax. In the nature of things, in view of several transactions that may be entered into between dealers. the same share of which the provisions of the said clause seek to avoid. [634 G H] (2) The expression "on demand" in r.27A is not ' obligate but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned. It can be invoked only in a Case where the authorityconcerned is empowered to take additional evidence in respect thereof; but that does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim tax exemption. [ 631 B C] State of Orissa vs M.A. Tulloch and Co. Ltd., ; , followed. (3) The language used in section 5 must be interpreted as laying down a condition for giving the exemption, but only as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way. If so construed the dealer is precluded in this case where proviso cannot he strictly complied ws from producing any other relevant material to prove its eligibility to exemption. The. proviso and qualifies the substantive clause.

Allowing the writ petition, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The State of Bihar is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It is further the constitutional obligation of this court as the guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to enforce the fundamental right of the accused to speedy trial by issuing the necessary direc tions to the State which may include taking of positive action, such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery setting up new courts, building new court houses providing more staff and equipment to the courts. [537F G]. 1.2 In order to enable the Court to discharge this constitutional obligation, it is necessary that the Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. The Constitution is an additional weapon to protect the poor and the needy is an essential element of any 'reasonable, fair and just procedure guaranteed by Article 21. [540C D] Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, [1978] 3 SCR 621, referred to. 1.3 The constitutional obligation is of this Court as the trust of the Constitution as the justices who are to seek his liberation through the court process that he should have legal services available to him. free legal serv ice to the poor, and the affluent is an important element of reasonableness, fair, just and proper procedure for a person accused of an offence and it must be held implicit in the guarantee of Article 21.[541G H] Maneka Shastri vs Union Territory of Delhi, ; @ p. 550; Maneka Gandhi v Union of lndia, ; Maneka Gandhi (1978) 1 SCR 621; Maneka public services ' Union vs Union for India, ; at p. 730, referred: 1 : 1.4 The Constitution guarantees free legal service is an inalienable element of reasonable fair and 'reasonable procedure guaranteed to Article 21 and it is the constitutional imperative of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trials to the accused.[541A B] Manekaary Procedure Co. vs Union lndian, ; , Maneka Gandhi V. Union of I ndia, [19911] 2 SCR 621 at p : 92; Maneka Gopalan V. State of Jammu Kashmir and Ors., ; , referred to: 1: 1 The right to be heard would be in many cases of little avail if it did not comprehend the right to he heard by counsel. The right of one charged with crime to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trials in some countries but is in ours. [541D E] 2 :3 It is well settled that a procedure which does not make available legal services to an accused person who is too poor to afford a lawyer and who would, therefore, have to go through the trial without their legal assistance, cannot possibly be regarded as 'reasonable fair and reasonable ' just ' procedure. [543E] Maneka Nehru Gandhi vs State of Punjab, ; ; Maneka instrumentality of India vs Union Of lndicia, and Maneka Gandhi mean vs Union 11 S.C.R. 348; Maneka Mandal (1978), 3 SCR 489 at pg.

The dispute was whether the tenant was entitled to the protection contained in this clause, HELD: Section 34(2 A), which provides for a notice of ejectment, prescribes certain conditions subject to which the right to terminate the tenancy shall be exercised. It may be that section 34 (1) requires one year 's notice in order to exercise this right to terminating, but flubs. The restriction of sub section (2 A) on the right of the landlord to terminate ' the tenancy and does not survive after the expiry of the notice. Therefore the Amending Act did not affect any vested right of landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated. [575 A B] According to section 34, a notice issued before the Amending Distord 's intention to terminate a tenancy shall have to be taken into consideration in determining the right for the landlord in the matter of the termination of tenancy, for the Amending of Act put certain fetters on this right of termination. In the circumstances, the decision of the High Court is correct and sub section A would apply to all cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending act, the amendment required a notice Of one year. [574 B C] There is no force in this contention. [573 E] Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (I.L.R. LX Cal. 1037), Pandit Durlabhbhai F ulbhai vs J. Jhaveribhai Bhikubhai (I L.R., Bom.

The assessee company was running at a loss as a result of which in 1952, the assessee company decided to instal a plant for manufacture of worsted yarn from imported wool, by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952. The assessee Company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee Company to the extent of Rs 2,50000 each and the assessee agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to 9% commission on net sale proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into by the assessee with M/ s Murlidhar Chiranjit Lal The selling agents entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which the latter were appointed as the managing agents on specified conditions and the important terms of which was that the " agency" was to finance The assessee company agreed to a deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the appellant Company from their remuneration. There were two other conditions with which he agreed to share losses to the amount made by them, 1% commission to the selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by it in order to earn profits and would, therefore, fall within the ambit of section 10(2) (xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The question whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal rightly held that the sums in question were not legal deductions as contemplated under section 10 (2)(xv) was not decided by this Court in Dharamvir Dhir vs Commissioner of Income tax Bihar & Orissa, ; and the High Court relied on certain materials which were not found by the Tribunal in its order nor did it consider the same as a valid deduction under the provisions of the Act.

The assessee was the Managing Director of a private limited company called R. K. V. Motors & Timber (P) Ltd., and during that year it had become indebted to the Company in the sum of Rs. 3,757.04 np. His drawings increased and as on March 31, 1959 as the total amount due by him stood at Rs. 25107.22np. This figure was worked out on the basis that a sum of RS. 11,000 as a provision for tax and of Rs 6,900 as a pro priate provision for dividend had to be adjusted against the balance of Rs 18,950. The Income Tax Officer rejected this contention on the ground that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2(6A)(e) could not be construed as including current profits. He arrived at this figure by including the current profits of the company for the account year ending March 31. 1959. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed an appeal filed by the assessee. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the word "accuable profits" occurring in section 6(2A)(a) had to include current profits in the expression 'accumulated profits ' and that the only reference application, it was pointed out, before the Appellate Tribunal was the reference application filed by Commissioner of Income Tax. It therefore allowed the assessee 's second appeal and held that the expression "accumbumulated profit" occurring therein could not in any sense be construed to include future profits for the purpose of section 2 (6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In this Court, it appeared from the record that the High Court was alive to the possibility of a winning party being deprived of the right to raise questions of law which could properly arise as further questions because they would be intimately involved in a decision on the questions referred at the instance of the applicant, but it failed to classify such a case separately from the case where a non applicant seeking a reference of questions of Law raised by that party. Not being a party aggrieved by the result of the appeal, it is not open to that party to file a reference application. But on a reference being filed by another party the basis of his claim that a question of law sought by him should be referred.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan which was comprised in Mouza Nala forming part of permanently settled estate of Burdwan, and were Mal lands assessed to revenue. The question for determination in this appeal arose whether on the materials on record the Courts below were right in presuming a lost grant in favour of the defendants. Held, that the burden of proving a lost Grant on the facts of this case was not discharged by the High Court. The suit properties formed part of the Mal or assessed lands of the estate and if a grant had been made in favour thereof it must have been made by the Mahant.
