The appellant is an agriculturist. In a suit for specific performance of contract, the appellant contended that (a) the land which was the subject matter of contract was covered by the provisions of section 63 of the Tenancy Act; and (b) the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, Section 63 of Indian Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land, and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions in section 70(a), read with sections 85 and 85A of the Bombay Tenancy Act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The trial court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On a further appeal by the respondent defendant, the High Court agreed with the trial Court observing that when an issue arises whether the plaintiff is an agriculturists or not he would have jurisdiction to decide the issue as required under section 85A. In the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: (1) The jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide and deal with any question which arises under the Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act and which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by any competent authority under the Bombay tenancy Act would alone be barred under section85. It is a debatable point whether the defendant is an agnate tenant or protected tenant, and that he must also hold that he is a trespasser in order to determine that he was not a tenant or a protected tenant and even while strictly construing the provisions, the legislature has left to the Mamlatdar to decide those issues only in some proceeding before him under some specific provision of the Land Act. [595 G] (2) The Court cannot lend support to the submission that past enancy being a subsidiary issue, as such was within the competence of the civil court. [596 E F] In the context of these facts, it is held that even though civil court had no jurisdiction to determine whether the acquisition would become invalid but there is nothing in section 78 or any other provision of tho Tenancy Act which excludes the Civil Courts ' jurisdiction to decree specific performance. If there was an issue which has to be decided, decided and dealt with in accordance with the decision recorded by the competent authority on the relevant issues, then notwithstanding the fact that it arises in an incidental manner in a civil suit cognizable by the Civil court, it would have been referred to the competent jurisdiction under the Land Reforms Act. The High Court was of the view that the jurisdiction of Civil Courts to settle the question would alone possess jurisdiction under section 70 (mb) and that the trial court had rightly dismissed the suit.

The assessee appellants carried on the business of heavy engineering, doing fabrication and for that purpose the assessee was purchasing the spare parts, forgings and castings from outside. Hence the Tribunal held that the new industrial undertakings were formed out of the existing 'business to come within the mischief of the exclusion clause in section 15C(2)(i). The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the asses see. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. A welfare legislation which seeks to promote a modern industry as one of its objects is necessary so as to facilitate development of new industrial industries by providing for provi sions to encourage setting up of new industries and for the establishment of new Industrial undertakings on account of which exemption of tax under section 15A may be claimed, will benefit in that perspective, namely, the setting up or reading of new business already in existence. This has not happened here in the case of two undertakings which are separate and distinct. It is clear that the principal business of the assessee is heavy engineering in the course of which it manufactures boilers, wagons, etc., If an industrial undertaking produce certain machines or parts which are, by themselves, identi fiable units being marketable commodities and the undertak ing can exist even after the cessation of the principal trade of the asses sees, it cannot be anything but a new and separate industrial undertaking to qualify for exemption under section . [764 H; 770A B] 1.2. The idea of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one Industrial unit sets up another industrial unit. This had not happened in the instant case In order that the old industrial undertakings are separate, and independent production units ' in the sense that the commodities produced or the results achieved are commercially tangible products and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business, they are not to be treated as being formed by reconstruction of the old registered concern. [767A C] 2.1 The primary object of section 15 C is to encourage set up of industrial undertakings by offering tax incentive within a period of 13 years from April 1, 1948. This section was inserted in the Indian Income Tax Act in 1949 by section 13 of the Taxation Laws (Extensions)Act, 1949 extending the benefit to the actual manufacture or production of arti cles commencing from a prior date, namely April 1. 1948. Under sub section (1) of section 25C the tax shall not be payable by an assessee on profits not exceeding six per cent per annum on the capital employed in the new Industrial Undertaking from the profits which alone exemption is claimed. [774A B; 773E] Commissioner of Income Tax West Bengal vs Textile Machinery Corporation, ; , referred to.

The inams were originally granted to the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. The inam Commission confirmed the grants of the inams in favour of the hereditary officeholders then rendering the services. Where there was an alienation of the inam either before or after 1934, and even apart from section 44 B which provided that in 1863 the inam might be resumed on any of the three grounds mentioned therein, no inam whatever its nature could be resumed for failure to perform the conditions of the grant, ranting the inam lands to any subordinate interest in the inams was illegal and a nullity. Held, that the inam was resumable under section 44B(2)(a) (i). Even apart from s. 44 B where there has been an alienation at any time the first ground ,exists and the inam may be resumed under s.44 B. The words 'has failed ' in sub section (2)(A)(ii) and the words 'have ceased" and 'has become 'in section 2(a)(iii). The circumstances, therefore, showed that the land was being enjoyed by the inamdars and were granted as inams. The fact that the original grant was made to the deity before 1886, did not alter the position of the lands in respect of which no appeal had been filed by the appellants in the plaint. The land was really granted to them for the service of Sree Padam Thangi which was then then rendered, and was enjoyed by them as remuneration for the services to be rendered by them. It was not properly called retrospective 'because a part of the requisites for its action is drawn from a time antecedent to its passing" [543 E; 540 C D] Case law reviewed.

Section 76(1) provides that such repeal shall not affect the validity or invalidity of anything already done under any of the enactments. The respondents as trustees of a charitable trust were the owners of certain houses situate in Indore City. Prior to January 26, 1954 the Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore city Municipal Act 4 of 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by that Act the municipality used to levy and collect house tax at the rate of 7% of their gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs, or on any account whatsoever. On January 26 ' 1954 the appellant Municipality was regulated by the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1958 which came into force on January 26. 1954. By a notification issued under section 6(a) of the Act, the Municipality had imposed the tax on buildings at the rates of 7 % of their total gross annual net letting value. The respondent as trustees filed a suit for recovery of the excess amount and contended that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual rental rent less 10 per cent statutory allowance. The Trial Court decreed the suit and the appeals filed by the Corporation in the District Court and the High Court were dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Under section 2(c) where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year the provisions of sections 75 and 76 shall be applicable as if a new assessment list has been completed at the commencement of that particular official year. But sub sec. 2 of section 79 provides expressly that when such a previous list is adopted for a particular officialyear it can be done subject to the procedure laid down in SS 75 and 78. [131C] The expression, "if" appearing in sub sec.(2) of s.79 is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if". because the word "if," standing by itself makes no sense at all, it has to be construed to mean that though a Municipality need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year and need prepare such a list once in every 4 years and can adopt an earlier assessment list such adopted list becomes the assessment list for that particular year as if it was a new list and "to which sections 75 & 76 apply.
